\chapter{Simulation Stack Development}
\label{ch:sim-stack}

% Guideline recommends 10-20 pages per methodology chapter.
% TODO: add figures - a URDF joint-tree diagram, a screenshot of the
% Gazebo model, and an odometry-drift plot from Sec. 3.6 would all
% strengthen this chapter with minimal extra writing.

This chapter documents the development of the simulation-side
navigation stack that Chapters~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge}
through~\ref{ch:nav-integration} later migrate onto physical
hardware. The stack went through two full drive-architecture
migrations before reaching the form used for hardware bridging
(Sections~\ref{sec:baseline-manual}--\ref{sec:second-migration}), and
along the way surfaced a middleware-level parser defect
(Section~\ref{sec:colon-bug}) and a four-part vehicle-dynamics bug
pattern that recurred, largely unchanged, across two sibling packages
(Section~\ref{sec:not-moving-bug}). The chapter closes with a
behaviour-tree fix specific to Ackermann-steered vehicles
(Section~\ref{sec:bt-fix}).

\section{Baseline: Manual Bicycle-Model Inversion}
\label{sec:baseline-manual}

The navigation stack's earliest drive architecture used two
independent \texttt{ros2\_control} \texttt{JointGroup} controllers
(\texttt{drive\_controller} for wheel velocity,
\texttt{steering\_controller} for hub position) driven by a
hand-written node, \texttt{cmd\_vel\_to\_drive.py}, that manually
inverted the bicycle-model relationship of
Equations~\ref{eq:bicycle-x}--\ref{eq:bicycle-theta} to compute a
per-wheel velocity and steering-hub angle from an incoming
\texttt{geometry\_msgs/Twist} on \texttt{/cmd\_vel}. This
architecture worked, but duplicated the Ackermann inverse-kinematics
logic that a purpose-built controller would otherwise provide, and --
more importantly for a navigation stack meant to reach physical
hardware -- could not support Nav2's recovery behaviours that require
reversing, since the manual node had no reverse-driving logic of its
own.

\section{First Migration: \texttt{ros2\_control}'s \texttt{AckermannSteeringController}}
\label{sec:first-migration}

The first architectural migration replaced both custom
\texttt{JointGroup} controllers and \texttt{cmd\_vel\_to\_drive.py}
with \texttt{ros2\_control}'s own
\texttt{ackermann\_steering\_controller} / \texttt{AckermannSteeringController}
plugin, configured via \texttt{config/qcar\_controllers.yaml}. This
controller performs the same Ackermann inverse kinematics internally,
and additionally publishes its own wheel-based odometry -- which
this project deliberately adopted as the vehicle's \texttt{/odom}
source in place of Gazebo's \texttt{gazebo\_ros\_p3d} ground-truth
plugin (the latter was kept running, but remapped to
\texttt{/ground\_truth/odom} for debugging comparison only). This was
a considered choice, not a default: ground-truth odometry is
trivially available in simulation but has no equivalent on the
physical robot, whose odometry can only ever be a real,
drift-prone dead-reckoning estimate (Section~\ref{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}).
Developing and tuning the navigation stack against the same
\emph{kind} of odometry it would have to work with on hardware, from
the start, avoided deferring that discrepancy to the eventual
hardware migration.

Because Nav2, AMCL, and \texttt{bt\_navigator} all hard-code an
expectation that odometry arrives on \texttt{/odom} and driving
commands are consumed from \texttt{/cmd\_vel}, and the new controller
instead exposes these under its own namespaced topics
(\texttt{\textasciitilde/odometry}, \texttt{\textasciitilde/reference\_unstamped}),
two \texttt{topic\_tools relay} nodes were added to the launch files
to bridge the naming mismatch without modifying Nav2 itself.

\subsection{A Wheel-Axis Bug Exposed by the Migration}
\label{sec:wheel-axis-bug}

The migration exposed a latent URDF defect that had been silently
compensated for by the old manual node and had therefore never
produced a visible symptom before. The rear-left drive wheel joint
(\texttt{base\_wheelrl\_joint}) had its \texttt{<origin>} yawed by
\ang{180} for correct mesh mirroring, but retained the \emph{same}
\texttt{<axis>} direction as the corresponding right-side joint --
which, combined with the yaw flip, silently inverted that wheel's
effective rotation sense relative to a positive commanded velocity.
The old \texttt{cmd\_vel\_to\_drive.py} had manually compensated for
this by commanding \texttt{[-speed, +speed]} to the left/right wheel
velocities respectively; the new controller had no such
compensation, and computed wheel odometry that did not match the
vehicle's real motion direction. The fix -- correcting the
\texttt{<axis>} declaration on the affected joint directly, rather
than perpetuating a sign-flip workaround downstream in every
consumer of that joint -- illustrates a pattern worth stating
explicitly: a URDF geometry defect that is silently absorbed by one
consumer's ad hoc compensation will resurface, often with a confusing
symptom, the moment that consumer is replaced.

\subsection{A URDF Parser Defect in \texttt{gazebo\_ros2\_control}}
\label{sec:colon-bug}

While adding explanatory comments to the URDF for the wheel-axis fix
above, \texttt{controller\_manager} began failing to start
altogether -- with all downstream symptoms that implies
(\texttt{joint\_state\_broadcaster} and the new controller never
spawning, \texttt{/odom} never appearing, and no \texttt{map} TF
being published either, since nothing in the chain that would
produce it ever started). The failure was silent: no controller
spawner logged an error explaining \emph{why} it timed out waiting
for \texttt{controller\_manager}.

Isolating the cause required a delta-debugging-style bisection of the
URDF file against the actual parsing code path, since multi-line
comments, apostrophes, and file length were all plausible-looking red
herrings that turned out not to matter. The root cause was found in
how \texttt{gazebo\_ros2\_control} starts its internally-managed
\texttt{controller\_manager} node: the plugin passes the entire
processed URDF as a single \texttt{--param
robot\_description:=<xml>} command-line-style argument, which
\texttt{rcl}'s parameter-override grammar parses looking for a
\texttt{node\_name:param\_name} pattern. That grammar treats
\emph{any} colon immediately followed by a space --
\texttt{": "} -- anywhere in the argument string as a potential
separator, including inside an XML comment that a human reader would
never consider part of the "real" content. A direct reproduction
using \texttt{rclpy}'s own argument parser confirmed the mechanism
precisely: \texttt{"hello: world"} fails to parse while
\texttt{"hello:world"} (no space) succeeds, and \texttt{package://}
URIs or \texttt{foo:=bar} remappings are unaffected since neither
places a bare space directly after a colon.

This is not specific to this project's URDF; it is a property of any
\texttt{gazebo\_ros2\_control}-based setup, and is recorded here as a
general finding: \textbf{a URDF or xacro file must never contain the
literal sequence colon-followed-by-space, including inside comments},
or \texttt{controller\_manager} fails to start with no diagnostic
pointing at the actual cause.

\section{Porting the Navigation Stack to ROS~2 Humble / Gazebo Classic}
\label{sec:humble-conversion}

A sibling package in this project's workspace had been authored
against ROS~2 Jazzy and the newer Gazebo Sim (Harmonic) simulator --
the \texttt{gz sim} binary family, \texttt{ros\_gz\_sim} /
\texttt{ros\_gz\_bridge} integration, and \texttt{gz-sim-*-system}
world plugins -- none of which are available on this project's
ROS~2 Humble / Ubuntu 22.04 / Gazebo Classic~11 host. Rather than
install a second, newer simulator stack alongside the one already
validated and working for the rest of this thesis's packages
(Section~\ref{sec:first-migration}), the package was converted to
Gazebo Classic, matching every other package in this project.
Table~\ref{tab:gz-sim-conversion} summarises the conversion, which
generalises directly to any future package encountered that was
authored against Gazebo Sim / Jazzy-era tutorials.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Gazebo Sim (Jazzy) to Gazebo Classic (Humble) translation table.}
  \label{tab:gz-sim-conversion}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}p{4.2cm}p{4.2cm}p{5.5cm}@{}}
    \toprule
    Gazebo Sim (source) & Gazebo Classic (target) & Notes \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{ros\_gz\_sim} / \texttt{ros\_gz\_bridge} (package.xml) & \texttt{gazebo\_ros} / \texttt{gazebo\_plugins} & \\
    \texttt{gpu\_lidar} sensor + gz-sim system plugin & \texttt{type="ray"} + \texttt{libgazebo\_ros\_ray\_sensor.so} & \\
    gz-sim \texttt{imu} sensor & classic \texttt{imu} + \texttt{libgazebo\_ros\_imu\_sensor.so} & \\
    \texttt{gz-sim-joint-state-publisher-system} & removed entirely & Not needed; the drive plugin's own \texttt{publish\_wheel\_tf} broadcasts wheel/steering TF directly \\
    \texttt{gz-sim-ackermann-steering-system} & \texttt{libgazebo\_ros\_ackermann\_drive.so} & Classic plugin auto-computes wheelbase/track/radius from URDF geometry; the gz-sim system required stating them explicitly \\
    5$\times$ \texttt{<plugin filename="gz-sim-*-system">} (world SDF) & deleted entirely & Classic's \texttt{gzserver} has physics, scene broadcast, and sensors built into its core, not opt-in systems \\
    \texttt{gz sim} + \texttt{ros\_gz\_sim create} spawn + \texttt{ros\_gz\_bridge} node & \texttt{gazebo}/\texttt{gzserver} + \texttt{gazebo\_ros spawn\_entity.py} & No bridge node needed; classic plugins publish onto ROS~2 topics directly \\
    \texttt{GZ\_SIM\_RESOURCE\_PATH} env-var for mesh resolution & not needed & \texttt{gazebo\_ros} registers its own \texttt{package://} resolver \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

One element of the original file required \emph{no} change: the
\texttt{<gazebo reference="link"><material>Gazebo/X</material></gazebo>}
material-script blocks are classic-Gazebo-native syntax that happened
to already be present and compatible, a reminder that a systematic
conversion still benefits from checking each element rather than
assuming every gz-sim-authored construct needs translating.

\section{Second Migration: The Direct Drive Plugin}
\label{sec:second-migration}

The navigation stack's final drive architecture -- the one this
thesis's hardware bridge (Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge}) targets
-- drops \texttt{ros2\_control} entirely in favour of driving the
robot through \texttt{libgazebo\_ros\_ackermann\_drive.so} directly,
declared in a \texttt{<gazebo>} block in the URDF rather than through
a separate controller-manager configuration file, matching the
approach already adopted for the sibling package during the Humble
conversion above. This plugin subscribes to \texttt{/cmd\_vel} and
publishes \texttt{/odom} and the \texttt{odom} $\rightarrow$
\texttt{base} TF transform directly, again auto-computing wheelbase,
track width, and wheel radius from URDF joint and collision geometry
at spawn time -- removing an entire category of configuration
drift risk where a controller's stated geometry parameters could
silently fall out of sync with the URDF's actual geometry, which had
been possible (if not observed) under the first migration's
\texttt{ros2\_control} YAML-based configuration. This is the
architecture described in Section~\ref{sec:gazebo}'s account of the
drive plugin, and the one whose real-world calibration
Chapter~\ref{ch:calibration} presents.

\section{The ``Robot Not Moving Forward'' Bug Pattern}
\label{sec:not-moving-bug}

Both the sibling package's Humble conversion (Section~\ref{sec:humble-conversion})
and this project's own second migration (Section~\ref{sec:second-migration})
independently produced the same surface symptom immediately
afterward: the simulated vehicle did not drive forward under a
sustained \texttt{/cmd\_vel} command. In both cases, this single
symptom turned out to be caused by a stack of independent bugs, each
one masking the next until the previous was fixed -- a pattern
significant enough, and confirmed to recur closely enough between
the two packages, to warrant treating as a general defect signature
for this plugin/vehicle combination rather than two unrelated
incidents. Table~\ref{tab:not-moving-bugs} summarises all bugs found
across both occurrences.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{The recurring ``not moving forward'' bug pattern, as found in both affected packages.}
  \label{tab:not-moving-bugs}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.6cm}p{5.3cm}p{7cm}@{}}
    \toprule
    \# & Bug & Symptom / mechanism \\
    \midrule
    1 & Wheel \texttt{<collision>} was the visual STL mesh, not a primitive shape & The plugin's radius auto-detection only supports cylinder/sphere collisions; a mesh collision silently returns radius 0, so \texttt{target\_linear / wheel\_radius} becomes infinite, poisoning the velocity PID regardless of gain. Fixed by keeping the STL for \texttt{<visual>} but using an explicit \texttt{<cylinder radius="0.036" length="0.0245"/>} for \texttt{<collision>}. \\
    2 & Zero Coulomb friction on the wheel links & Even with a correct wheel radius, the wheel spins at exactly the commanded angular velocity forever while the chassis never translates -- 100\% slip. Fixed with \texttt{<mu1>1.0</mu1><mu2>1.0</mu2>} on every wheel link. \\
    3 & Absurd ground-plane friction (\texttt{mu=100}, \texttt{mu2=50}) & Once wheel friction is fixed, this combination produces a real physics instability/NaN blow-up on contact. Fixed by lowering to a realistic \texttt{mu=1}, \texttt{mu2=1}. \\
    4 & Razor-thin wheel/ground clearance (only $\sim$0.38\,mm geometric overlap at the original 0.033\,m collision radius) & Enough overlap to rest on the ground without falling through, but not enough consistent contact-normal force to generate real traction even at correct friction -- chassis twist stayed near zero despite full wheel spin. Fixed by padding the collision cylinder radius to 0.036\,m (+3\,mm), which alone flipped the vehicle from ``spins in place'' to sustained forward motion. \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

The first occurrence of this pattern also included a preceding, more
basic defect specific to that package: its mesh URIs
(\texttt{package://.../models/qcar/QCarBody.stl}-style paths) pointed
at a directory layout copy-pasted from this project's own package
rather than the sibling's actual \texttt{meshes/} layout and file
names, so the robot had \emph{no} collision geometry at all and fell
through the simulated ground plane -- confirmed directly via
\texttt{/odom} tracking a $z$-position reaching approximately
$-38{,}000$\,m. This is worth recording as a separate, more
fundamental lesson: Gazebo Classic's URDF-to-SDF loader silently
rewrites \texttt{package://} mesh URIs to \texttt{model://}, which
only resolves via the \texttt{GAZEBO\_MODEL\_PATH} environment
variable -- and since neither package's \texttt{package.xml} exports
the \texttt{<gazebo\_ros gazebo\_model\_path=.../>} tag required for
that resolution, correcting the path string alone would not have
been sufficient. The fix instead used xacro's \texttt{\$(find)}
substitution to build \texttt{file://} URIs directly, which bypass
package-path resolution entirely.

The second occurrence additionally required a numerical-stability
fix not initially anticipated: wheel rotational inertia values that
were physically correct for a solid disk of the wheel's real mass and
radius, but small enough in absolute terms to interact badly with the
plugin's 100\,Hz PID control loop, producing an
\texttt{Ogre::AxisAlignedBox::setExtents} assertion crash a few
seconds into driving. Bumping wheel inertia roughly 20$\times$
(\texttt{ixx=izz=0.0012}, \texttt{iyy=0.0022}) together with lowering
the steering and linear-velocity PID gains resolved the crash; this
value combination, once found working in the first occurrence, was
reused directly in the second and confirmed stable there as well.

A further gain-tuning finding, specific to the second occurrence and
worth stating as a general caution for reusing PID values across
otherwise-identical vehicle configurations: a steering PID gain
verified stable and accurate on a \emph{frictionless} wheel
configuration produced a real turning radius roughly $6\times$ larger
than commanded once realistic wheel friction (bug~2 above) was added,
because the same low gain that was previously sufficient (with no
resistive torque to overcome) could no longer turn the front hubs
against a now-gripping, rolling tyre. The fix -- raising
\texttt{left/right\_steering\_pid\_gain} from \texttt{0.02} to
\texttt{3.0} -- was verified directly via TF lookups on the
steering-hub joints during a commanded 1.0\,m-radius turn, confirming
hub angles converging to the correct $\sim$\ang{15}--\ang{18}
Ackermann inner/outer split, and via a circle fit to the resulting
odometry trace, which recovered a turning radius of 0.87\,m against
the 1.0\,m commanded -- a reasonable margin given the real-vs-ideal
gap between the single-track model of
Section~\ref{sec:ackermann-kinematics} and the vehicle's true
four-wheel geometry.

\subsection{Diagnostic Method}
\label{sec:diagnostic-method}

A methodological point generalises from both occurrences of this bug
pattern: none of these four bugs are visible from \texttt{ros2 topic
list} or a static inspection of the URDF alone. A simulated robot
that appears correctly configured can simultaneously be in freefall,
frozen inside a crashed-but-still-running \texttt{gzserver} process,
or driving its wheels at 100\% slip with zero real chassis motion --
and none of these states are distinguishable without directly
comparing \texttt{/odom} position over several seconds of sustained
commanded motion, cross-checked against the Gazebo server log for
silent \texttt{[Err]}/assertion lines. This became this project's
standard verification method for any subsequent URDF or physics
change to the simulation stack.

\section{A Behaviour-Tree Fix for Ackermann Recovery}
\label{sec:bt-fix}

A separate, functional (rather than purely physics-level) issue
appeared once the vehicle was reliably driving: Nav2's default
recovery behaviour tree round-robins through
\texttt{[ClearCostmaps, Spin(1.57\,rad), Wait(5\,s), BackUp(0.3\,m)]}
whenever the active controller reports it cannot make further
progress. The \texttt{Spin} recovery commands a pure in-place
rotation -- physically impossible for an Ackermann-steered vehicle,
whose steering angle has no effect while linear velocity is zero, so
the vehicle simply cannot rotate without also translating. Roughly
one in three recovery attempts was therefore a guaranteed no-op that
burned its full timeout without attempting any corrective motion.

The fix was to remove \texttt{<Spin>} from the recovery action list
in local copies of Nav2's stock behaviour-tree XML files
(\texttt{navigate\_to\_pose\_w\_replanning\_and\_recovery.xml} and
its through-poses equivalent), wired into the launch configuration
via a \texttt{RewrittenYaml} substitution. This required one
non-obvious step: \texttt{RewrittenYaml} only overwrites
\emph{existing} leaf keys in a YAML file, it does not add new ones,
so the parameter keys pointing at these custom BT file paths
(\texttt{default\_nav\_to\_pose\_bt\_xml} /
\texttt{default\_nav\_through\_poses\_bt\_xml}) had to already exist
as placeholder entries in \texttt{nav2\_params.yaml} before the
launch-time substitution could take effect.

\section{Summary of the Simulation-Stack Architecture}
\label{sec:sim-stack-summary}

By the end of this chapter's work, the simulation-side navigation
stack consists of: a URDF-described vehicle driven directly by
\texttt{libgazebo\_ros\_ackermann\_drive.so} (Section~\ref{sec:second-migration}),
publishing its own dead-reckoning \texttt{/odom} rather than Gazebo
ground truth (Section~\ref{sec:first-migration}), with corrected
wheel collision geometry, friction, and inertia
(Section~\ref{sec:not-moving-bug}), tuned PID gains for both drive
and steering, and a custom Ackermann-aware recovery behaviour tree
(Section~\ref{sec:bt-fix}). This is the configuration
Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge} treats as the reference to be
matched -- as closely as the physical robot's own constraints allow
-- when bridging to hardware.

1	\chapter{Real-Hardware Bridge Architecture}
2	\label{ch:hardware-bridge}
3	
4	% TODO: add a sequence diagram (goal -> Nav2 -> /cmd_vel -> relay ->
5	% TCP -> bridge -> HAL -> motor) - this chapter describes the exact
6	% data flow in prose/tables, but a single figure would help the reader
7	% a lot given how many hops are involved.
8	
9	This chapter presents the architecture built to connect the
10	simulation-validated navigation stack of Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}
11	to the physical QCar~2. Section~\ref{sec:rmw-incompatibility}
12	establishes why native ROS~2 communication with the robot's onboard
13	compute is not available, which motivates the TCP/JSON bridge
14	architecture of Section~\ref{sec:bridge-architecture}. The remaining
15	sections document the sensor and actuator correctness issues found
16	while bringing that bridge up to the same fidelity as the simulation
17	stack: LiDAR angle convention (Section~\ref{sec:lidar-angle}),
18	odometry (Section~\ref{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}), steering trim
19	(Section~\ref{sec:steering-trim}), and inter-machine clock
20	synchronisation (Section~\ref{sec:clock-offset}).
21	
22	\section{The ROS~2 Dashing / Humble Incompatibility}
23	\label{sec:rmw-incompatibility}
24	
25	As described in Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}, the QCar~2's onboard
26	Jetson TX2 ships with ROS~2 Dashing (released 2019) pre-installed,
27	while this project's navigation stack targets ROS~2 Humble (released
28	2022). Section~\ref{sec:ros2-model} established that ROS~2 nodes
29	communicate via DDS participants that must share a compatible
30	discovery and wire protocol to find each other at all; the working
31	hypothesis at the start of this thesis's hardware phase was that this
32	would be a soft compatibility problem -- degraded performance,
33	perhaps, but not a hard failure.
34	
35	This was tested directly, not assumed. A minimal ROS~2 publisher
36	(\texttt{demo\_nodes\_cpp talker}) on the QCar and a minimal
37	subscriber (\texttt{demo\_nodes\_py listener}) on the development PC,
38	both configured with the same \texttt{ROS\_DOMAIN\_ID}, never
39	established communication across three repeated attempts, with the
40	talker independently confirmed to be actively publishing each time.
41	The network layer itself was systematically ruled out before
42	concluding this was a middleware-level problem: raw UDP unicast
43	passed cleanly in both directions, including on the exact Fast~DDS
44	discovery port for the domain in use; no firewall was active on
45	either host; and an explicit unicast-peers Fast~DDS XML profile,
46	which bypasses multicast-based discovery entirely, still failed to
47	achieve discovery. This isolates the failure to the DDS protocol
48	implementation itself -- a genuine Fast~DDS protocol-version
49	incompatibility between the versions bundled with ROS~2 Dashing and
50	ROS~2 Humble respectively \cite{eprosima_fastdds}, not a network,
51	firewall, or configuration problem that could be worked around within
52	ROS~2 itself.
53	
54	This result rules out every architecture that assumes native ROS~2
55	interoperability between the two machines, including running a
56	Humble-compatible container on the QCar: a Humble Docker container
57	was considered early on, but does not address a protocol-version
58	incompatibility at the DDS transport layer, since the Dashing side of
59	the link is fixed by what physically runs on the vehicle's ROS~2
60	partition and cannot itself be upgraded without departing from the
61	vendor-supported software image.
62	
63	\section{Bridge Architecture Overview}
64	\label{sec:bridge-architecture}
65	
66	The architecture built in response uses no ROS~2 at all on the
67	QCar's own compute. Two plain Python processes run directly on the
68	Jetson TX2 (no \texttt{colcon} build, invoked as
69	\texttt{python3 <script>.py}):
70	
71	\begin{itemize}
72	  \item \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} -- a TCP server (port 5555) wrapping
73	    the Quanser HAL/PAL \texttt{QCar} object (Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}):
74	    receives newline-delimited JSON drive/steering commands and
75	    responds with odometry JSON over the same full-duplex connection.
76	  \item \texttt{qcar\_lidar\_node.py} -- a second TCP server (port
77	    5556) wrapping the LiDAR driver, streaming scan data as
78	    newline-delimited JSON.
79	\end{itemize}
80	
81	On the development PC, a single node, \texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py},
82	is the sole point of contact between ROS~2 and this TCP/JSON
83	protocol: it subscribes to \texttt{/cmd\_vel} and forwards commands
84	into the motor socket, and publishes \texttt{sensor\_msgs/LaserScan}
85	on \texttt{/scan} and \texttt{nav\_msgs/Odometry} plus the
86	\texttt{odom} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{base} TF on \texttt{/odom} from
87	data received back over both sockets. Every other node in the
88	navigation stack -- Nav2, AMCL, Cartographer, RViz -- interacts with
89	this relay node exactly as it would with the simulation's own drive
90	plugin, requiring no awareness that the underlying vehicle is real
91	hardware reached over a bespoke protocol rather than a co-located
92	Gazebo simulation.
93	% TODO: insert a figure here illustrating the full path from a
94	% Nav2-issued velocity command to the physical motor (Nav2 ->
95	% /cmd_vel -> qcar_relay_node.py -> TCP -> qcar_bridge.py -> HAL ->
96	% motor). Give it \label{fig:bridge-architecture} and reference it
97	% with Figure~\ref{fig:bridge-architecture} in the sentence above once
98	% added.
99	
100	Both onboard TCP servers were built to handle \texttt{SIGTERM}
101	identically to \texttt{SIGINT} -- a deliberate correctness fix, not a
102	default: Python does not automatically translate a plain
103	\texttt{pkill}'s default \texttt{SIGTERM} into a caught, clean-exit
104	signal the way it does for \texttt{SIGINT} (Ctrl-C), and an earlier
105	plain \texttt{pkill} against the LiDAR process left the physical
106	LiDAR unit spinning after the owning process had already exited,
107	which is both a battery drain and a safety concern for anyone near
108	the vehicle. Section~\ref{sec:safe-shutdown} presents the resulting
109	documented shutdown procedure in full.
110	
111	\section{LiDAR Angle-Convention Correction}
112	\label{sec:lidar-angle}
113	
114	The first sensor-correctness issue found while bringing up
115	visualisation of the bridged data (\texttt{robot\_state\_publisher} +
116	\texttt{joint\_state\_publisher} + RViz, no Gazebo) was a LiDAR
117	angle-binning defect in \texttt{qcar\_lidar\_node.py}: obstacles
118	rendered in RViz did not appear at their true bearing relative to the
119	rendered robot model. This required \emph{two} stacked, independent
120	corrections, not one -- a clockwise-to-counter-clockwise direction
121	flip \emph{and} a $+\ang{90}$ rotational offset between the LiDAR's
122	zero-reference bearing and the vehicle's own forward direction. The
123	first attempted fix (direction only) produced a result that was
124	itself the tell that a second error remained: it exactly mirrored the
125	original error about the vehicle's forward axis rather than
126	correcting it, which is the expected signature of fixing only a sign
127	error while a separate rotational offset error is still present. The
128	final, verified-correct transform is
129	
130	\begin{equation}
131	  \theta_{\text{target}} = \operatorname{wrap}_{(-\pi,\,\pi]}\!\left(-\theta_{\text{lidar}} + \frac{\pi}{2}\right), \label{eq:lidar-angle-fix}
132	\end{equation}
133	
134	verified against a real obstacle at a known bearing (the vehicle's
135	physical right side), cross-checked against the rendered robot
136	model's own orientation in RViz rather than the screen's raw
137	left/right, which depends on the RViz camera's own facing direction
138	and is therefore not a reliable reference on its own.
139	
140	\section{Wheel Odometry over the Bridge}
141	\label{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}
142	
143	Mapping (Cartographer, Section~\ref{sec:cartographer}) was
144	successfully brought up on real hardware using scan-matching alone,
145	with \texttt{use\_odometry: false} / \texttt{provide\_odom\_frame:
146	true} in the Cartographer configuration -- meaning the initial bridge
147	implementation required no odometry extension at all for mapping to
148	work end-to-end. Localisation (AMCL) does not share this property:
149	unlike Cartographer's self-contained scan matching, AMCL looks up a
150	live \texttt{odom} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{base} TF at every scan
151	callback as its motion-model input, so the wheel-odometry extension
152	originally scoped only for the mapping phase became a hard
153	requirement once navigation (Nav2/AMCL) was brought up.
154	
155	\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} was extended with an \texttt{Odometry} class
156	implementing the same bicycle-model dead-reckoning integration as
157	Equations~\ref{eq:bicycle-x}--\ref{eq:bicycle-theta}, sent back to
158	the relay over the same already-full-duplex TCP connection the drive
159	commands arrive on (the reverse direction of this connection had
160	previously been opened but its data discarded).
161	\texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py} parses this stream and publishes both
162	\texttt{/odom} and the corresponding TF. Tested in isolation before
163	layering Nav2 on top, the resulting odometry published at
164	approximately 45\,Hz, and a 3-second commanded straight-line drive at
165	\SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} produced $x \approx \SI{1.25}{\meter}$,
166	$v \approx \SI{0.37}{\meter\per\second}$, $y \approx 0$ -- consistent
167	with straight-line motion at close to the commanded speed, and
168	confirmed working before the full navigation stack was brought up on
169	top of it.
170	
171	\section{Steering-Trim Calibration}
172	\label{sec:steering-trim}
173	
174	A small but consistent steering bias -- the physical vehicle drifting
175	laterally under a nominally straight (zero-steering) command -- was
176	present on this specific chassis, and the physical steering linkage
177	could not be adjusted to correct it mechanically. The fix was
178	implemented in software instead, as a constant offset
179	(\texttt{STEERING\_TRIM}, ultimately \SI{-0.08}{\radian}) applied
180	only at the point the steering command is written to the servo.
181	Calibration proceeded in two stages: an initial static test (motor
182	off, holding candidate angles and judging visually against a
183	reference, preserved as \texttt{calibrate\_steering.py} for future
184	re-calibration) narrowed the value to roughly the right range, and a
185	series of real straight-line driving tests (drive a known distance,
186	measure the resulting lateral offset, compute
187	$\delta_{\text{trim}} = \arctan(\text{offset}/\text{distance})$)
188	refined it further. This data carried real measurement noise --
189	lateral offset depends on the vehicle's initial aim at the start of
190	each test run, not purely on trim -- so the calibration deliberately
191	did not over-fit a precise value from only two data points; a
192	consistent directional nudge toward zero observed drift converged
193	faster in practice than attempting a precise interpolation. The final
194	value was accepted once a \SI{4.4}{\meter} test drive showed no
195	reported drift; this is described as ``almost accurate,'' a
196	deliberate acceptance of a small residual rather than a claim of
197	exact zero.
198	
199	\subsection{A Trim-Placement Bug and the ``Apply at the Actuator Boundary'' Principle}
200	\label{sec:trim-boundary-principle}
201	
202	The first implementation of this trim contained a real bug worth
203	recording as a general principle for any per-unit hardware
204	calibration constant, not only this one. It folded the trim into the
205	\emph{same} steering value used both for the real servo command
206	\emph{and} for the odometry dead-reckoning calculation in
207	Section~\ref{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}. Since the entire purpose of
208	the trim is to make the real wheels read approximately zero deflection
209	despite a nonzero servo command, feeding that same trimmed value into
210	odometry made the dead-reckoning model believe the wheels were
211	deflected by the trim amount even while the vehicle was, in reality,
212	driving dead straight. A live test briefly exposed this directly: a
213	straight-line drive of approximately \SI{2.8}{\meter} produced a
214	fictitious $y \approx \SI{-1.72}{\meter}$ in the odometry output, a
215	spurious $\sim$\ang{30} curve that did not correspond to any real
216	vehicle motion.
217	
218	The fix separated \texttt{compute\_steering()} (returns the
219	untrimmed, kinematic steering angle, used for odometry) from a new
220	\texttt{apply\_trim()} (computes the real servo command, called only
221	immediately before the HAL write). Re-verified with the same drive
222	command, the odometry then correctly read $y \approx 0$. The general
223	principle this illustrates -- and which is stated here explicitly
224	because it is expected to generalise to any future per-unit hardware
225	calibration constant on this or a similar platform -- is that a
226	calibration constant compensating for a specific actuator's physical
227	imperfection should be applied \emph{as late as possible, immediately
228	at the actuator boundary}, and never upstream of any computation
229	(such as odometry) that treats its input as an accurate, ground-truth
230	kinematic quantity.
231	
232	\section{Clock Synchronisation and the Receipt-vs-Capture Timestamp Bug}
233	\label{sec:clock-offset}
234	
235	The first real navigation-goal test run independently by this
236	project's author, after mapping, localisation, and the fixes above
237	were all in place, surfaced a new symptom: sudden AMCL localisation
238	jumps and visible path deviation on both straight and curved
239	segments. The description of what was actually observed --
240	LiDAR scan shape stays internally coherent, but the entire scan
241	rigidly shifts and appears to track the robot's motion, ``like the
242	skeleton of the map is moving'' -- together with an explicit
243	instinct that this might be a transform-related issue rather than a
244	tuning problem, pointed toward a \emph{timing} rather than a spatial
245	or gain-tuning cause, and this proved correct.
246	
247	\texttt{/scan} (port 5556) and \texttt{/odom} (port 5555) are two
248	independent TCP streams, each subject to its own, uncorrelated
249	network jitter -- this link had already been measured showing
250	\SIrange{87}{300}{\milli\second} of variable latency.
251	\texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py} had been stamping both incoming
252	streams with \texttt{self.get\_clock().now()} at the moment of TCP
253	\emph{receipt} on the development PC, rather than at the moment of
254	sensor \emph{capture} on the QCar. Because the two streams' receipt
255	times are decorrelated, a late-arriving scan could be paired --
256	purely by receipt-time coincidence -- against an odometry sample
257	that, in real physical time, was already stale by a different,
258	independent amount. This produces exactly the observed symptom: a
259	LiDAR scan that is internally self-consistent but rigidly offset
260	relative to the map, tracking the robot's own recent motion.
261	
262	The fix required both machines' clocks to be related, not merely
263	each stream's own internal timing corrected. A round-trip-corrected
264	NTP-style offset measurement (five clustered trials of
265	$\text{offset} = t_{\text{remote}} - (t_1+t_2)/2$ around an SSH
266	\texttt{date} call) found a genuine $\sim$\SI{0.50}{\second} clock
267	offset between the two machines -- a naive sequential comparison
268	without the round-trip correction would have overstated this by also
269	counting SSH connection-setup time as clock skew. This offset was
270	deliberately \emph{not} corrected via a system-level NTP/chrony
271	configuration, since the QCar is shared laboratory hardware, and a
272	persistent system configuration pointing it at one researcher's
273	personal development machine as a time reference is not appropriate
274	to leave on shared infrastructure. Instead, \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}
275	and \texttt{qcar\_lidar\_node.py} were changed to stamp every message
276	with their own local \texttt{time.time()} at the moment of capture (a
277	\texttt{'t'} field in the JSON payload), and
278	\texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py} gained a \texttt{qcar\_clock\_offset}
279	parameter and a \texttt{qcar\_time\_to\_stamp()} helper that converts
280	a QCar-local capture timestamp into its development-PC-clock
281	equivalent, applied consistently to both the \texttt{/odom}+TF and
282	\texttt{/scan} publication paths.
283	
284	\begin{table}[htbp]
285	  \centering
286	  \caption{Diagnostic measurements underlying the clock-offset fix.}
287	  \label{tab:clock-offset}
288	  \begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
289	    \toprule
290	    Quantity & Value \\
291	    \midrule
292	    Network latency (TCP link, both ports) & \SIrange{87}{300}{\milli\second} (variable) \\
293	    Measured clock offset (round-trip corrected) & $\approx \SI{0.50}{\second}$ \\
294	    \texttt{qcar\_clock\_offset} launch parameter (verified session) & \texttt{0.50} \\
295	    \bottomrule
296	  \end{tabular}
297	\end{table}
298	
299	\section{Safe Shutdown Procedure}
300	\label{sec:safe-shutdown}
301	
302	Because two of the four processes in this bridge run directly on
303	physical hardware with no supervising ROS~2 lifecycle to fall back
304	on, this project established and documented a fixed shutdown
305	sequence, using \texttt{SIGINT} exclusively rather than a plain
306	\texttt{pkill} (per the signal-handling fix in
307	Section~\ref{sec:bridge-architecture}):
308	(1)~stop \texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py} on the development PC;
309	(2)~stop the visualisation launch process group (RViz may itself

\chapter{Real-Hardware Bridge Architecture}
\label{ch:hardware-bridge}

% TODO: add a sequence diagram (goal -> Nav2 -> /cmd_vel -> relay ->
% TCP -> bridge -> HAL -> motor) - this chapter describes the exact
% data flow in prose/tables, but a single figure would help the reader
% a lot given how many hops are involved.

This chapter presents the architecture built to connect the
simulation-validated navigation stack of Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}
to the physical QCar~2. Section~\ref{sec:rmw-incompatibility}
establishes why native ROS~2 communication with the robot's onboard
compute is not available, which motivates the TCP/JSON bridge
architecture of Section~\ref{sec:bridge-architecture}. The remaining
sections document the sensor and actuator correctness issues found
while bringing that bridge up to the same fidelity as the simulation
stack: LiDAR angle convention (Section~\ref{sec:lidar-angle}),
odometry (Section~\ref{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}), steering trim
(Section~\ref{sec:steering-trim}), and inter-machine clock
synchronisation (Section~\ref{sec:clock-offset}).

\section{The ROS~2 Dashing / Humble Incompatibility}
\label{sec:rmw-incompatibility}

As described in Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}, the QCar~2's onboard
Jetson TX2 ships with ROS~2 Dashing (released 2019) pre-installed,
while this project's navigation stack targets ROS~2 Humble (released
2022). Section~\ref{sec:ros2-model} established that ROS~2 nodes
communicate via DDS participants that must share a compatible
discovery and wire protocol to find each other at all; the working
hypothesis at the start of this thesis's hardware phase was that this
would be a soft compatibility problem -- degraded performance,
perhaps, but not a hard failure.

This was tested directly, not assumed. A minimal ROS~2 publisher
(\texttt{demo\_nodes\_cpp talker}) on the QCar and a minimal
subscriber (\texttt{demo\_nodes\_py listener}) on the development PC,
both configured with the same \texttt{ROS\_DOMAIN\_ID}, never
established communication across three repeated attempts, with the
talker independently confirmed to be actively publishing each time.
The network layer itself was systematically ruled out before
concluding this was a middleware-level problem: raw UDP unicast
passed cleanly in both directions, including on the exact Fast~DDS
discovery port for the domain in use; no firewall was active on
either host; and an explicit unicast-peers Fast~DDS XML profile,
which bypasses multicast-based discovery entirely, still failed to
achieve discovery. This isolates the failure to the DDS protocol
implementation itself -- a genuine Fast~DDS protocol-version
incompatibility between the versions bundled with ROS~2 Dashing and
ROS~2 Humble respectively \cite{eprosima_fastdds}, not a network,
firewall, or configuration problem that could be worked around within
ROS~2 itself.

This result rules out every architecture that assumes native ROS~2
interoperability between the two machines, including running a
Humble-compatible container on the QCar: a Humble Docker container
was considered early on, but does not address a protocol-version
incompatibility at the DDS transport layer, since the Dashing side of
the link is fixed by what physically runs on the vehicle's ROS~2
partition and cannot itself be upgraded without departing from the
vendor-supported software image.

\section{Bridge Architecture Overview}
\label{sec:bridge-architecture}

The architecture built in response uses no ROS~2 at all on the
QCar's own compute. Two plain Python processes run directly on the
Jetson TX2 (no \texttt{colcon} build, invoked as
\texttt{python3 <script>.py}):

\begin{itemize}
  \item \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} -- a TCP server (port 5555) wrapping
    the Quanser HAL/PAL \texttt{QCar} object (Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}):
    receives newline-delimited JSON drive/steering commands and
    responds with odometry JSON over the same full-duplex connection.
  \item \texttt{qcar\_lidar\_node.py} -- a second TCP server (port
    5556) wrapping the LiDAR driver, streaming scan data as
    newline-delimited JSON.
\end{itemize}

On the development PC, a single node, \texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py},
is the sole point of contact between ROS~2 and this TCP/JSON
protocol: it subscribes to \texttt{/cmd\_vel} and forwards commands
into the motor socket, and publishes \texttt{sensor\_msgs/LaserScan}
on \texttt{/scan} and \texttt{nav\_msgs/Odometry} plus the
\texttt{odom} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{base} TF on \texttt{/odom} from
data received back over both sockets. Every other node in the
navigation stack -- Nav2, AMCL, Cartographer, RViz -- interacts with
this relay node exactly as it would with the simulation's own drive
plugin, requiring no awareness that the underlying vehicle is real
hardware reached over a bespoke protocol rather than a co-located
Gazebo simulation.
% TODO: insert a figure here illustrating the full path from a
% Nav2-issued velocity command to the physical motor (Nav2 ->
% /cmd_vel -> qcar_relay_node.py -> TCP -> qcar_bridge.py -> HAL ->
% motor). Give it \label{fig:bridge-architecture} and reference it
% with Figure~\ref{fig:bridge-architecture} in the sentence above once
% added.

Both onboard TCP servers were built to handle \texttt{SIGTERM}
identically to \texttt{SIGINT} -- a deliberate correctness fix, not a
default: Python does not automatically translate a plain
\texttt{pkill}'s default \texttt{SIGTERM} into a caught, clean-exit
signal the way it does for \texttt{SIGINT} (Ctrl-C), and an earlier
plain \texttt{pkill} against the LiDAR process left the physical
LiDAR unit spinning after the owning process had already exited,
which is both a battery drain and a safety concern for anyone near
the vehicle. Section~\ref{sec:safe-shutdown} presents the resulting
documented shutdown procedure in full.

\section{LiDAR Angle-Convention Correction}
\label{sec:lidar-angle}

The first sensor-correctness issue found while bringing up
visualisation of the bridged data (\texttt{robot\_state\_publisher} +
\texttt{joint\_state\_publisher} + RViz, no Gazebo) was a LiDAR
angle-binning defect in \texttt{qcar\_lidar\_node.py}: obstacles
rendered in RViz did not appear at their true bearing relative to the
rendered robot model. This required \emph{two} stacked, independent
corrections, not one -- a clockwise-to-counter-clockwise direction
flip \emph{and} a $+\ang{90}$ rotational offset between the LiDAR's
zero-reference bearing and the vehicle's own forward direction. The
first attempted fix (direction only) produced a result that was
itself the tell that a second error remained: it exactly mirrored the
original error about the vehicle's forward axis rather than
correcting it, which is the expected signature of fixing only a sign
error while a separate rotational offset error is still present. The
final, verified-correct transform is

\begin{equation}
  \theta_{\text{target}} = \operatorname{wrap}_{(-\pi,\,\pi]}\!\left(-\theta_{\text{lidar}} + \frac{\pi}{2}\right), \label{eq:lidar-angle-fix}
\end{equation}

verified against a real obstacle at a known bearing (the vehicle's
physical right side), cross-checked against the rendered robot
model's own orientation in RViz rather than the screen's raw
left/right, which depends on the RViz camera's own facing direction
and is therefore not a reliable reference on its own.

\section{Wheel Odometry over the Bridge}
\label{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}

Mapping (Cartographer, Section~\ref{sec:cartographer}) was
successfully brought up on real hardware using scan-matching alone,
with \texttt{use\_odometry: false} / \texttt{provide\_odom\_frame:
true} in the Cartographer configuration -- meaning the initial bridge
implementation required no odometry extension at all for mapping to
work end-to-end. Localisation (AMCL) does not share this property:
unlike Cartographer's self-contained scan matching, AMCL looks up a
live \texttt{odom} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{base} TF at every scan
callback as its motion-model input, so the wheel-odometry extension
originally scoped only for the mapping phase became a hard
requirement once navigation (Nav2/AMCL) was brought up.

\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} was extended with an \texttt{Odometry} class
implementing the same bicycle-model dead-reckoning integration as
Equations~\ref{eq:bicycle-x}--\ref{eq:bicycle-theta}, sent back to
the relay over the same already-full-duplex TCP connection the drive
commands arrive on (the reverse direction of this connection had
previously been opened but its data discarded).
\texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py} parses this stream and publishes both
\texttt{/odom} and the corresponding TF. Tested in isolation before
layering Nav2 on top, the resulting odometry published at
approximately 45\,Hz, and a 3-second commanded straight-line drive at
\SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} produced $x \approx \SI{1.25}{\meter}$,
$v \approx \SI{0.37}{\meter\per\second}$, $y \approx 0$ -- consistent
with straight-line motion at close to the commanded speed, and
confirmed working before the full navigation stack was brought up on
top of it.

\section{Steering-Trim Calibration}
\label{sec:steering-trim}

A small but consistent steering bias -- the physical vehicle drifting
laterally under a nominally straight (zero-steering) command -- was
present on this specific chassis, and the physical steering linkage
could not be adjusted to correct it mechanically. The fix was
implemented in software instead, as a constant offset
(\texttt{STEERING\_TRIM}, ultimately \SI{-0.08}{\radian}) applied
only at the point the steering command is written to the servo.
Calibration proceeded in two stages: an initial static test (motor
off, holding candidate angles and judging visually against a
reference, preserved as \texttt{calibrate\_steering.py} for future
re-calibration) narrowed the value to roughly the right range, and a
series of real straight-line driving tests (drive a known distance,
measure the resulting lateral offset, compute
$\delta_{\text{trim}} = \arctan(\text{offset}/\text{distance})$)
refined it further. This data carried real measurement noise --
lateral offset depends on the vehicle's initial aim at the start of
each test run, not purely on trim -- so the calibration deliberately
did not over-fit a precise value from only two data points; a
consistent directional nudge toward zero observed drift converged
faster in practice than attempting a precise interpolation. The final
value was accepted once a \SI{4.4}{\meter} test drive showed no
reported drift; this is described as ``almost accurate,'' a
deliberate acceptance of a small residual rather than a claim of
exact zero.

\subsection{A Trim-Placement Bug and the ``Apply at the Actuator Boundary'' Principle}
\label{sec:trim-boundary-principle}

The first implementation of this trim contained a real bug worth
recording as a general principle for any per-unit hardware
calibration constant, not only this one. It folded the trim into the
\emph{same} steering value used both for the real servo command
\emph{and} for the odometry dead-reckoning calculation in
Section~\ref{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}. Since the entire purpose of
the trim is to make the real wheels read approximately zero deflection
despite a nonzero servo command, feeding that same trimmed value into
odometry made the dead-reckoning model believe the wheels were
deflected by the trim amount even while the vehicle was, in reality,
driving dead straight. A live test briefly exposed this directly: a
straight-line drive of approximately \SI{2.8}{\meter} produced a
fictitious $y \approx \SI{-1.72}{\meter}$ in the odometry output, a
spurious $\sim$\ang{30} curve that did not correspond to any real
vehicle motion.

The fix separated \texttt{compute\_steering()} (returns the
untrimmed, kinematic steering angle, used for odometry) from a new
\texttt{apply\_trim()} (computes the real servo command, called only
immediately before the HAL write). Re-verified with the same drive
command, the odometry then correctly read $y \approx 0$. The general
principle this illustrates -- and which is stated here explicitly
because it is expected to generalise to any future per-unit hardware
calibration constant on this or a similar platform -- is that a
calibration constant compensating for a specific actuator's physical
imperfection should be applied \emph{as late as possible, immediately
at the actuator boundary}, and never upstream of any computation
(such as odometry) that treats its input as an accurate, ground-truth
kinematic quantity.

\section{Clock Synchronisation and the Receipt-vs-Capture Timestamp Bug}
\label{sec:clock-offset}

The first real navigation-goal test run independently by this
project's author, after mapping, localisation, and the fixes above
were all in place, surfaced a new symptom: sudden AMCL localisation
jumps and visible path deviation on both straight and curved
segments. The description of what was actually observed --
LiDAR scan shape stays internally coherent, but the entire scan
rigidly shifts and appears to track the robot's motion, ``like the
skeleton of the map is moving'' -- together with an explicit
instinct that this might be a transform-related issue rather than a
tuning problem, pointed toward a \emph{timing} rather than a spatial
or gain-tuning cause, and this proved correct.

\texttt{/scan} (port 5556) and \texttt{/odom} (port 5555) are two
independent TCP streams, each subject to its own, uncorrelated
network jitter -- this link had already been measured showing
\SIrange{87}{300}{\milli\second} of variable latency.
\texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py} had been stamping both incoming
streams with \texttt{self.get\_clock().now()} at the moment of TCP
\emph{receipt} on the development PC, rather than at the moment of
sensor \emph{capture} on the QCar. Because the two streams' receipt
times are decorrelated, a late-arriving scan could be paired --
purely by receipt-time coincidence -- against an odometry sample
that, in real physical time, was already stale by a different,
independent amount. This produces exactly the observed symptom: a
LiDAR scan that is internally self-consistent but rigidly offset
relative to the map, tracking the robot's own recent motion.

The fix required both machines' clocks to be related, not merely
each stream's own internal timing corrected. A round-trip-corrected
NTP-style offset measurement (five clustered trials of
$\text{offset} = t_{\text{remote}} - (t_1+t_2)/2$ around an SSH
\texttt{date} call) found a genuine $\sim$\SI{0.50}{\second} clock
offset between the two machines -- a naive sequential comparison
without the round-trip correction would have overstated this by also
counting SSH connection-setup time as clock skew. This offset was
deliberately \emph{not} corrected via a system-level NTP/chrony
configuration, since the QCar is shared laboratory hardware, and a
persistent system configuration pointing it at one researcher's
personal development machine as a time reference is not appropriate
to leave on shared infrastructure. Instead, \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}
and \texttt{qcar\_lidar\_node.py} were changed to stamp every message
with their own local \texttt{time.time()} at the moment of capture (a
\texttt{'t'} field in the JSON payload), and
\texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py} gained a \texttt{qcar\_clock\_offset}
parameter and a \texttt{qcar\_time\_to\_stamp()} helper that converts
a QCar-local capture timestamp into its development-PC-clock
equivalent, applied consistently to both the \texttt{/odom}+TF and
\texttt{/scan} publication paths.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Diagnostic measurements underlying the clock-offset fix.}
  \label{tab:clock-offset}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
    \toprule
    Quantity & Value \\
    \midrule
    Network latency (TCP link, both ports) & \SIrange{87}{300}{\milli\second} (variable) \\
    Measured clock offset (round-trip corrected) & $\approx \SI{0.50}{\second}$ \\
    \texttt{qcar\_clock\_offset} launch parameter (verified session) & \texttt{0.50} \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Safe Shutdown Procedure}
\label{sec:safe-shutdown}

Because two of the four processes in this bridge run directly on
physical hardware with no supervising ROS~2 lifecycle to fall back
on, this project established and documented a fixed shutdown
sequence, using \texttt{SIGINT} exclusively rather than a plain
\texttt{pkill} (per the signal-handling fix in
Section~\ref{sec:bridge-architecture}):
(1)~stop \texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py} on the development PC;
(2)~stop the visualisation launch process group (RViz may itself
segfault on exit, a known, harmless Qt/OpenGL quirk on this system --
worth confirming it has actually exited rather than assuming);
(3)~stop \texttt{qcar\_lidar\_node.py} on the QCar;
(4)~stop \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} on the QCar (requires \texttt{sudo}).
This project's own operational experience found it is not sufficient
to trust that the sequence \emph{was run} -- on one occasion the
motor bridge was still listening on its TCP port after the operator
believed it had been stopped -- so the documented procedure
explicitly includes confirming both TCP ports (5555, 5556) are
released on the QCar (\texttt{ss -tlnp}) before considering the
vehicle idle.

\section{Summary}
\label{sec:hardware-bridge-summary}

This chapter's bridge architecture makes the physical QCar~2 appear,
from the perspective of every ROS~2 node in the navigation stack, as
an ordinary \texttt{/cmd\_vel}-in, \texttt{/odom}/\texttt{/scan}-out
robot -- despite the underlying reality of two incompatible ROS~2
distributions connected by a bespoke TCP/JSON protocol. Getting the
data flowing across that bridge to a fidelity usable by AMCL and
Nav2, however, required four further, independently discovered
corrections (LiDAR angle convention, wheel odometry, steering trim,
and inter-machine clock synchronisation) beyond simply moving bytes
across the link. Chapter~\ref{ch:calibration} continues directly from
here, addressing the one remaining discrepancy this chapter's fixes
do not touch: the relationship between a commanded velocity and the
vehicle's actual physical speed.

    target = -angle + math.pi / 2
    normalized = math.atan2(math.sin(target), math.cos(target))
    idx = int(round((normalized + math.pi) / increment)) % NUM_MEASUREMENTS
    if RANGE_MIN <= dist <= RANGE_MAX:
        ranges[idx] = float(dist)

+ranges = [float('inf')] * NUM_MEASUREMENTS

Listing~\ref{lst:odometry-class} shows the \texttt{Odometry} class in
full: \texttt{update()} is called once per control-loop cycle with
the raw encoder count and the current commanded steering angle, and
directly implements the bicycle-model relationship of
Equations~\ref{eq:bicycle-x}--\ref{eq:bicycle-theta} -- encoder-count
deltas become a travelled distance via the fixed
\texttt{METERS\_PER\_COUNT} conversion, from which velocity and yaw
rate follow, and $x$/$y$/yaw are then integrated forward exactly as
in the continuous-time model.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Bicycle-model dead-reckoning odometry (\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}).},label={lst:odometry-class}]
class Odometry:
    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 0.0
        self.y = 0.0
        self.yaw = 0.0
        self.last_encoder = None

    def update(self, encoder_counts, steering, dt):
        if self.last_encoder is None:
            self.last_encoder = encoder_counts
        delta_counts = encoder_counts - self.last_encoder
        self.last_encoder = encoder_counts

        distance = delta_counts * METERS_PER_COUNT
        v = distance / dt
        yaw_rate = v * math.tan(steering) / WHEELBASE

        self.yaw += yaw_rate * dt
        self.x += distance * math.cos(self.yaw)
        self.y += distance * math.sin(self.yaw)

        return {'x': self.x, 'y': self.y, 'yaw': self.yaw,
                'v': v, 'yaw_rate': yaw_rate}
\end{lstlisting}

    # Returns the KINEMATIC (untrimmed) angle - used for odometry.

    return max(-MAX_STEER_CMD,

\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Converting a QCar-local capture timestamp to the development PC's clock (\texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py}).},label={lst:clock-offset-code}]
def qcar_time_to_stamp(qcar_time, qcar_clock_offset):
    '''Converts a QCar-clock time.time() reading into a
    builtin_interfaces/Time on this machine's clock, correcting for
    the measured offset between the two machines' independent,
    unsynchronized clocks.'''
    corrected = qcar_time - qcar_clock_offset
    sec = int(corrected)
    nanosec = int(round((corrected - sec) * 1e9))
    return Time(sec=sec, nanosec=nanosec)
\end{lstlisting}

1	\chapter{System Identification and Calibration}
2	\label{ch:calibration}
3	
4	% TODO: this is the thesis's strongest evidentiary chapter - consider
5	% pulling the six-point sweep and the readMode before/after table into
6	% actual plotted figures (velocity-vs-time traces) rather than tables
7	% only, if you still have the raw CSV/rosbag data from the sessions
8	% referenced here.
9	
10	This chapter documents the longest and most consequential
11	investigation of the project: a real-hardware symptom in which the
12	vehicle, commanded to travel a fixed distance and then stop,
13	consistently travelled substantially further -- in the worst observed
14	case, roughly three times as far -- before actually coming to rest.
15	What began as a search for a physical explanation (drivetrain
16	coasting) ended in the discovery of a stale-data artefact in the
17	vendor hardware abstraction layer described in
18	Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}, with the true physical residual
19	turning out to be small once that artefact was removed. The chapter
20	also documents a control-design attempt that was tested on physical
21	hardware without adequate prior validation and produced a genuine,
22	dangerous oscillation -- included here in full because it is as
23	methodologically important as the investigation's eventual successful
24	resolution.
25	
26	\section{Problem Statement}
27	\label{sec:stop-distance-problem}
28	
29	With the bridge of Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge} operational, a
30	simple closed-loop test was used throughout this investigation: drive
31	the vehicle at a fixed commanded speed toward a target distance,
32	using odometry to detect when the target is crossed, and stop.
33	Repeated trials showed the vehicle travelling substantially further
34	than the commanded target before settling, with the overshoot
35	growing, not shrinking, across repeated sessions under otherwise
36	similar conditions -- an early indication that the effect was
37	systematic and reproducible rather than simple measurement noise.
38	
39	\section{Ruling Out Simpler Explanations}
40	\label{sec:ruled-out}
41	
42	Several plausible causes were tested directly and eliminated before
43	the investigation's eventual resolution:
44	
45	\begin{itemize}
46	  \item \textbf{AMCL/localisation.} The original suspect. Investigating
47	    it produced one genuine, separately valid fix -- raising AMCL's
48	    \texttt{recovery\_alpha\_fast}/\texttt{recovery\_alpha\_slow} from
49	    \texttt{0.0} to \texttt{0.1}/\texttt{0.001}, since a value of
50	    \texttt{0.0} allows the particle filter to freeze permanently once
51	    it (incorrectly) converges to zero uncertainty under real sensor
52	    noise, a failure mode that a clean simulation environment does not
53	    expose. This fix was kept, but does not explain the stop-distance
54	    symptom, which persisted after it was applied.
55	  \item \textbf{Command-delivery delay.} Measured directly on the
56	    QCar's own local clock (eliminating any network-latency
57	    contribution) at approximately \SI{0.2}{\second} from decision to
58	    applied throttle -- normal, and not large enough to explain
59	    metre-scale overshoot at the tested speeds.
60	  \item \textbf{A backlog of stale \texttt{/cmd\_vel} commands.}
61	    Hypothesised as queuing behind a blocking socket \texttt{send}
62	    call in the relay's single-threaded executor. Two increasingly
63	    careful fixes were built and deployed -- a staleness timestamp
64	    check, then a full non-blocking sender-thread architecture -- and
65	    both were tested directly on hardware. \textbf{Neither made any
66	    measurable difference}, ruling this out as the cause.
67	  \item \textbf{Logging/print buffering artefacts.} The timing of
68	    QCar-local debug samples during the ``coast'' period was a steady
69	    \SIrange{20}{35}{\milli\second} throughout, not a rapid burst
70	    consistent with a draining backlog -- ruled out.
71	\end{itemize}
72	
73	\section{Active Braking: A Control-Design Attempt and a Safety Incident}
74	\label{sec:active-braking}
75	
76	With the above ruled out, the leading hypothesis shifted to genuine
77	drivetrain (motor and gearbox) rotational inertia keeping the wheels
78	turning for a period after commanded throttle reached zero -- a
79	physically plausible mechanism, and one apparently consistent with
80	QCar-local encoder readings that showed real velocity persisting for
81	several seconds after a stop was commanded.
82	
83	A corrective control law was implemented directly in
84	\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}: a reverse-throttle brake pulse proportional
85	to the residual measured velocity, intended to actively cancel the
86	coasting motion. \textbf{This was deployed directly to physical
87	hardware without first being traced through by hand or tested in
88	simulation.} On its first test, it produced a genuine, dangerous
89	oscillation: the vehicle lurched forward and backward repeatedly,
90	reaching \SI{-0.88}{\meter\per\second} in reverse and still
91	accelerating, and had to be stopped manually via an SSH-issued kill
92	command mid-test. The root cause, in hindsight, is a textbook control
93	failure mode: a continuous proportional reaction to \emph{any}
94	nonzero residual velocity, including reverse velocity, with no
95	deadband and no explicit disarm condition, means every correction's
96	own overshoot looks to the controller like a fresh error requiring
97	correction -- an undamped hunting loop with no mechanism to settle.
98	
99	A revised, ``one-shot'' design was implemented -- braking fires
100	exactly once per drive-to-stop transition and permanently disarms the
101	instant measured velocity crosses zero, rather than re-arming from
102	residual drift -- and \textbf{reproduced the same oscillation on
103	retest}. Given the repeated safety failure, this control approach was
104	abandoned entirely rather than iterated on further. Both modified
105	files were reverted to their exact pre-investigation state, verified
106	byte-identical to the known-good version by hash comparison, with the
107	failure documented directly in a source-code comment so that it is
108	not blindly re-attempted in a future session.
109	
110	This incident is the clearest instance in this project of the general
111	principle stated in Section~\ref{sec:methodology-overview}: a
112	reactive feedback controller acting on a live sensor reading, on a
113	system already confirmed to have real actuator lag and inertia,
114	should be traced through by hand for an overshoot scenario -- or
115	tested in simulation first -- before it is ever sent to physical
116	hardware. ``The control theory seems sound'' was not, on its own,
117	sufficient justification here, and this project treats that as a
118	standing rule for any future reactive control logic on this
119	platform, not merely a lesson learned in retrospect.
120	
121	\section{Sim-versus-Real Comparison}
122	\label{sec:sim-vs-real}
123	
124	Following a methodology suggested by the author's academic
125	supervisor, the identical closed-loop stop-distance test (drive $N$
126	metres at a fixed speed, stop the instant odometry crosses the
127	target) was reproduced in both the physical robot and the Gazebo
128	simulation of Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}, using the same launch stack
129	with only the drive target switched from simulated to real hardware.
130	
131	A six-point sweep across three target distances
132	(\SIlist{1.0;1.5;2.0}{\meter}) and three commanded speeds
133	(\SIlist{0.20;0.25;0.30}{\meter\per\second}) found real
134	hardware overshoot in the range \SIrange{0.58}{2.12}{\meter} across
135	two sessions roughly one hour apart, with \emph{every} tested
136	condition worse in the second session by a broadly consistent margin
137	-- evidence of real, reproducible drift (plausibly battery voltage or
138	floor/tyre condition) rather than measurement noise. The matched
139	simulation sweep, over the same six conditions, showed overshoot of
140	only \SIrange{0.044}{0.067}{\meter} -- \SIrange{10}{30}{}$\times$
141	smaller, and only weakly sensitive to speed, in contrast to the real
142	hardware overshoot, which scaled roughly with the cube of speed. A
143	dedicated, isolated comparison at \SI{2}{\meter} /
144	\SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} sharpened this further: the simulated
145	vehicle settled at \SI{2.067}{\meter} (an extra \SI{0.067}{\meter}),
146	while the real vehicle settled at \SI{3.91}{\meter} (an extra
147	\SI{1.90}{\meter}) -- a $\sim$28$\times$ difference for an identical
148	software command. This result strongly supports a real-hardware-specific
149	controller/dynamics cause rather than something inherent to the
150	stop-command approach itself, and directly motivated the calibration
151	work in the remainder of this chapter.
152	
153	\section{Throttle Calibration}
154	\label{sec:throttle-calibration}
155	
156	\subsection{The Uncalibrated Gain Hypothesis}
157	\label{sec:throttle-gain-hypothesis}
158	
159	\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}'s mapping from \texttt{cmd\_vel}'s
160	\texttt{linear.x} (in \si{\meter\per\second}) to the HAL's PWM duty
161	cycle had, since early in the project, used a placeholder gain
162	(\texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN = 1/3}), explicitly documented in its own
163	source comment as uncalibrated. Direct measurement from the sweep
164	data above confirmed this mattered: commanding
165	\SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} produced a real, QCar-local
166	encoder-measured cruise velocity averaging
167	$\approx$\SI{0.8}{\meter\per\second} -- roughly $2.6$--$2.7\times$ the
168	commanded speed, consistent across two independent measurements.
169	Since coasting distance from momentum scales with the square of
170	velocity, this alone predicts roughly a $6.9\times$ larger coast
171	distance than a genuine \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} stop would
172	produce -- a substantial fraction of the sim-vs-real gap found above,
173	and a reminder that the sim-vs-real comparison in
174	Section~\ref{sec:sim-vs-real} was not, at that point, comparing truly
175	matched real speeds.
176	
177	\subsection{First Calibration Attempt: A Deadband Discovered, Then Reverted}
178	\label{sec:deadband-discovery}
179	
180	A dedicated measurement tool, \texttt{check\_stop\_latency.py}, was
181	built to measure cruise velocity and stop latency in a single run. An
182	initial correction -- lowering \texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN} by dividing by
183	the previously measured $2.67\times$ ratio -- was deployed to
184	hardware and immediately surfaced a second, independent, hard
185	non-linearity: at the old gain, a commanded \SI{0.25}{\meter\per\second}
186	($\sim$8\% duty) sat completely motionless for
187	$\approx$\SI{2.1}{\second} before suddenly breaking static friction
188	and moving, while \SIlist{0.20;0.15}{\meter\per\second}
189	($\sim$6.7\%/5\% duty) never moved at all across
190	\SIrange{8}{10}{\second} of commanding. This static-friction deadband
191	is a genuine physical property of the vehicle, not a linear gain
192	error, and it interacts badly with a naive linear-gain correction: the
193	lowered gain restored accurate cruise-speed tracking at higher
194	commanded speeds, but pushed the duty cycle for normal teleoperation
195	speeds below the deadband threshold entirely, making the vehicle stop
196	responding to real driving commands. The gain correction was reverted
197	the same day to restore usable teleoperation.
198	
199	This reframes the calibration problem: gain and deadband are not
200	independent. Any solution must jointly (a) track commanded speed
201	accurately at normal operating speeds and (b) keep every one of those
202	same commands above the static-friction threshold -- which a single
203	linear multiplier applied to the whole range cannot do, since scaling
204	the gain down to fix (a) simultaneously worsens (b) for exactly the
205	commands that were already only barely clearing the threshold.
206	
207	\subsection{Final Calibration: An Empirical Duty Sweep}
208	\label{sec:final-calibration}
209	
210	Given that finding, the calibration approach was reframed entirely:
211	rather than extrapolating a linear gain from one or two data points,
212	\texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN} was forced to zero and a dedicated,
213	lighter-weight tool (\texttt{drive\_and\_log.py}) was used to sweep
214	fixed PWM duty values directly, with the vehicle on the ground under
215	real load throughout. Table~\ref{tab:duty-sweep} summarises the
216	resulting duty-response curve.

288	\subsection{A Stray-Process False Positive}
289	\label{sec:stray-process}
290	
291	While iterating on this calibration, a separate, purely diagnostic
292	false alarm is worth recording as a general debugging caution. A
293	prior \texttt{check\_stop\_latency.py} test process, left running in
294	the background rather than exiting automatically once its measurement
295	completed, continued publishing \texttt{linear.x=0.0} on
296	\texttt{/cmd\_vel} at 20\,Hz, silently racing against a separately
297	launched teleoperation node publishing on the same topic. The
298	resulting symptom -- the vehicle briefly registering a throttle
299	command and then immediately reverting to zero within one control
300	cycle -- looked exactly like a gain, deadband, or logic bug, and was
301	initially investigated as one. ROS~2 does not warn about multiple
302	publishers on the same topic; it simply interleaves messages, with
303	whichever publisher's message arrives last in a given control cycle
304	taking effect. The actual fix was operational, not code: kill the
305	stray process. This project subsequently adopted two standing
306	practices as a result -- checking \texttt{pgrep -af} for
307	topic-related script names (or \texttt{ros2 topic info /cmd\_vel
308	--verbose} for publisher count) before deep-diving into a control-logic
309	theory whenever real behaviour contradicts an issued command, and
310	designing one-shot diagnostic nodes to exit automatically once their
311	measurement is complete rather than spinning indefinitely.
