\paragraph{From raw encoder counts to metres.}
\texttt{METERS\_PER\_COUNT} (documented in \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} as
$\frac{0.01977}{2880}$) is itself a small derived constant, not a
directly measured one: 2880 is the number of raw encoder counts per
one full revolution of the motor shaft, as documented in the Quanser
HAL manual for this drive motor/encoder pairing, and
\SI{0.01977}{\meter} is the linear distance one rear-wheel revolution
advances the vehicle (i.e.\ the wheel's rolling circumference,
folding in the fixed gear ratio between motor shaft and wheel), so
their ratio converts a raw encoder delta directly into a travelled
distance in one multiplication, with no separate gear-ratio or
wheel-circumference term needed at the call site.

\paragraph{The integration is forward Euler, not an exact arc.}
Line-by-line, \texttt{update()} performs a standard forward-Euler
discretisation of Equations~\ref{eq:bicycle-x}--\ref{eq:bicycle-theta}:
it advances \texttt{self.yaw} by \texttt{yaw\_rate * dt} \emph{first},
then immediately uses that already-updated yaw to project the
travelled \texttt{distance} onto $x$ and $y$ via
$\cos(\text{yaw})$/$\sin(\text{yaw})$ -- effectively assuming the
vehicle's heading was already at its new value for the entirety of
this cycle's straight-line displacement, rather than integrating the
true curved arc the vehicle followed while turning during the
interval. This is a standard, deliberate simplification (matching how
Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}'s simulation-side plugin also integrates
its own motion incrementally rather than analytically per step), and
its error shrinks toward zero as the control loop's period
\texttt{dt} shrinks, but it is not exact for any nonzero
\texttt{yaw\_rate * dt} -- at this project's \SI{50}{\hertz} control
rate (Section~\ref{sec:bridge-architecture}), \texttt{dt} is small
enough that the resulting error is negligible next to this thesis's
other, much larger sources of odometry inaccuracy (steering trim,
throttle calibration), but it is worth naming explicitly as a
non-zero, if small, contributor to dead-reckoning drift over a long
enough drive.

73	\section{Active Braking: A Control-Design Attempt and a Safety Incident}
74	\label{sec:active-braking}
75	
76	With the above ruled out, the leading hypothesis shifted to genuine
77	drivetrain (motor and gearbox) rotational inertia keeping the wheels
78	turning for a period after commanded throttle reached zero -- a
79	physically plausible mechanism, and one apparently consistent with
80	QCar-local encoder readings that showed real velocity persisting for
81	several seconds after a stop was commanded.
82	
83	A corrective control law was implemented directly in
84	\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}: a reverse-throttle brake pulse proportional
85	to the residual measured velocity, intended to actively cancel the
86	coasting motion. \textbf{This was deployed directly to physical
87	hardware without first being traced through by hand or tested in
88	simulation.} On its first test, it produced a genuine, dangerous
89	oscillation: the vehicle lurched forward and backward repeatedly,
90	reaching \SI{-0.88}{\meter\per\second} in reverse and still
91	accelerating, and had to be stopped manually via an SSH-issued kill
92	command mid-test. The root cause, in hindsight, is a textbook control
93	failure mode: a continuous proportional reaction to \emph{any}
94	nonzero residual velocity, including reverse velocity, with no
95	deadband and no explicit disarm condition, means every correction's
96	own overshoot looks to the controller like a fresh error requiring
97	correction -- an undamped hunting loop with no mechanism to settle.
98	
99	Since both attempts were reverted, no implementation of this control
100	law survives in the repository to quote directly; Listing~\ref{lst:active-braking-comment}
101	instead reproduces the comment left in its place in
102	\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}, at the site the code once occupied -- the
103	project's own permanent record of what was tried, why it failed, and
104	why it must not be blindly re-attempted.
105	
106	\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Comment documenting the rejected active-braking design, left in place of the reverted code (\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}).},label={lst:active-braking-comment}]
107	# Tried active braking (brief reverse-throttle pulse proportional to
108	# residual speed when a stop is commanded) to counter drivetrain coast -
109	# REJECTED, not just untuned. It's a proportional loop on velocity sign
110	# with no deadband and one-cycle-stale (~20ms) feedback: if the pulse
111	# overshoots past zero into real reverse motion, the next cycle reads a
112	# negative v and "corrects" with a forward push, which can itself
113	# overshoot - a genuine undamped hunting oscillation, not a bad gain
114	# value. Confirmed on hardware (twice - it was reverted once already
115	# before this comment, then re-tried and reproduced the same result):
116	# car visibly lurched forward/back repeatedly and fast, had to be
117	# killed manually. Do not re-add this without a real deadband/
118	# hysteresis or a one-shot (non-continuous) brake pulse design -
119	# retuning BRAKE_GAIN alone will not fix it.
120	\end{lstlisting}
121	
122	A revised, ``one-shot'' design was implemented -- braking fires
123	exactly once per drive-to-stop transition and permanently disarms the
124	instant measured velocity crosses zero, rather than re-arming from
125	residual drift -- and \textbf{reproduced the same oscillation on
126	retest}. Given the repeated safety failure, this control approach was
127	abandoned entirely rather than iterated on further. Both modified
128	files were reverted to their exact pre-investigation state, verified
129	byte-identical to the known-good version by hash comparison, with the
130	failure documented directly in a source-code comment so that it is
131	not blindly re-attempted in a future session.
132	
133	This incident is the clearest instance in this project of the general
134	principle stated in Section~\ref{sec:methodology-overview}: a
135	reactive feedback controller acting on a live sensor reading, on a
136	system already confirmed to have real actuator lag and inertia,
137	should be traced through by hand for an overshoot scenario -- or
138	tested in simulation first -- before it is ever sent to physical
139	hardware. ``The control theory seems sound'' was not, on its own,
140	sufficient justification here, and this project treats that as a
141	standing rule for any future reactive control logic on this
142	platform, not merely a lesson learned in retrospect.
143	
144	\section{Sim-versus-Real Comparison}
145	\label{sec:sim-vs-real}
146	
147	Following a methodology suggested by the author's academic
148	supervisor, the identical closed-loop stop-distance test (drive $N$
149	metres at a fixed speed, stop the instant odometry crosses the
150	target) was reproduced in both the physical robot and the Gazebo

152	with only the drive target switched from simulated to real hardware.
153

158	two sessions roughly one hour apart, with \emph{every} tested

172	controller/dynamics cause rather than something inherent to the

coasting motion. \textbf{This was deployed directly to physical
hardware without first being traced through by hand or tested in
simulation.} On its first test, it produced a genuine, dangerous
oscillation: the vehicle lurched forward and backward repeatedly,
reaching \SI{-0.88}{\meter\per\second} in reverse and still
accelerating, and had to be stopped manually via an SSH-issued kill
command mid-test. The root cause, in hindsight, is a textbook control
failure mode: a continuous proportional reaction to \emph{any}
nonzero residual velocity, including reverse velocity, with no
deadband and no explicit disarm condition, means every correction's
own overshoot looks to the controller like a fresh error requiring
correction -- an undamped hunting loop with no mechanism to settle.

Since both attempts were reverted, no implementation of this control
law survives in the repository to quote directly; Listing~\ref{lst:active-braking-comment}
instead reproduces the comment left in its place in
\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}, at the site the code once occupied -- the
project's own permanent record of what was tried, why it failed, and
why it must not be blindly re-attempted.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Comment documenting the rejected active-braking design, left in place of the reverted code (\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}).},label={lst:active-braking-comment}]
# Tried active braking (brief reverse-throttle pulse proportional to
# residual speed when a stop is commanded) to counter drivetrain coast -
# REJECTED, not just untuned. It's a proportional loop on velocity sign
# with no deadband and one-cycle-stale (~20ms) feedback: if the pulse
# overshoots past zero into real reverse motion, the next cycle reads a
# negative v and "corrects" with a forward push, which can itself
# overshoot - a genuine undamped hunting oscillation, not a bad gain
# value. Confirmed on hardware (twice - it was reverted once already
# before this comment, then re-tried and reproduced the same result):
# car visibly lurched forward/back repeatedly and fast, had to be
# killed manually. Do not re-add this without a real deadband/
# hysteresis or a one-shot (non-continuous) brake pulse design -
# retuning BRAKE_GAIN alone will not fix it.
\end{lstlisting}

A revised, ``one-shot'' design was implemented -- braking fires
exactly once per drive-to-stop transition and permanently disarms the
instant measured velocity crosses zero, rather than re-arming from
residual drift -- and \textbf{reproduced the same oscillation on
retest}. Given the repeated safety failure, this control approach was
abandoned entirely rather than iterated on further. Both modified
files were reverted to their exact pre-investigation state, verified
byte-identical to the known-good version by hash comparison, with the
failure documented directly in a source-code comment so that it is
not blindly re-attempted in a future session.

This incident is the clearest instance in this project of the general
principle stated in Section~\ref{sec:methodology-overview}: a
reactive feedback controller acting on a live sensor reading, on a
system already confirmed to have real actuator lag and inertia,
should be traced through by hand for an overshoot scenario -- or
tested in simulation first -- before it is ever sent to physical
hardware. ``The control theory seems sound'' was not, on its own,
sufficient justification here, and this project treats that as a
standing rule for any future reactive control logic on this
platform, not merely a lesson learned in retrospect.

\label{sec:sim-vs-real}

Following a methodology suggested by the author's academic
supervisor, the identical closed-loop stop-distance test (drive $N$

with only the drive target switched from simulated to real hardware.

two sessions roughly one hour apart, with \emph{every} tested
condition worse in the second session by a broadly consistent margin

stop-command approach itself, and directly motivated the calibration

\end{equation}

governed entirely by the magnitude of $(1 - aK)$: the residual
velocity decays toward zero only if $|1 - aK| < 1$, i.e.\

critically, that oscillation \emph{grows} in magnitude, without

multiplied by a factor more negative than $-1$. This single
inequality is the formal statement of exactly what the source comment

\subsection{First Calibration Attempt: A Deadband Discovered, Then Reverted}
\label{sec:deadband-discovery}

A dedicated measurement tool, \texttt{check\_stop\_latency.py}, was
built to measure cruise velocity and stop latency in a single run. An
initial correction -- lowering \texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN} by dividing by
the previously measured $2.67\times$ ratio -- was deployed to
hardware and immediately surfaced a second, independent, hard
non-linearity: at the old gain, a commanded \SI{0.25}{\meter\per\second}
($\sim$8\% duty) sat completely motionless for
$\approx$\SI{2.1}{\second} before suddenly breaking static friction
and moving, while \SIlist{0.20;0.15}{\meter\per\second}
($\sim$6.7\%/5\% duty) never moved at all across
\SIrange{8}{10}{\second} of commanding. This static-friction deadband
is a genuine physical property of the vehicle, not a linear gain
error, and it interacts badly with a naive linear-gain correction: the
lowered gain restored accurate cruise-speed tracking at higher
commanded speeds, but pushed the duty cycle for normal teleoperation
speeds below the deadband threshold entirely, making the vehicle stop
responding to real driving commands. The gain correction was reverted
the same day to restore usable teleoperation.

This reframes the calibration problem: gain and deadband are not
independent. Any solution must jointly (a) track commanded speed
accurately at normal operating speeds and (b) keep every one of those
same commands above the static-friction threshold -- which a single
linear multiplier applied to the whole range cannot do, since scaling
the gain down to fix (a) simultaneously worsens (b) for exactly the
commands that were already only barely clearing the threshold.

\paragraph{This is a different friction phenomenon from Section~\ref{sec:friction-theory}'s.}
It is worth being precise about which friction is responsible here,
since this thesis discusses two physically distinct friction
phenomena under similar language. Section~\ref{sec:friction-theory}'s
Coulomb tyre-ground friction (the simulation's \texttt{mu1}/\texttt{mu2})
governs whether a spinning wheel's rotation converts into forward
chassis thrust at all, and is essentially instantaneous -- it has no
notion of a wheel being ``stuck.'' The deadband characterised here is
a different phenomenon internal to the real drivetrain itself (motor
brushes, gearbox mesh, bearing seats): \emph{static} friction (often
called stiction) resists the onset of relative motion between two
surfaces up to some breakaway force threshold, while \emph{kinetic}
friction, which applies once motion has actually begun, is often
measurably lower than that static threshold for the same
surface pair. A commanded duty cycle below the static threshold
produces zero motion no matter how long it is held, since the applied
torque never exceeds the force needed to break static friction in the
first place; once duty is raised just past that threshold, the
\emph{lower} kinetic friction then applies to an already-moving
system, so the same duty cycle that only barely broke static friction
can accelerate substantially further than expected once moving -- the
stick-slip signature Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration} identifies
directly in the duty-sweep data (Table~\ref{tab:duty-sweep}'s
\texttt{0.085} row, which \emph{runs away} rather than settling,
despite that same duty needing no help at all breaking away from a
standstill).

\subsection{Root Cause: a Ring-Buffer I/O Mode}
\label{sec:readmode-rootcause}

The root cause, found in the vendor HAL source
(\texttt{pal/products/qcar.py}) on the QCar itself, is exactly the
\texttt{readMode} distinction introduced in
Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}. \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} constructed
its \texttt{QCar} object with \texttt{readMode=1} (task-based I/O),
which starts a background acquisition task \emph{at object
construction time} -- before the bridge's listening TCP socket has
even opened -- filling a ring buffer of \texttt{frequency}$\times 2$
samples (at this project's \SI{50}{\hertz} read rate, exactly 100
samples, i.e.\ \SI{2.0}{\second}) with overwrite-on-overflow
behaviour. Each call to \texttt{car.read()} dequeues one buffered
sample. Because \texttt{car.read()} is not actually called until a
relay client connects -- which can take many seconds after the bridge
process starts -- the buffer fills and cycles during that idle gap.
Once reads begin at a consumption rate matching the production rate
exactly, the read stream is permanently stuck approximately 100
samples (\SI{2.0}{\second}) behind real time, because the backlog
never has an opportunity to drain.

This single mechanism explains every property of the symptom observed
across this entire chapter: the near-exact \SI{2.0}{\second} to
\SI{2.1}{\second} figure (matching the buffer's mathematically exact
2.0\,s capacity), its remarkable stability across sessions, vehicle
speeds, and physical conditions (a fixed buffer depth is indifferent
to any of these), and its symmetric appearance on both the start side
(the ``stiction delay'' of Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery}) and

\paragraph{Formalising the lag: why it is exactly the buffer depth, forever.}
Let the background task write into the ring buffer at a fixed
production index $p$, incrementing by one every $1/f$ seconds
($f = \SI{50}{\hertz}$ here), and let \texttt{car.read()} calls
advance a separate consumption index $c$, each call returning the
sample at position $c \bmod B$ (buffer capacity $B = 100$) and then
incrementing $c$. Production begins at object construction, $t = 0$;
consumption begins only once a relay client connects, at
$t = T_{\text{idle}}$. During $[0, T_{\text{idle}}]$, $p$ advances
alone (production with no consumption at all), so by the time
consumption starts, $p = f \cdot T_{\text{idle}}$ while $c = 0$ --
a gap of $f \cdot T_{\text{idle}}$ samples between them. If
$T_{\text{idle}} > B/f$ (true here, since a relay connecting takes
several seconds while $B/f = \SI{2.0}{\second}$), the overwrite-on-overflow
buffer has already wrapped around at least once by
$T_{\text{idle}}$, meaning the oldest sample still available to read
is not the very first one produced, but the one produced exactly
$B$ samples before $p$'s current value -- so the very first
\texttt{car.read()} call, at $t = T_{\text{idle}}$, necessarily
returns a sample captured at $t = T_{\text{idle}} - B/f$, a lag of
exactly $B/f = \SI{2.0}{\second}$, regardless of how much larger than
$B/f$ the idle gap $T_{\text{idle}}$ itself was. From that point
onward, because production and consumption both advance at the
identical rate $f$ (one \texttt{car.read()} per control-loop cycle,
matching the background task's own sampling rate), the gap between
$p$ and $c$ -- and therefore the lag between ``now'' and whatever
sample is being read -- stays fixed at exactly $B$ samples
indefinitely: neither index ever gains on the other, so the backlog
that accumulated during the idle gap is carried forward forever
rather than draining over time. This is precisely why the lag proved
so exactly reproducible (always $B/f = \SI{2.0}{\second}$, never more
and never less, regardless of how long the QCar sat idle before a
relay connected) and why it never improved on its own the longer the
system ran.

\section{Porting the Nav2 Configuration to Hardware}
\label{sec:nav2-porting}

The Nav2 parameter set developed and tuned in simulation
(Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}) required a small, mechanical set of
changes to run against physical hardware rather than Gazebo: every
occurrence of \texttt{use\_sim\_time} (13 in total, across the
costmap, planner, controller, and AMCL parameter blocks) was switched
from \texttt{true} to \texttt{false}, since the physical robot has no
simulation clock to synchronise against. Both mapping and navigation
launch files were given a real-hardware branch, gated on
\texttt{launch\_sim}, alongside the existing Gazebo branch, with
real hardware as the default and simulation opt-in
(\texttt{launch\_sim:=true}) -- a deliberate inversion of which mode
is the default, made once hardware became the project's active
development target, while keeping the simulation path fully intact
for future regression testing rather than removing it.

The AMCL \texttt{recovery\_alpha\_fast}/\texttt{recovery\_alpha\_slow}
fix from Section~\ref{sec:ruled-out} was carried forward
proactively into the hardware configuration at this point, rather
than left to be independently rediscovered against hardware, since
the underlying cause (particle-filter freeze under real sensor noise
that a clean simulation does not exercise) is a property of AMCL
itself, not specific to any one deployment target.

\paragraph{How this cost actually changes which trajectory wins.}
Connecting this directly to Section~\ref{sec:mppi-math}'s softmax
weighting (Equation~\ref{eq:mppi-weight}): \texttt{data.costs} is the
same per-trajectory accumulator every enabled critic adds into, so
this critic's contribution
$\left(\overline{\Delta\theta} \cdot \texttt{weight\_}\right)^{\texttt{power\_}}$
(the early-steps-averaged angular difference $\overline{\Delta\theta}$
from the listing's \texttt{cost} variable, scaled and exponentiated by
its own configured weight and power) is simply summed alongside the
stock critics' own contributions into $S(\tau^{(k)})$ before
Equation~\ref{eq:mppi-weight}'s exponential weighting is applied.
Concretely: of two sampled trajectories approaching the same curve,
one that begins turning toward the near-term path point immediately
accrues a small $\overline{\Delta\theta}$ over its first
\texttt{early\_time\_steps}, while one that continues driving straight
before reacting accrues a much larger one -- inflating that second
trajectory's total cost $S(\tau^{(k)})$, which Equation~\ref{eq:mppi-weight}
translates into an \emph{exponentially} smaller importance weight
$w^{(k)}$ relative to the early-turning trajectory. Because the
executed control is the weight-averaged sum over all $K$ sampled
trajectories, systematically suppressing the weight of every
late-turning sample -- rather than merely marking one specific
trajectory as disqualified -- is what actually shifts the controller's
averaged output toward beginning the turn earlier, without ever
needing to identify or select a single ``best'' trajectory explicitly.

\item \textbf{A QoS durability mismatch.} The actual publisher QoS
    for \texttt{/navigate\_to\_pose/\_action/status} is
    \texttt{RELIABLE} + \texttt{TRANSIENT\_LOCAL}. \texttt{rclpy}'s
    default subscription QoS, constructed by passing a plain integer
    depth, leaves durability at \texttt{VOLATILE} -- technically
    QoS-compatible by specification (a subscriber may request less
    than a publisher offers), but this delivered \emph{zero} messages
    in practice, confirmed twice on real hardware. The fix required
    constructing an explicit \texttt{QoSProfile} matching the
    publisher exactly, a reminder that formal QoS compatibility rules
    do not guarantee the practical behaviour a developer expects
    (Section~\ref{sec:ros2-model}).

constructing an explicit \texttt{QoSProfile} matching the
    publisher exactly, a reminder that formal QoS compatibility rules
    do not guarantee the practical behaviour a developer expects
    (Section~\ref{sec:ros2-model}). This is exactly the
    \texttt{TRANSIENT\_LOCAL}-publisher / \texttt{VOLATILE}-subscriber
    case Table~\ref{tab:qos-compatibility} marks as formally
    compatible: durability governs whether \emph{already-published}
    samples are replayed to a newly matched subscriber, and a
    low-frequency topic like action status may not publish a fresh
    sample again for a long time, so a \texttt{VOLATILE} subscriber
    that missed the replay is left waiting with no error raised on
    either side.

excluding TOC/bibliography/appendix. Starting from an earlier ~50-page
draft, every chapter was substantially deepened in one pass: Chapter 2

actual Gazebo plugin source, not just the single-track approximation),
PID control theory, the Coulomb/friction-cone model, the full MPPI
softmax-weighting math, and the full AMCL particle-filter + augmented-MCL
recovery math; Chapters 3-6 each gained "how the code actually works"
walkthroughs for every bug/fix already introduced - worked numerical
traces, a formal ring-buffer lag derivation, a formal discrete-time
instability proof for the rejected active-braking controller, and
more. Body text alone is now roughly 23,000 words (up from ~15,500) -
compile it and check the actual page count, since code listings,
equations, and tables render less densely than prose and a words/page
heuristic will underestimate them.

additions:** reading the actual `gazebo_ros_ackermann_drive.cpp`
source (Chapter 3, Section "A Quiet Regression") found that the
final simulation drive plugin's `/odom` is computed from
`model_->WorldPose()`/`WorldLinearVel()` - literal Gazebo ground
truth - not the genuine wheel-encoder dead reckoning the thesis
originally (and incorrectly) claimed for it. Every place that claim
appeared (Chapter 3's second-migration section and summary, Chapter
8's summary) has been corrected; only the physical QCar's own
odometry (Chapter 4) is actually dead reckoning. This is now presented
as a real finding (a structural, not just measured, source of the

# Master's Thesis - working project

Source for the Master's thesis on the QCar~2 sim-to-real navigation
migration, formatted against the Deggendorf Institute of Technology
(DIT) "Thesis Guideline" (Version 1.0, 27.06.2023).

## How to compile (Overleaf)

1. Overleaf -> **New Project -> Upload Project** -> select
   `qcar-master-thesis.zip` (not a blank project + drag-and-drop,
   which flattens the folder structure).
2. Confirm the main document is `main.tex` (project menu -> Main
   document; usually auto-detected).
3. Compiler: **pdfLaTeX** (default). The bibliography uses plain
   BibTeX (`\bibliographystyle{plain}` + `\bibliography{...}`), not
   biblatex/biber, and the abbreviations index is a plain table, not
   the `glossaries` package - both deliberately, to keep the compile
   chain short (`pdflatex -> bibtex -> pdflatex -> pdflatex`) instead
   of the much longer `pdflatex -> biber -> makeglossaries -> pdflatex
   -> pdflatex` chain, which is what was tripping the free plan's
   compile-time limit. Overleaf runs `bibtex` automatically; no manual
   step needed beyond a normal Recompile.
4. If you still hit a compile-timeout on the free plan (e.g. after
   adding a lot more content or large figures), the usual next levers
   are: compress/downsize any image you add under `figures/`, or drop
   `microtype` from `preamble.tex` (cosmetic justification polish
   only, not required by the guideline) - both reduce per-pass time
   without changing the document's structure or content.

## What's done vs. what's left

**Done - full structural compliance with the guideline:**
page geometry, font sizes, line spacing, heading style, page
numbering (roman front matter / arabic body), section numbering
depth, figure/table caption style, and a numeric DIN-style
bibliography. All required sections exist: title page, statement of
authorship, index of abbreviations, abstract, introduction,
groundwork, four methodology chapters, results, summary & prospects,
bibliography, appendix.

**Done - substantial real technical content**, pulled directly from
the underlying project's development history (session memory,
READMEs, CHANGELOGs): the Ackermann-drive migration, the Gazebo
Classic/Humble conversion, the four-bug "not moving forward" pattern,
the TCP/JSON hardware bridge design, the LiDAR/odometry/steering-trim
fixes, the full stop-distance investigation (including the active-
braking safety incident and the `readMode=1` HAL buffering root
cause), and the Nav2/MPPI integration and display-lag investigation.

**Done - 14 code listings with explanation**, verbatim from the
actual `qcar_updated` source (URDF/xacro, the behaviour-tree XML, the
onboard bridge and relay Python, and the `EarlyCommitCritic` C++
plugin), each introduced by a paragraph explaining what it does and
why - spread across Chapters 3-6, one or two per major fix discussed
in the prose. `\usepackage{listings}` (already in `preamble.tex`)
renders these with syntax highlighting and line numbers; no extra
Overleaf configuration needed.

**TODO - search every chapter file for the literal string `TODO`**
(`grep -rn TODO .` from this directory) - each marks something only
you can fill in or decide:

- Title page fields (`main.tex`): title, programme, supervisor,
  matriculation number, and submission date are filled in. Only the
  exact degree title (M.Eng./M.Sc./etc.) is still a TODO - confirm
  with the Centre for Studies.
- Acknowledgement (optional, `frontmatter/acknowledgement.tex`) - not
  currently included in the build; uncomment its `\input` line in
  `main.tex` if you want one.
- Statement of Authorship: sign the exported/printed copy by hand.
- Two measurements flagged in Chapters 6-7 as taken *before* the
  final `readMode=0` fix (Section 6.5 / 7.3) - re-running
  `monitor_goal_timing.py` and the six-point sim-vs-real sweep
  post-fix, if you can still get QCar lab time, would let those
  sections report final rather than provisional numbers.
- Bibliography (`bibliography.bib`): verify every entry's exact
  volume/issue/page numbers against the publisher before submission.
- Figures: several `% TODO: add figure` comments mark where a
  diagram, screenshot, or plot would strengthen a chapter - none of
  the current content depends on them being added, they're additive.
- Appendix source-code/data availability pointer (`appendix/appendix.tex`).

## Page count

Guideline target for a Master's thesis: ~80 text pages (±10%),
excluding TOC/bibliography/appendix. This draft's eight chapters are
a complete, technically substantive first pass covering every
required section, but are not yet padded or expanded to hit that
exact page count - per the guideline's own advice
("content-related quality... does not rise proportionally with page
count"), expand depth (more literature in Ch. 2, more figures
throughout, deeper discussion in Ch. 7) rather than length for its
own sake once your supervisor has reviewed this draft's structure and
content.

## Source reference

`docs/guideline-source.md` (in this directory) has a page-by-page
summary of the DIT guideline this draft was built against, for quick
reference without re-opening the original PDF.

24	\section{Porting the Nav2 Configuration to Hardware}
25	\label{sec:nav2-porting}
26	
27	The Nav2 parameter set developed and tuned in simulation
28	(Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}) required a small, mechanical set of
29	changes to run against physical hardware rather than Gazebo: every
30	occurrence of \texttt{use\_sim\_time} (13 in total, across the
31	costmap, planner, controller, and AMCL parameter blocks) was switched
32	from \texttt{true} to \texttt{false}, since the physical robot has no
33	simulation clock to synchronise against. Both mapping and navigation
34	launch files were given a real-hardware branch, gated on
35	\texttt{launch\_sim}, alongside the existing Gazebo branch, with
36	real hardware as the default and simulation opt-in
37	(\texttt{launch\_sim:=true}) -- a deliberate inversion of which mode
38	is the default, made once hardware became the project's active
39	development target, while keeping the simulation path fully intact
40	for future regression testing rather than removing it.
41	
42	The AMCL \texttt{recovery\_alpha\_fast}/\texttt{recovery\_alpha\_slow}
43	fix from Section~\ref{sec:ruled-out} was carried forward
44	proactively into the hardware configuration at this point, rather
45	than left to be independently rediscovered against hardware, since
46	the underlying cause -- Section~\ref{sec:amcl-math}'s augmented-MCL
47	random-particle-injection mechanism being permanently disabled at
48	$\alpha_{\text{slow}} = \alpha_{\text{fast}} = 0$, leaving the filter
49	with no way to recover from an overconfident convergence once real
50	sensor noise (which a clean simulation rarely exercises) triggers one
51	-- is a property of AMCL's own resampling algorithm, not specific to
52	any one deployment target.
53	
54	\section{Custom MPPI Critic: \texttt{EarlyCommitCritic}}
55	\label{sec:mppi-critic}
56	
57	Early navigation testing showed a specific weakness in the stock MPPI
58	critic set (Section~\ref{sec:nav2}) for this vehicle: the standard
59	path-following critics evaluate a sampled trajectory's alignment and
60	progress against the path as a whole, which can leave the controller
61	driving further into an approaching curve before it begins reacting
62	to it, rather than beginning the turn as early as physically sensible
63	-- a behaviour more forgiving for a differential-drive robot's tight
64	turning radius than for an Ackermann-steered vehicle with the
65	finite minimum turning radius of Table~\ref{tab:qcar-geometry}.
66	
67	A custom MPPI critic plugin, \texttt{EarlyCommitCritic}, was
68	developed and built into the navigation package to address this: it
69	scores only the first \texttt{early\_time\_steps} of each sampled
70	trajectory rollout against the bearing to a near-term path point,
71	with no distance or angle gating, so that MPPI is pushed to begin
72	turning toward the path immediately rather than waiting until deeper
73	into the curve. It is gated by an \texttt{active\_path\_points}
74	parameter so that it stops influencing the controller once the
75	vehicle has made genuine progress along the route, avoiding
76	interference with the stock critics' normal path-tracking behaviour
77	during straight segments. A later direction-awareness refinement
78	extended the critic to handle reversing and K-turn path segments
79	correctly, where a naive ``always turn toward the next point''
80	bearing calculation would otherwise fight the vehicle's intended
81	direction of travel.
82	
83	Building this plugin required matching \texttt{xtensor}/\texttt{xsimd}
84	compile definitions exactly against Nav2's own MPPI controller build
85	-- a mismatch here does not produce a compile-time error, but a
86	silent ABI incompatibility that crashes the navigation container on
87	the first control cycle that touches vectorised critic math, making
88	it a notably unforgiving class of build-configuration bug to diagnose
89	from its symptom alone.
90	
91	Listing~\ref{lst:early-commit-critic} shows the critic's
92	\texttt{score()} method in full. It computes the bearing from each
93	sampled trajectory's own starting position to a near-term path target
94	(\texttt{offset\_from\_furthest} points ahead of the furthest point
95	the robot has already reached), then, for only the first
96	\texttt{early\_time\_steps} of that trajectory, accumulates the
97	angular distance between the trajectory's actual yaw and that
98	bearing -- scoring every sampled rollout independently, not just the
99	robot's single current pose. The early return on
100	\texttt{active\_path\_points} is what confines this to the start of a
101	path, and the \texttt{forward\_preference\_}-gated minimum of the
102	forward- and reverse-bearing angular distances is the
103	direction-awareness refinement mentioned above, letting a trajectory
104	be scored against whichever of the bearing or its reverse it is
105	actually closer to, rather than penalising a legitimate reversing
106	manoeuvre.

9	This chapter documents the development of the simulation-side
10	navigation stack that Chapters~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge}
11	through~\ref{ch:nav-integration} later migrate onto physical
12	hardware. The stack went through two full drive-architecture
13	migrations before reaching the form used for hardware bridging
14	(Sections~\ref{sec:baseline-manual}--\ref{sec:second-migration}), and
15	along the way surfaced a middleware-level parser defect
16	(Section~\ref{sec:colon-bug}) and a four-part vehicle-dynamics bug
17	pattern that recurred, largely unchanged, across two sibling packages
18	(Section~\ref{sec:not-moving-bug}). The chapter closes with a
19	behaviour-tree fix specific to Ackermann-steered vehicles
20	(Section~\ref{sec:bt-fix}).
21	
22	\section{Baseline: Manual Bicycle-Model Inversion}
23	\label{sec:baseline-manual}
24	
25	The navigation stack's earliest drive architecture used two
26	independent \texttt{ros2\_control} \texttt{JointGroup} controllers
27	(\texttt{drive\_controller} for wheel velocity,
28	\texttt{steering\_controller} for hub position) driven by a
29	hand-written node, \texttt{cmd\_vel\_to\_drive.py}, that manually
30	inverted the bicycle-model relationship of
31	Equations~\ref{eq:bicycle-x}--\ref{eq:bicycle-theta} to compute a
32	per-wheel velocity and steering-hub angle from an incoming
33	\texttt{geometry\_msgs/Twist} on \texttt{/cmd\_vel}. This
34	architecture worked, but duplicated the Ackermann inverse-kinematics
35	logic that a purpose-built controller would otherwise provide, and --
36	more importantly for a navigation stack meant to reach physical
37	hardware -- could not support Nav2's recovery behaviours that require
38	reversing, since the manual node had no reverse-driving logic of its
39	own.
40	
41	\section{First Migration: \texttt{ros2\_control}'s \texttt{AckermannSteeringController}}
42	\label{sec:first-migration}
43	
44	The first architectural migration replaced both custom
45	\texttt{JointGroup} controllers and \texttt{cmd\_vel\_to\_drive.py}
46	with \texttt{ros2\_control}'s own
47	\texttt{ackermann\_steering\_controller} / \texttt{AckermannSteeringController}
48	plugin, configured via \texttt{config/qcar\_controllers.yaml}. This
49	controller performs the same Ackermann inverse kinematics internally,
50	and additionally publishes its own wheel-based odometry -- which
51	this project deliberately adopted as the vehicle's \texttt{/odom}
52	source in place of Gazebo's \texttt{gazebo\_ros\_p3d} ground-truth
53	plugin (the latter was kept running, but remapped to
54	\texttt{/ground\_truth/odom} for debugging comparison only). This was
55	a considered choice, not a default: ground-truth odometry is
56	trivially available in simulation but has no equivalent on the
57	physical robot, whose odometry can only ever be a real,
58	drift-prone dead-reckoning estimate (Section~\ref{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}).
59	Developing and tuning the navigation stack against the same
60	\emph{kind} of odometry it would have to work with on hardware, from
61	the start, avoided deferring that discrepancy to the eventual
62	hardware migration.
63	
64	Because Nav2, AMCL, and \texttt{bt\_navigator} all hard-code an
65	expectation that odometry arrives on \texttt{/odom} and driving
66	commands are consumed from \texttt{/cmd\_vel}, and the new controller
67	instead exposes these under its own namespaced topics
68	(\texttt{\textasciitilde/odometry}, \texttt{\textasciitilde/reference\_unstamped}),
69	two \texttt{topic\_tools relay} nodes were added to the launch files
70	to bridge the naming mismatch without modifying Nav2 itself.
71	
72	\subsection{A Wheel-Axis Bug Exposed by the Migration}
73	\label{sec:wheel-axis-bug}
74	
75	The migration exposed a latent URDF defect that had been silently
76	compensated for by the old manual node and had therefore never
77	produced a visible symptom before. The rear-left drive wheel joint
78	(\texttt{base\_wheelrl\_joint}) had its \texttt{<origin>} yawed by
79	\ang{180} for correct mesh mirroring, but retained the \emph{same}
80	\texttt{<axis>} direction as the corresponding right-side joint --
81	which, combined with the yaw flip, silently inverted that wheel's
82	effective rotation sense relative to a positive commanded velocity.
83	The old \texttt{cmd\_vel\_to\_drive.py} had manually compensated for
84	this by commanding \texttt{[-speed, +speed]} to the left/right wheel
85	velocities respectively; the new controller had no such
86	compensation, and computed wheel odometry that did not match the
87	vehicle's real motion direction. The fix -- correcting the
88	\texttt{<axis>} declaration on the affected joint directly, rather
89	than perpetuating a sign-flip workaround downstream in every
90	consumer of that joint -- illustrates a pattern worth stating
91	explicitly: a URDF geometry defect that is silently absorbed by one
92	consumer's ad hoc compensation will resurface, often with a confusing
93	symptom, the moment that consumer is replaced.
94	
95	Listing~\ref{lst:wheel-axis} shows the two rear drive-wheel joints as
96	they stand in the corrected URDF: the left joint's mesh-mirroring yaw
97	(\texttt{rpy="0 0 3.14"}) is paired with a negated \texttt{<axis>} so
98	that a positive commanded wheel velocity turns both wheels in the
99	same physical sense, whereas the right joint needs no such
100	compensation since its origin carries no mirroring rotation.
101

104	    <parent link="base" />
105	    <child link="wheelrl" />
106	    <origin rpy="0 0 3.14" xyz="-0.12765 0.05610 0.03338" />

This makes `listings` use our definitions instead of ever touching the broken bundled files — same comment/string highlighting, just without pulling in the buggy code. No changes needed to any of the 14 individual code listings themselves.

\chapter{Appendix}
\label{ch:appendix}

% Guideline 4.2.7: separate title page from the main body (the
% \chapter above + \appendix numbering in main.tex provides this),
% own numbering (A1, A1.1, ... below), source code referenced but not
% printed in full.

\section{QCar Hardware Safety Limits}
\label{app:safety-limits}

Table~\ref{tab:app-safety-limits} lists the documented hardware
safety limits enforced throughout every piece of drive-control code
presented in this thesis (Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}).

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{QCar documented hardware safety limits.}
  \label{tab:app-safety-limits}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
    \toprule
    Limit & Value \\
    \midrule
    PWM duty cycle saturation & $\pm 30\%$ \\
    PWM duty cycle rate limit & $100\%/\mathrm{s}$ \\
    Battery auto-shutdown & below \SI{10.0}{\volt} \\
    Battery low-voltage warning & below \SI{10.5}{\volt} \\
    Steering command range & $\pm 0.5$~rad \\
    Max.\ physical steering angle & $\pm 0.5236$~rad ($\pm\ang{30}$) \\
    Overcurrent protection & \SI{5}{\ampere}/\SI{8}{\second}, \SI{10}{\ampere}/\SI{2}{\second}, or \SI{15}{\ampere}/\SI{0.5}{\second} $\to$ forced Neutral mode \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Diagnostic and Calibration Tooling Reference}
\label{app:tooling}

Table~\ref{tab:app-tooling} summarises the diagnostic scripts
developed and used throughout Chapters~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge}
--\ref{ch:nav-integration}. Full source is maintained in the
project's version-controlled repository (electronic submission), not
reproduced here in full per the guideline's recommendation that
programming code be supplied on the electronic data carrier rather
than printed.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Diagnostic and calibration scripts referenced in this thesis.}
  \label{tab:app-tooling}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}p{3.8cm}p{9.5cm}@{}}
    \toprule
    Script & Purpose \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{calibrate\_steering.py} & Static steering-trim calibration aid (Section~\ref{sec:steering-trim}) \\
    \texttt{drive\_and\_log.py} & Drive to a target distance at a fixed speed, log \texttt{/odom} to CSV, exit automatically (Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration}) \\
    \texttt{check\_stop\_latency.py} & As above, plus reports cruise velocity and stop latency directly (Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery}) \\
    \texttt{monitor\_goal\_timing.py} & Instruments one Nav2 goal end-to-end: goal-sent, real/displayed motion start and stop, goal-reached (Section~\ref{sec:monitor-goal-timing}) \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Real-Hardware Bring-Up Command Reference}
\label{app:commands}

For reproducibility, the full bring-up sequence used throughout
Chapters~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge}--\ref{ch:nav-integration} is
reproduced here.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash,caption={Real-hardware bring-up (two QCar terminals, two development-PC terminals).}]
# --- On the QCar (two terminals) ---
sudo -E env PYTHONPATH=/home/nvidia/Documents/python \
    python3 ~/ros2_amit/src/onboard_bridge/qcar_bridge.py

PYTHONPATH=/home/nvidia/Documents/python \
    python3 ~/ros2_amit/src/onboard_bridge/qcar_lidar_node.py

# --- On the development PC ---
ros2 run qcar_updated qcar_relay_node.py --ros-args \
    -p qcar_ip:=<qcar-ip> -p qcar_clock_offset:=<measured-offset>

ros2 launch qcar_updated qcar_nav2.launch.py launch_sim:=false
\end{lstlisting}

\texttt{qcar\_clock\_offset} (Section~\ref{sec:clock-offset}) and the
QCar's DHCP-assigned IP address both drift session to session and
must be re-measured / re-checked before each bring-up, not reused
from a previous session.

\subsection{Safe Shutdown Sequence}
\label{app:shutdown}

The shutdown sequence established in Section~\ref{sec:safe-shutdown}
must be followed in order, using \texttt{SIGINT} (Ctrl-C) exclusively:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Stop \texttt{qcar\_relay\_node.py} (development PC).
  \item Stop the visualisation launch process group (development PC).
  \item Stop \texttt{qcar\_lidar\_node.py} (QCar).
  \item Stop \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} (QCar, requires \texttt{sudo}).
  \item Confirm both TCP ports are released on the QCar:
    \texttt{sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E "5555|5556"} should print nothing.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Source Code and Data Availability}
\label{app:source-availability}

% TODO: fill in with however your faculty/supervisor wants source
% code and raw data supplied - e.g. a git repository URL, or "supplied
% on the accompanying electronic data carrier as specified in
% guideline Section 4.2.7". If any data is restricted (see guideline
% Section 4.1.2), note that here instead.

The complete, version-controlled source code for the simulation
stack (Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}), the hardware bridge
(Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge}), and all calibration/diagnostic
tooling (Appendix~\ref{app:tooling}) referenced throughout this
thesis is supplied on the accompanying electronic data carrier /
repository: \texttt{TODO: path or URL}.

% Abstract - guideline 4.1.6: optional, 120-150 words recommended,
% describes the problem and results, with key words.

\chapter*{Abstract}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Abstract}

% TODO: this draft is ~150 words; trim or adjust once the final
% results chapter numbers are locked in, and re-check the word count.

Autonomous mobile robots are typically developed in simulation before
being deployed on physical hardware, yet the transfer from simulator to
real platform routinely exposes gaps that no amount of simulated
testing predicts. This thesis documents the end-to-end migration of a
ROS~2 Nav2 navigation stack for an Ackermann-steered vehicle, the
Quanser QCar, from a Gazebo simulation onto the physical robot. A
protocol-level incompatibility between the robot's onboard ROS~2
Dashing distribution and a ROS~2 Humble development host made native
ROS~2 communication impossible, motivating a custom TCP/JSON bridge.
The thesis presents the bridge's design, the calibration of an
open-loop throttle model against real actuator behaviour, and the
root-cause diagnosis of a hardware abstraction-layer buffering defect
that had been misattributed to physical drivetrain coasting. The
resulting system is validated through closed-loop Nav2 goal-reaching
tests on the physical vehicle, and the observed sim-to-real
discrepancies are quantified and discussed.

\vspace{0.5cm}
\noindent\textbf{Key words:} ROS~2, Nav2, Ackermann steering, sim-to-real
transfer, Gazebo, Model Predictive Path Integral control, mobile robot
navigation, Quanser QCar

import re, glob

def count_cols(spec):
    # remove @{...} and p{...}/m{...}/b{...} column-sep/width groups first
    spec = re.sub(r'@\{[^}]*\}', '', spec)
    spec = re.sub(r'[pmb]\{[^}]*\}', 'X', spec)
    return len(re.findall(r'[lcrX]', spec))

for f in glob.glob('chapters/*.tex') + glob.glob('appendix/*.tex') + glob.glob('frontmatter/*.tex'):
    lines = open(f).read().splitlines()
    i = 0
    while i < len(lines):
        m = re.search(r'\\begin\{(tabular|longtable)\}\{(.*)\}\s*$', lines[i])
        if m:
            env = m.group(1)
            spec = m.group(2)
            ncols = count_cols(spec)
            start = i
            i += 1
            while i < len(lines) and f'\\end{{{env}}}' not in lines[i]:
                line = lines[i]
                stripped = line.strip()
                if stripped and not stripped.startswith('%') and any(k in stripped for k in ['\\\\']) and '\\toprule' not in stripped and '\\midrule' not in stripped and '\\bottomrule' not in stripped:
                    # count top-level & (ignore inside \text{} etc - good enough heuristic)
                    namps = line.count('&')
                    if namps > 0 and namps + 1 != ncols:
                        print(f"{f}:{i+1}: declared {ncols} cols but row has {namps+1} cells -> {stripped[:80]}")
                i += 1
        i += 1
EOF

\chapter{Results}
\label{ch:results}

This chapter consolidates the quantitative results produced across
Chapters~\ref{ch:sim-stack}--\ref{ch:nav-integration} and evaluates
them directly against the target state defined in
Section~\ref{sec:problem-statement}: a Nav2 navigation stack that
reaches goal poses reliably on the physical QCar, with the
sim-to-real gap identified and, where practical, corrected. Results
are presented here without re-opening their diagnosis; interpretation
and generalisation are deferred to Chapter~\ref{ch:summary}.

\section{Actuator Calibration Accuracy}
\label{sec:results-throttle}

Table~\ref{tab:results-throttle-summary} restates the throttle
calibration validation of Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration}
alongside the uncalibrated baseline it replaced.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Commanded-versus-real cruise speed, before and after calibration.}
  \label{tab:results-throttle-summary}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
    \toprule
    Commanded speed & Baseline ratio (uncalibrated $\text{THROTTLE\_GAIN}=1/3$) & Calibrated ratio (Eq.~\ref{eq:throttle-calibration}) \\
    \midrule
    \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} & $\approx$2.6--2.7 & 1.05 \\
    \SI{0.4}{\meter\per\second} & -- (not separately measured) & 1.05 \\
    \SI{0.5}{\meter\per\second} & -- (not separately measured) & 1.00 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

The commanded-to-real speed ratio was reduced from
$\approx$2.6--2.7$\times$ to within 5\% across the
\SIrange{0.3}{0.5}{\meter\per\second} range validated. Below
$\approx$\SI{0.25}{\meter\per\second}, both the calibrated and
uncalibrated mappings are unreliable in an open-loop sense, since the
vehicle's static-friction deadband (Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery})
sits in that range independently of gain calibration; commanding
\SI{0.2}{\meter\per\second} moved the vehicle in only some trials.

\section{Stop-Distance and Latency}
\label{sec:results-stop-distance}

Table~\ref{tab:results-stop-distance} restates the
\texttt{readMode=0} fix's effect (Section~\ref{sec:readmode-validation})
across all five tested conditions, alongside the residual physical
explanation for what remains.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Stop-latency and extra-distance results, before and after the \texttt{readMode=0} fix.}
  \label{tab:results-stop-distance}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
    \toprule
    Test condition & Stiction delay & Extra distance & Stop latency \\
    & (before $\to$ after) & (before $\to$ after) & (before $\to$ after) \\
    \midrule

    \SI{2}{\meter} @ \SI{0.5}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.14}{0.116}{\second} & \SIrange{0.923}{0.154}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.55}{0.550}{\second} \\

decay predicts exactly 50\%), rather than indicating any further

\section{Sim-versus-Real Overshoot}
\label{sec:results-sim-vs-real}

Table~\ref{tab:results-sim-vs-real} restates the sim-versus-real
comparison of Section~\ref{sec:sim-vs-real}. Because this comparison
was run \emph{before} both the throttle calibration
(Section~\ref{sec:throttle-calibration}) and the buffering-defect fix

    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Navigation Goal-Reaching}
\label{sec:results-goal-reaching}

Closed-loop \texttt{navigate\_to\_pose} goals requiring both straight
driving and real turning were completed successfully on the physical
QCar on multiple occasions across this project, confirmed both by
\texttt{bt\_navigator}'s own \texttt{Goal succeeded} status and, in
the final validation of Section~\ref{sec:final-validation}, by the
operator's direct observation that localisation tracked the vehicle's
real motion closely throughout the goal, rather than exhibiting the
map-shift artefact of Section~\ref{sec:display-lag}. The one
navigation timing measurement available (Table~\ref{tab:display-lag})
was taken under the pre-\texttt{readMode=0} bridge configuration and
should be read as an upper bound on the true post-fix pipeline
latency and stop-coast behaviour during a live goal, not as the final
figure, per the caveat in Section~\ref{sec:display-lag-interpretation}.

\section{Applicability of the Results}
\label{sec:results-applicability}

\subsection{Beyond This Specific QCar Unit}
\label{sec:applicability-unit}

The throttle deadband/gain values (Equation~\ref{eq:throttle-calibration})
and the steering-trim value (Section~\ref{sec:steering-trim}) are
per-unit calibration constants, expected to differ, potentially
substantially, on a different physical QCar chassis, or even on
this same chassis under different tyre wear, floor surface, or
battery charge conditions -- the calibration explicitly found this
floor to drift within a single session (Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery}).
The \emph{method} used to find them -- an empirical fixed-duty sweep
under real load, rather than an analytically derived or single-point
gain estimate -- is expected to transfer directly to any similarly
actuated small-scale ground vehicle, independent of the specific
numeric result.

\subsection{Beyond the QCar Platform}
\label{sec:applicability-platform}

The \texttt{readMode} buffering defect (Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug})
is specific to the Quanser HAL's task-based I/O mode, but the general
failure class it represents -- a background acquisition task started
at object-construction time, with a read-consumption rate that
happens to match its production rate closely enough that a
start-up-gap backlog never drains -- is a generic ring-buffer hazard
that is not specific to this vendor's library, and is worth checking
for in any hardware abstraction layer offering a buffered or
task-based I/O mode as an alternative to immediate/polled reads,
particularly where the buffer is initialised eagerly rather than on
first read. The diagnostic principle that resolved it -- when an
internally self-consistent software abstraction (here, the
\texttt{Odometry} class) produces a value that contradicts direct
physical observation, verify the abstraction's own \emph{input}, not
only its internal consistency -- is a general debugging principle,
not specific to this project at all.

\subsection{Beyond Navigation}
\label{sec:applicability-domain}

The active-braking safety incident (Section~\ref{sec:active-braking})
and its resolution generalise directly to any reactive
feedback-control design intended for direct hardware deployment on a
system with confirmed actuator lag or inertia, regardless of
application domain: this project's standing rule -- trace new
reactive control logic through by hand for an overshoot scenario, or
validate it in simulation, before it reaches a physical actuator --
is a general control-engineering caution reinforced, not discovered,
by this project's own experience.

1	\chapter{System Identification and Calibration}
2	\label{ch:calibration}
3	
4	% TODO: this is the thesis's strongest evidentiary chapter - consider
5	% pulling the six-point sweep and the readMode before/after table into
6	% actual plotted figures (velocity-vs-time traces) rather than tables

10	This chapter documents the longest and most consequential
11	investigation of the project: a real-hardware symptom in which the
12	vehicle, commanded to travel a fixed distance and then stop,
13	consistently travelled substantially further -- in the worst observed
14	case, roughly three times as far -- before actually coming to rest.
15	What began as a search for a physical explanation (drivetrain
16	coasting) ended in the discovery of a stale-data artefact in the
17	vendor hardware abstraction layer described in
18	Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}, with the true physical residual
19	turning out to be small once that artefact was removed. The chapter
20	also documents a control-design attempt that was tested on physical
21	hardware without adequate prior validation and produced a genuine,
22	dangerous oscillation -- included here in full because it is as
23	methodologically important as the investigation's eventual successful
24	resolution.
25	
26	\section{Problem Statement}
27	\label{sec:stop-distance-problem}
28	
29	With the bridge of Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge} operational, a
30	simple closed-loop test was used throughout this investigation: drive
31	the vehicle at a fixed commanded speed toward a target distance,
32	using odometry to detect when the target is crossed, and stop.
33	Repeated trials showed the vehicle travelling substantially further
34	than the commanded target before settling, with the overshoot
35	growing, not shrinking, across repeated sessions under otherwise
36	similar conditions -- an early indication that the effect was
37	systematic and reproducible rather than simple measurement noise.
38	
39	\section{Ruling Out Simpler Explanations}
40	\label{sec:ruled-out}
41	
42	Several plausible causes were tested directly and eliminated before
43	the investigation's eventual resolution:
44	
45	\begin{itemize}
46	  \item \textbf{AMCL/localisation.} The original suspect. Investigating
47	    it produced one genuine, separately valid fix -- raising AMCL's
48	    \texttt{recovery\_alpha\_fast}/\texttt{recovery\_alpha\_slow} from
49	    \texttt{0.0} to \texttt{0.1}/\texttt{0.001}, since a value of
50	    \texttt{0.0} allows the particle filter to freeze permanently once
51	    it (incorrectly) converges to zero uncertainty under real sensor
52	    noise, a failure mode that a clean simulation environment does not
53	    expose. This fix was kept, but does not explain the stop-distance
54	    symptom, which persisted after it was applied.
55	  \item \textbf{Command-delivery delay.} Measured directly on the
56	    QCar's own local clock (eliminating any network-latency
57	    contribution) at approximately \SI{0.2}{\second} from decision to
58	    applied throttle -- normal, and not large enough to explain
59	    metre-scale overshoot at the tested speeds.
60	  \item \textbf{A backlog of stale \texttt{/cmd\_vel} commands.}
61	    Hypothesised as queuing behind a blocking socket \texttt{send}
62	    call in the relay's single-threaded executor. Two increasingly
63	    careful fixes were built and deployed -- a staleness timestamp
64	    check, then a full non-blocking sender-thread architecture -- and
65	    both were tested directly on hardware. \textbf{Neither made any
66	    measurable difference}, ruling this out as the cause.
67	  \item \textbf{Logging/print buffering artefacts.} The timing of
68	    QCar-local debug samples during the ``coast'' period was a steady
69	    \SIrange{20}{35}{\milli\second} throughout, not a rapid burst
70	    consistent with a draining backlog -- ruled out.
71	\end{itemize}
72	
73	\section{Active Braking: A Control-Design Attempt and a Safety Incident}
74	\label{sec:active-braking}
75	
76	With the above ruled out, the leading hypothesis shifted to genuine
77	drivetrain (motor and gearbox) rotational inertia keeping the wheels
78	turning for a period after commanded throttle reached zero -- a
79	physically plausible mechanism, and one apparently consistent with
80	QCar-local encoder readings that showed real velocity persisting for
81	several seconds after a stop was commanded.
82	
83	A corrective control law was implemented directly in
84	\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}: a reverse-throttle brake pulse proportional
85	to the residual measured velocity, intended to actively cancel the
86	coasting motion. \textbf{This was deployed directly to physical
87	hardware without first being traced through by hand or tested in
88	simulation.} On its first test, it produced a genuine, dangerous
89	oscillation: the vehicle lurched forward and backward repeatedly,
90	reaching \SI{-0.88}{\meter\per\second} in reverse and still
91	accelerating, and had to be stopped manually via an SSH-issued kill
92	command mid-test. The root cause, in hindsight, is a textbook control
93	failure mode: a continuous proportional reaction to \emph{any}
94	nonzero residual velocity, including reverse velocity, with no
95	deadband and no explicit disarm condition, means every correction's
96	own overshoot looks to the controller like a fresh error requiring
97	correction -- an undamped hunting loop with no mechanism to settle.
98	
99	Since both attempts were reverted, no implementation of this control
100	law survives in the repository to quote directly; Listing~\ref{lst:active-braking-comment}
101	instead reproduces the comment left in its place in
102	\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}, at the site the code once occupied -- the
103	project's own permanent record of what was tried, why it failed, and
104	why it must not be blindly re-attempted.
105	
106	\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Comment documenting the rejected active-braking design, left in place of the reverted code (\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}).},label={lst:active-braking-comment}]
107	# Tried active braking (brief reverse-throttle pulse proportional to
108	# residual speed when a stop is commanded) to counter drivetrain coast -
109	# REJECTED, not just untuned. It's a proportional loop on velocity sign
110	# with no deadband and one-cycle-stale (~20ms) feedback: if the pulse
111	# overshoots past zero into real reverse motion, the next cycle reads a
112	# negative v and "corrects" with a forward push, which can itself
113	# overshoot - a genuine undamped hunting oscillation, not a bad gain
114	# value. Confirmed on hardware (twice - it was reverted once already
115	# before this comment, then re-tried and reproduced the same result):
116	# car visibly lurched forward/back repeatedly and fast, had to be
117	# killed manually. Do not re-add this without a real deadband/
118	# hysteresis or a one-shot (non-continuous) brake pulse design -
119	# retuning BRAKE_GAIN alone will not fix it.
120	\end{lstlisting}
121	
122	\paragraph{A minimal model of why this design cannot be stable.}
123	The instability the comment above describes can be shown formally
124	with a deliberately simplified discrete-time model that keeps only
125	the mechanism responsible, not the full nonlinear vehicle dynamics.
126	Let $v_k$ be the residual measured velocity at control cycle $k$, and
127	let the brake law command a throttle proportional to that residual
128	with gain $K$: $u_k = -K v_k$. If the vehicle's velocity responds to
129	one cycle's throttle command with an effective per-cycle gain $a$
130	(lumping motor response, control period, and vehicle mass into a
131	single constant, and ignoring natural friction/drag for this minimal
132	model), the resulting closed-loop update is
133	
134	\begin{equation}
135	  v_{k+1} = v_k + a\,u_k = v_k(1 - aK).
136	  \label{eq:brake-instability}
137	\end{equation}
138	
139	This is a first-order linear recurrence, and its behaviour is
140	governed entirely by the magnitude of $(1 - aK)$: the residual
141	velocity decays toward zero only if $|1 - aK| < 1$, i.e.\
142	$0 < aK < 2$; it oscillates in sign every cycle if $aK > 1$; and,
143	critically, that oscillation \emph{grows} in magnitude, without
144	bound, whenever $aK > 2$, since each successive $v_k$ is then
145	multiplied by a factor more negative than $-1$. This single
146	inequality is the formal statement of exactly what the source comment
147	describes qualitatively -- a correction that overshoots past zero
148	into real reverse motion, prompting a next-cycle correction in the
149	opposite direction that itself overshoots by more -- and it shows
150	directly why \emph{no} amount of retuning $K$ alone guarantees safety
151	here: $a$ (the vehicle's true, real per-cycle response to a given
152	throttle command) was never independently measured before this
153	control law was deployed, so there was no way to have verified
154	$aK < 2$ in advance from the gain value alone. A one-shot design
155	avoids re-arming after the first correction, but Equation~\ref{eq:brake-instability}'s
156	single-step overshoot condition does not require re-arming to
157	manifest -- if the very first correction alone satisfies $aK > 2$, it
158	already produces a reverse velocity larger in magnitude than the
159	original residual it was meant to cancel, which is consistent with
160	the one-shot retest reproducing the same oscillation rather than
161	being protected by its disarm condition. This is precisely the kind
162	of hand-traceable instability check Section~\ref{sec:methodology-overview}'s
163	standing rule asks for \emph{before} hardware deployment, not after.
164	
165	A revised, ``one-shot'' design was implemented -- braking fires
166	exactly once per drive-to-stop transition and permanently disarms the
167	instant measured velocity crosses zero, rather than re-arming from
168	residual drift -- and \textbf{reproduced the same oscillation on
169	retest}. Given the repeated safety failure, this control approach was
170	abandoned entirely rather than iterated on further. Both modified
171	files were reverted to their exact pre-investigation state, verified
172	byte-identical to the known-good version by hash comparison, with the
173	failure documented directly in a source-code comment so that it is
174	not blindly re-attempted in a future session.
175	
176	This incident is the clearest instance in this project of the general
177	principle stated in Section~\ref{sec:methodology-overview}: a
178	reactive feedback controller acting on a live sensor reading, on a
179	system already confirmed to have real actuator lag and inertia,
180	should be traced through by hand for an overshoot scenario -- or
181	tested in simulation first -- before it is ever sent to physical
182	hardware. ``The control theory seems sound'' was not, on its own,
183	sufficient justification here, and this project treats that as a
184	standing rule for any future reactive control logic on this
185	platform, not merely a lesson learned in retrospect.
186	
187	\section{Sim-versus-Real Comparison}
188	\label{sec:sim-vs-real}
189	
190	Following a methodology suggested by the author's academic
191	supervisor, the identical closed-loop stop-distance test (drive $N$
192	metres at a fixed speed, stop the instant odometry crosses the
193	target) was reproduced in both the physical robot and the Gazebo
194	simulation of Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}, using the same launch stack
195	with only the drive target switched from simulated to real hardware.
196	
197	A six-point sweep across three target distances
198	(\SIlist{1.0;1.5;2.0}{\meter}) and three commanded speeds
199	(\SIlist{0.20;0.25;0.30}{\meter\per\second}) found real
200	hardware overshoot in the range \SIrange{0.58}{2.12}{\meter} across
201	two sessions roughly one hour apart, with \emph{every} tested
202	condition worse in the second session by a broadly consistent margin
203	-- evidence of real, reproducible drift (plausibly battery voltage or
204	floor/tyre condition) rather than measurement noise. The matched
205	simulation sweep, over the same six conditions, showed overshoot of
206	only \SIrange{0.044}{0.067}{\meter} -- \SIrange{10}{30}{}$\times$
207	smaller, and only weakly sensitive to speed, in contrast to the real
208	hardware overshoot, which scaled roughly with the cube of speed. A
209	dedicated, isolated comparison at \SI{2}{\meter} /
210	\SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} sharpened this further: the simulated
211	vehicle settled at \SI{2.067}{\meter} (an extra \SI{0.067}{\meter}),
212	while the real vehicle settled at \SI{3.91}{\meter} (an extra
213	\SI{1.90}{\meter}) -- a $\sim$28$\times$ difference for an identical
214	software command. This result strongly supports a real-hardware-specific
215	controller/dynamics cause rather than something inherent to the
216	stop-command approach itself, and directly motivated the calibration
217	work in the remainder of this chapter.
218	
219	\section{Throttle Calibration}
220	\label{sec:throttle-calibration}
221	
222	\subsection{The Uncalibrated Gain Hypothesis}
223	\label{sec:throttle-gain-hypothesis}
224	
225	\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}'s mapping from \texttt{cmd\_vel}'s
226	\texttt{linear.x} (in \si{\meter\per\second}) to the HAL's PWM duty
227	cycle had, since early in the project, used a placeholder gain
228	(\texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN = 1/3}), explicitly documented in its own
229	source comment as uncalibrated. Direct measurement from the sweep
230	data above confirmed this mattered: commanding
231	\SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} produced a real, QCar-local
232	encoder-measured cruise velocity averaging
233	$\approx$\SI{0.8}{\meter\per\second} -- roughly $2.6$--$2.7\times$ the
234	commanded speed, consistent across two independent measurements.
235	Since coasting distance from momentum scales with the square of
236	velocity, this alone predicts roughly a $6.9\times$ larger coast
237	distance than a genuine \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} stop would
238	produce -- a substantial fraction of the sim-vs-real gap found above,
239	and a reminder that the sim-vs-real comparison in
240	Section~\ref{sec:sim-vs-real} was not, at that point, comparing truly
241	matched real speeds.
242	
243	\subsection{First Calibration Attempt: A Deadband Discovered, Then Reverted}
244	\label{sec:deadband-discovery}
245	
246	A dedicated measurement tool, \texttt{check\_stop\_latency.py}, was
247	built to measure cruise velocity and stop latency in a single run. An
248	initial correction -- lowering \texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN} by dividing by
249	the previously measured $2.67\times$ ratio -- was deployed to
250	hardware and immediately surfaced a second, independent, hard
251	non-linearity: at the old gain, a commanded \SI{0.25}{\meter\per\second}
252	($\sim$8\% duty) sat completely motionless for
253	$\approx$\SI{2.1}{\second} before suddenly breaking static friction
254	and moving, while \SIlist{0.20;0.15}{\meter\per\second}
255	($\sim$6.7\%/5\% duty) never moved at all across
256	\SIrange{8}{10}{\second} of commanding. This static-friction deadband
257	is a genuine physical property of the vehicle, not a linear gain
258	error, and it interacts badly with a naive linear-gain correction: the
259	lowered gain restored accurate cruise-speed tracking at higher
260	commanded speeds, but pushed the duty cycle for normal teleoperation
261	speeds below the deadband threshold entirely, making the vehicle stop
262	responding to real driving commands. The gain correction was reverted
263	the same day to restore usable teleoperation.
264	
265	\paragraph{This is a different friction phenomenon from Section~\ref{sec:friction-theory}'s.}
266	It is worth being precise about which friction is responsible here,
267	since this thesis discusses two physically distinct friction
268	phenomena under similar language. Section~\ref{sec:friction-theory}'s
269	Coulomb tyre-ground friction (the simulation's \texttt{mu1}/\texttt{mu2})
270	governs whether a spinning wheel's rotation converts into forward
271	chassis thrust at all, and is essentially instantaneous -- it has no
272	notion of a wheel being ``stuck.'' The deadband characterised here is
273	a different phenomenon internal to the real drivetrain itself (motor
274	brushes, gearbox mesh, bearing seats): \emph{static} friction (often
275	called stiction) resists the onset of relative motion between two
276	surfaces up to some breakaway force threshold, while \emph{kinetic}
277	friction, which applies once motion has actually begun, is often
278	measurably lower than that static threshold for the same
279	surface pair. A commanded duty cycle below the static threshold
280	produces zero motion no matter how long it is held, since the applied
281	torque never exceeds the force needed to break static friction in the
282	first place; once duty is raised just past that threshold, the
283	\emph{lower} kinetic friction then applies to an already-moving
284	system, so the same duty cycle that only barely broke static friction
285	can accelerate substantially further than expected once moving -- the
286	stick-slip signature Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration} identifies
287	directly in the duty-sweep data (Table~\ref{tab:duty-sweep}'s
288	\texttt{0.085} row, which \emph{runs away} rather than settling,
289	despite that same duty needing no help at all breaking away from a
290	standstill).
291	
292	This reframes the calibration problem: gain and deadband are not
293	independent. Any solution must jointly (a) track commanded speed
294	accurately at normal operating speeds and (b) keep every one of those
295	same commands above the static-friction threshold -- which a single
296	linear multiplier applied to the whole range cannot do, since scaling
297	the gain down to fix (a) simultaneously worsens (b) for exactly the
298	commands that were already only barely clearing the threshold.
299

304	rather than extrapolating a linear gain from one or two data points,
305	\texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN} was forced to zero and a dedicated,
306	lighter-weight tool (\texttt{drive\_and\_log.py}) was used to sweep
307	fixed PWM duty values directly, with the vehicle on the ground under
308	real load throughout. Table~\ref{tab:duty-sweep} summarises the
