402	\subsection{A Stray-Process False Positive}
403	\label{sec:stray-process}
404	
405	While iterating on this calibration, a separate, purely diagnostic
406	false alarm is worth recording as a general debugging caution. A
407	prior \texttt{check\_stop\_latency.py} test process, left running in
408	the background rather than exiting automatically once its measurement
409	completed, continued publishing \texttt{linear.x=0.0} on
410	\texttt{/cmd\_vel} at 20\,Hz, silently racing against a separately
411	launched teleoperation node publishing on the same topic. The
412	resulting symptom -- the vehicle briefly registering a throttle
413	command and then immediately reverting to zero within one control
414	cycle -- looked exactly like a gain, deadband, or logic bug, and was
415	initially investigated as one. ROS~2 does not warn about multiple
416	publishers on the same topic; it simply interleaves messages, with
417	whichever publisher's message arrives last in a given control cycle
418	taking effect. The actual fix was operational, not code: kill the
419	stray process. This project subsequently adopted two standing
420	practices as a result -- checking \texttt{pgrep -af} for
421	topic-related script names (or \texttt{ros2 topic info /cmd\_vel
422	--verbose} for publisher count) before deep-diving into a control-logic
423	theory whenever real behaviour contradicts an issued command, and
424	designing one-shot diagnostic nodes to exit automatically once their
425	measurement is complete rather than spinning indefinitely.
426	
427	\section{The Hardware Abstraction-Layer Buffering Defect}
428	\label{sec:readmode-bug}
429	
430	Even after the throttle calibration of
431	Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration} made commanded and real cruise
432	speed match closely, the original stop-distance symptom this chapter
433	opened with -- a multi-second coast after a stop command, with
434	substantial extra distance -- was still present, apparently
435	unaffected by the gain fix. This section documents how that residual
436	was ultimately traced to a defect in the vendor hardware abstraction
437	layer itself, not the vehicle's physical dynamics at all -- the
438	project's single most significant finding, both for its magnitude and
439	for the methodological lesson in how long an incorrect physical
440	explanation can survive against evidence that, in hindsight, directly
441	contradicted it.
442	
443	\subsection{An Initial, Incomplete Diagnosis}
444	\label{sec:coast-shape-analysis}
445	
446	A closer look at the raw coast-phase velocity trace from one of the
447	calibration validation runs (\SI{0.5}{\meter\per\second}) showed the
448	coast was \emph{not} a smooth decay: velocity remained essentially
449	flat -- if anything slightly \emph{elevated} relative to the
450	preceding cruise average -- for the first $\approx$\SI{2.0}{\second}
451	after ``stop'' was commanded, and only crashed sharply to zero in the
452	final \SIrange{0.3}{0.4}{\second}. This flat-plateau-then-cliff shape
453	is inconsistent with passive drivetrain momentum/friction coasting
454	(which predicts continuous, gradual decay starting immediately once
455	power is cut), and instead resembles the real motor continuing to be
456	\emph{actively driven} for roughly two seconds after the stop command
457	was issued. A review of the Quanser HAL documentation found no
458	mention of any drive-motor ramp, filter, or time constant that would
459	explain a two-second lag of this kind -- only a separate, documented
460	\SI{0.16}{\second} steering-servo time constant, unrelated to the
461	drive motor. This shifted the leading hypothesis toward a
462	command-delivery lag in the project's own bridge software rather than
463	physical coasting -- a genuine change of theory, captured here because
464	it turned out to still be one step short of the actual cause. A
465	diagnostic instrumentation pass (logging commanded velocity, the
466	bridge's own internally-ramped throttle value, and real encoder
467	velocity together, all on the QCar's local clock to eliminate network
468	timing) was begun but interrupted by the test vehicle's battery
469	running out mid-session, and resumed in a later session on a charged
470	battery.
471	
472	\subsection{Disproving Two Hypotheses, and the Argument That Found the Real Cause}
473	\label{sec:readmode-discovery}
474	
475	The resumed diagnostic trace showed the bridge's own internal
476	throttle value reaching exactly zero within \SI{52}{\milli\second} of
477	the stop command, while the encoder-reported velocity stayed elevated
478	for roughly two more seconds -- which correctly ruled out the
479	project's own throttle-ramping logic as the cause, but, as understood
480	in hindsight, did \emph{not} actually rule out a measurement or
481	reporting defect in the encoder-velocity reading itself, since the two
482	values are produced through entirely separate code paths. This
483	distinction was missed on the first pass through the data.
484	
485	At this point the person operating the vehicle directly and
486	repeatedly disputed the emerging conclusion: teleoperating the QCar
487	from a genuine standstill, the vehicle visibly starts and stops moving
488	\emph{instantly} in response to a command, flatly contradicting the
489	$\approx$2-second delay the automated test script was measuring. Two
490	further hypotheses were tested and disproven with direct hardware data
491	before the actual cause was found:
492	
493	\begin{itemize}
494	  \item \textbf{Duty-magnitude dependence} (a higher commanded speed
495	    produces more torque and a faster stiction breakaway): tested at
496	    \SI{0.7}{\meter\per\second} (duty 0.087, well above the normally
497	    tested \SIrange{0.052}{0.075} range) -- the stiction delay was
498	    still \SI{2.092}{\second}, statistically identical to the
499	    low-speed tests. Disproven.
500	  \item \textbf{``\texttt{v} is a stale reading, not real motion.''}
501	    Disproven by the structure of the \texttt{Odometry} class's own
502	    update code: the reported velocity \texttt{v} and the accumulated
503	    position \texttt{x} are computed from the exact same
504	    \texttt{distance} variable within the same loop iteration, so if
505	    \texttt{v} were falsely indicating motion, the accumulated position
506	    would have to freeze at the same instant -- and it demonstrably did
507	    not; distance kept growing smoothly and matched the vehicle's real,
508	    physically measured settled position.
509	\end{itemize}
510	
511	The argument that ultimately identified the true cause was not a
512	further measurement, but a piece of physical reasoning offered
513	directly by the vehicle's operator: \emph{an encoder is a real-time
514	sensor -- it cannot have a built-in two-second lag by itself.} This
515	was correct, and it redirected the investigation to a question the
516	prior analysis had not actually asked: not whether the
517	\texttt{Odometry} class was internally self-consistent (it was), but
518	whether the value it was consuming as its own input -- the raw
519	\texttt{car.motorEncoder[0]} read -- was itself stale before the
520	\texttt{Odometry} class ever saw it. This prompted reading the vendor
521	HAL's own Python source directly, rather than continuing to reason
522	about it indirectly from documentation or from the \texttt{Odometry}
523	class's own behaviour.
524	
525	\subsection{Root Cause: a Ring-Buffer I/O Mode}
526	\label{sec:readmode-rootcause}
527	
528	The root cause, found in the vendor HAL source
529	(\texttt{pal/products/qcar.py}) on the QCar itself, is exactly the
530	\texttt{readMode} distinction introduced in
531	Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}. \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} constructed
532	its \texttt{QCar} object with \texttt{readMode=1} (task-based I/O),
533	which starts a background acquisition task \emph{at object
534	construction time} -- before the bridge's listening TCP socket has
535	even opened -- filling a ring buffer of \texttt{frequency}$\times 2$
536	samples (at this project's \SI{50}{\hertz} read rate, exactly 100
537	samples, i.e.\ \SI{2.0}{\second}) with overwrite-on-overflow
538	behaviour. Each call to \texttt{car.read()} dequeues one buffered
539	sample. Because \texttt{car.read()} is not actually called until a
540	relay client connects -- which can take many seconds after the bridge
541	process starts -- the buffer fills and cycles during that idle gap.
542	Once reads begin at a consumption rate matching the production rate
543	exactly, the read stream is permanently stuck approximately 100
544	samples (\SI{2.0}{\second}) behind real time, because the backlog
545	never has an opportunity to drain.
546	
547	\paragraph{Formalising the lag: why it is exactly the buffer depth, forever.}
548	Let the background task write into the ring buffer at a fixed
549	production index $p$, incrementing by one every $1/f$ seconds
550	($f = \SI{50}{\hertz}$ here), and let \texttt{car.read()} calls
551	advance a separate consumption index $c$, each call returning the
552	sample at position $c \bmod B$ (buffer capacity $B = 100$) and then
553	incrementing $c$. Production begins at object construction, $t = 0$;
554	consumption begins only once a relay client connects, at
555	$t = T_{\text{idle}}$. During $[0, T_{\text{idle}}]$, $p$ advances
556	alone (production with no consumption at all), so by the time
557	consumption starts, $p = f \cdot T_{\text{idle}}$ while $c = 0$ --
558	a gap of $f \cdot T_{\text{idle}}$ samples between them. If
559	$T_{\text{idle}} > B/f$ (true here, since a relay connecting takes
560	several seconds while $B/f = \SI{2.0}{\second}$), the overwrite-on-overflow
561	buffer has already wrapped around at least once by
562	$T_{\text{idle}}$, meaning the oldest sample still available to read
563	is not the very first one produced, but the one produced exactly
564	$B$ samples before $p$'s current value -- so the very first
565	\texttt{car.read()} call, at $t = T_{\text{idle}}$, necessarily
566	returns a sample captured at $t = T_{\text{idle}} - B/f$, a lag of
567	exactly $B/f = \SI{2.0}{\second}$, regardless of how much larger than
568	$B/f$ the idle gap $T_{\text{idle}}$ itself was. From that point
569	onward, because production and consumption both advance at the
570	identical rate $f$ (one \texttt{car.read()} per control-loop cycle,
571	matching the background task's own sampling rate), the gap between
572	$p$ and $c$ -- and therefore the lag between ``now'' and whatever
573	sample is being read -- stays fixed at exactly $B$ samples
574	indefinitely: neither index ever gains on the other, so the backlog
575	that accumulated during the idle gap is carried forward forever
576	rather than draining over time. This is precisely why the lag proved
577	so exactly reproducible (always $B/f = \SI{2.0}{\second}$, never more
578	and never less, regardless of how long the QCar sat idle before a
579	relay connected) and why it never improved on its own the longer the
580	system ran.
581	
582	This single mechanism explains every property of the symptom observed
583	across this entire chapter: the near-exact \SI{2.0}{\second} to
584	\SI{2.1}{\second} figure (matching the buffer's mathematically exact
585	2.0\,s capacity), its remarkable stability across sessions, vehicle
586	speeds, and physical conditions (a fixed buffer depth is indifferent
587	to any of these), and its symmetric appearance on both the start side
588	(the ``stiction delay'' of Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery}) and
589	the stop side (the ``coast''), since both are read through the same
590	buffered path.
591	
592	\textbf{Fix:} \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} now constructs the \texttt{QCar}
593	object as shown in Listing~\ref{lst:readmode-fix} -- immediate I/O,
594	reading current hardware state directly with no background task or
595	buffer involved at all.
596	
597	\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={The one-line HAL construction change that fixed the buffering defect (\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}).},label={lst:readmode-fix}]
598	# readMode=0 (immediate I/O) - was 1 (task-based I/O), which runs a
599	# background acquisition task into a 100-sample ring buffer
600	# (frequency*2) from the moment this object is constructed,
601	# independent of when car.read() actually starts being called. Since
602	# this object is created before the listening socket even opens, and
603	# car.read() isn't called until a relay connects, the buffer fills and
604	# starts overwriting during that gap - once reads begin at the matched
605	# 50Hz rate, they get permanently stuck ~100 samples (~2.0s) behind
606	# real-time, since the backlog never drains. Immediate I/O reads
607	# current hardware state directly, no task/buffer involved.
608	car = QCar(readMode=0, frequency=READ_RATE)
609	\end{lstlisting}
610	
611	\subsection{Validation}
612	\label{sec:readmode-validation}
613	
614	The full calibration test suite from Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration}
615	was re-run in its entirety on a freshly charged battery, with the
616	duty formula (Equation~\ref{eq:throttle-calibration}) unchanged, to
617	isolate the effect of this single fix. Table~\ref{tab:readmode-fix}
618	presents the results.
619	
620	\begin{table}[htbp]
621	  \centering
622	  \caption{Effect of the \texttt{readMode=0} fix on stiction delay, extra distance, and stop latency.}
623	  \label{tab:readmode-fix}
624	  \begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
625	    \toprule
626	    Test & Stiction delay & Extra distance & Stop latency \\
627	    & (before $\to$ after) & (before $\to$ after) & (before $\to$ after) \\
628	    \midrule
629	    \SI{2}{\meter} @ \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.09}{0.117}{\second} & \SIrange{0.520}{0.114}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.37}{0.598}{\second} \\
630	    \SI{2}{\meter} @ \SI{0.4}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.14}{0.001}{\second} & \SIrange{0.790}{0.114}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.40}{0.501}{\second} \\
631	    \SI{2}{\meter} @ \SI{0.5}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.14}{0.116}{\second} & \SIrange{0.923}{0.154}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.55}{0.550}{\second} \\
632	    \SI{1}{\meter} @ \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.14}{0.120}{\second} & \SIrange{0.641}{0.118}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.44}{0.572}{\second} \\
633	    \SI{3}{\meter} @ \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.08}{0.088}{\second} & \SIrange{0.583}{0.104}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.35}{0.509}{\second} \\
634	    \bottomrule
635	  \end{tabular}
636	\end{table}
637	
638	Stiction delay collapses to \SIrange{0.001}{0.12}{\second} -- an
639	essentially instantaneous breakaway response, matching direct
640	observation of the vehicle. Extra distance becomes small and roughly
641	constant, $\approx$\SIrange{0.10}{0.15}{\meter}, regardless of speed
642	or target distance, rather than scaling with cruise speed as
643	previously found -- confirming that the earlier ``extra distance
644	scales with speed'' relationship was itself an artefact of a
645	fixed-\emph{duration} buffering delay applied to different real
646	velocities, not a genuine vehicle property.
647	
648	The small residual that remains after this fix is real, and is fully
649	accounted for by ordinary physics rather than being a further open
650	mystery: dividing extra distance by stop latency (an implied average
651	coast velocity) yields \SIrange{54}{61}{\percent} of cruise velocity
652	in four of the five tests -- consistent with an ordinary, roughly
653	linear velocity decay to zero over the stop-latency window (a
654	perfectly linear decay predicts exactly 50\%). The one outlier
655	(\SI{2}{\meter} @ \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second}, 108\%) is attributable
656	to a data-analysis artefact (the ``cruise average'' window for that
657	specific test likely had not reached a true steady state, now that
658	the run has much less runway once stiction delay is near-instant)
659	rather than a physical inconsistency.
660	
661	\SI{0.2}{\meter\per\second} remains genuinely unreliable even after
662	this fix, sometimes failing to move the vehicle at all -- this is the
663	real, independent static-friction deadband characterised in
664	Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery}, and is unrelated to the
665	buffering defect resolved here.
666	
667	\section{Summary}
668	\label{sec:calibration-summary}
669	
670	This chapter's investigation began with a symptom -- travelling
671	roughly three times the commanded stop distance -- that had at least
672	three superficially plausible explanations (localisation error,
673	command-delivery delay, and physical drivetrain coasting), and ended
674	by identifying two genuinely independent, compounding causes: an
675	uncalibrated, non-linear throttle-to-speed mapping
676	(Section~\ref{sec:throttle-calibration}), and a fixed-duration
677	sensor-read buffering artefact in the vendor hardware abstraction
678	layer (Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug}) that had, for a period of this
679	project, been reasonably but incorrectly attributed to genuine
680	vehicle physics. Neither cause was found by reasoning from
681	documentation or first principles alone; both required direct,
682	targeted measurement on the physical robot, and the second was found
683	only after a direct physical argument from the vehicle's operator
684	prompted reading the vendor's own source code rather than continuing
685	to trust an internally self-consistent, but incompletely verified,
686	software abstraction. Chapter~\ref{ch:nav-integration} builds on this
687	chapter's calibrated, buffering-free bridge to bring up and validate
688	full closed-loop Nav2 navigation on the physical vehicle.
689

\chapter{System Identification and Calibration}
\label{ch:calibration}

% TODO: this is the thesis's strongest evidentiary chapter - consider
% pulling the six-point sweep and the readMode before/after table into
% actual plotted figures (velocity-vs-time traces) rather than tables
% only, if you still have the raw CSV/rosbag data from the sessions
% referenced here.

This chapter documents the longest and most consequential
investigation of the project: a real-hardware symptom in which the
vehicle, commanded to travel a fixed distance and then stop,
consistently travelled substantially further -- in the worst observed
case, roughly three times as far -- before actually coming to rest.
What began as a search for a physical explanation (drivetrain
coasting) ended in the discovery of a stale-data artefact in the
vendor hardware abstraction layer described in
Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}, with the true physical residual
turning out to be small once that artefact was removed. The chapter
also documents a control-design attempt that was tested on physical
hardware without adequate prior validation and produced a genuine,
dangerous oscillation -- included here in full because it is as
methodologically important as the investigation's eventual successful
resolution.

\section{Problem Statement}
\label{sec:stop-distance-problem}

With the bridge of Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge} operational, a
simple closed-loop test was used throughout this investigation: drive
the vehicle at a fixed commanded speed toward a target distance,
using odometry to detect when the target is crossed, and stop.
Repeated trials showed the vehicle travelling substantially further
than the commanded target before settling, with the overshoot
growing, not shrinking, across repeated sessions under otherwise
similar conditions -- an early indication that the effect was
systematic and reproducible rather than simple measurement noise.

\section{Ruling Out Simpler Explanations}
\label{sec:ruled-out}

Several plausible causes were tested directly and eliminated before
the investigation's eventual resolution:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{AMCL/localisation.} The original suspect. Investigating
    it produced one genuine, separately valid fix -- raising AMCL's
    \texttt{recovery\_alpha\_fast}/\texttt{recovery\_alpha\_slow} from
    \texttt{0.0} to \texttt{0.1}/\texttt{0.001}, since a value of
    \texttt{0.0} allows the particle filter to freeze permanently once
    it (incorrectly) converges to zero uncertainty under real sensor
    noise, a failure mode that a clean simulation environment does not
    expose. This fix was kept, but does not explain the stop-distance
    symptom, which persisted after it was applied.
  \item \textbf{Command-delivery delay.} Measured directly on the
    QCar's own local clock (eliminating any network-latency
    contribution) at approximately \SI{0.2}{\second} from decision to
    applied throttle -- normal, and not large enough to explain
    metre-scale overshoot at the tested speeds.
  \item \textbf{A backlog of stale \texttt{/cmd\_vel} commands.}
    Hypothesised as queuing behind a blocking socket \texttt{send}
    call in the relay's single-threaded executor. Two increasingly
    careful fixes were built and deployed -- a staleness timestamp
    check, then a full non-blocking sender-thread architecture -- and
    both were tested directly on hardware. \textbf{Neither made any
    measurable difference}, ruling this out as the cause.
  \item \textbf{Logging/print buffering artefacts.} The timing of
    QCar-local debug samples during the ``coast'' period was a steady
    \SIrange{20}{35}{\milli\second} throughout, not a rapid burst
    consistent with a draining backlog -- ruled out.
\end{itemize}

\section{Active Braking: A Control-Design Attempt and a Safety Incident}
\label{sec:active-braking}

With the above ruled out, the leading hypothesis shifted to genuine
drivetrain (motor and gearbox) rotational inertia keeping the wheels
turning for a period after commanded throttle reached zero -- a
physically plausible mechanism, and one apparently consistent with
QCar-local encoder readings that showed real velocity persisting for
several seconds after a stop was commanded.

A corrective control law was implemented directly in
\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}: a reverse-throttle brake pulse proportional
to the residual measured velocity, intended to actively cancel the
coasting motion. \textbf{This was deployed directly to physical
hardware without first being traced through by hand or tested in
simulation.} On its first test, it produced a genuine, dangerous
oscillation: the vehicle lurched forward and backward repeatedly,
reaching \SI{-0.88}{\meter\per\second} in reverse and still
accelerating, and had to be stopped manually via an SSH-issued kill
command mid-test. The root cause, in hindsight, is a textbook control
failure mode: a continuous proportional reaction to \emph{any}
nonzero residual velocity, including reverse velocity, with no
deadband and no explicit disarm condition, means every correction's
own overshoot looks to the controller like a fresh error requiring
correction -- an undamped hunting loop with no mechanism to settle.

Since both attempts were reverted, no implementation of this control
law survives in the repository to quote directly; Listing~\ref{lst:active-braking-comment}
instead reproduces the comment left in its place in
\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}, at the site the code once occupied -- the
project's own permanent record of what was tried, why it failed, and
why it must not be blindly re-attempted.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Comment documenting the rejected active-braking design, left in place of the reverted code (\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}).},label={lst:active-braking-comment}]
# Tried active braking (brief reverse-throttle pulse proportional to
# residual speed when a stop is commanded) to counter drivetrain coast -
# REJECTED, not just untuned. It's a proportional loop on velocity sign
# with no deadband and one-cycle-stale (~20ms) feedback: if the pulse
# overshoots past zero into real reverse motion, the next cycle reads a
# negative v and "corrects" with a forward push, which can itself
# overshoot - a genuine undamped hunting oscillation, not a bad gain
# value. Confirmed on hardware (twice - it was reverted once already
# before this comment, then re-tried and reproduced the same result):
# car visibly lurched forward/back repeatedly and fast, had to be
# killed manually. Do not re-add this without a real deadband/
# hysteresis or a one-shot (non-continuous) brake pulse design -
# retuning BRAKE_GAIN alone will not fix it.
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{A minimal model of why this design cannot be stable.}
The instability the comment above describes can be shown formally
with a deliberately simplified discrete-time model that keeps only
the mechanism responsible, not the full nonlinear vehicle dynamics.
Let $v_k$ be the residual measured velocity at control cycle $k$, and
let the brake law command a throttle proportional to that residual
with gain $K$: $u_k = -K v_k$. If the vehicle's velocity responds to
one cycle's throttle command with an effective per-cycle gain $a$
(lumping motor response, control period, and vehicle mass into a
single constant, and ignoring natural friction/drag for this minimal
model), the resulting closed-loop update is

\begin{equation}
  v_{k+1} = v_k + a\,u_k = v_k(1 - aK).
  \label{eq:brake-instability}
\end{equation}

This is a first-order linear recurrence, and its behaviour is
governed entirely by the magnitude of $(1 - aK)$: the residual
velocity decays toward zero only if $|1 - aK| < 1$, i.e.\
$0 < aK < 2$; it oscillates in sign every cycle if $aK > 1$; and,
critically, that oscillation \emph{grows} in magnitude, without
bound, whenever $aK > 2$, since each successive $v_k$ is then
multiplied by a factor more negative than $-1$. This single
inequality is the formal statement of exactly what the source comment
describes qualitatively -- a correction that overshoots past zero
into real reverse motion, prompting a next-cycle correction in the
opposite direction that itself overshoots by more -- and it shows
directly why \emph{no} amount of retuning $K$ alone guarantees safety
here: $a$ (the vehicle's true, real per-cycle response to a given
throttle command) was never independently measured before this
control law was deployed, so there was no way to have verified
$aK < 2$ in advance from the gain value alone. A one-shot design
avoids re-arming after the first correction, but Equation~\ref{eq:brake-instability}'s
single-step overshoot condition does not require re-arming to
manifest -- if the very first correction alone satisfies $aK > 2$, it
already produces a reverse velocity larger in magnitude than the
original residual it was meant to cancel, which is consistent with
the one-shot retest reproducing the same oscillation rather than
being protected by its disarm condition. This is precisely the kind
of hand-traceable instability check Section~\ref{sec:methodology-overview}'s
standing rule asks for \emph{before} hardware deployment, not after.

A revised, ``one-shot'' design was implemented -- braking fires
exactly once per drive-to-stop transition and permanently disarms the
instant measured velocity crosses zero, rather than re-arming from
residual drift -- and \textbf{reproduced the same oscillation on
retest}. Given the repeated safety failure, this control approach was
abandoned entirely rather than iterated on further. Both modified
files were reverted to their exact pre-investigation state, verified
byte-identical to the known-good version by hash comparison, with the
failure documented directly in a source-code comment so that it is
not blindly re-attempted in a future session.

This incident is the clearest instance in this project of the general
principle stated in Section~\ref{sec:methodology-overview}: a
reactive feedback controller acting on a live sensor reading, on a
system already confirmed to have real actuator lag and inertia,
should be traced through by hand for an overshoot scenario -- or
tested in simulation first -- before it is ever sent to physical
hardware. ``The control theory seems sound'' was not, on its own,
sufficient justification here, and this project treats that as a
standing rule for any future reactive control logic on this
platform, not merely a lesson learned in retrospect.

\section{Sim-versus-Real Comparison}
\label{sec:sim-vs-real}

Following a methodology suggested by the author's academic
supervisor, the identical closed-loop stop-distance test (drive $N$
metres at a fixed speed, stop the instant odometry crosses the
target) was reproduced in both the physical robot and the Gazebo
simulation of Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}, using the same launch stack
with only the drive target switched from simulated to real hardware.

A six-point sweep across three target distances
(\SIlist{1.0;1.5;2.0}{\meter}) and three commanded speeds
(\SIlist{0.20;0.25;0.30}{\meter\per\second}) found real
hardware overshoot in the range \SIrange{0.58}{2.12}{\meter} across
two sessions roughly one hour apart, with \emph{every} tested
condition worse in the second session by a broadly consistent margin
-- evidence of real, reproducible drift (plausibly battery voltage or
floor/tyre condition) rather than measurement noise. The matched
simulation sweep, over the same six conditions, showed overshoot of
only \SIrange{0.044}{0.067}{\meter} -- \SIrange{10}{30}{}$\times$
smaller, and only weakly sensitive to speed, in contrast to the real
hardware overshoot, which scaled roughly with the cube of speed. A
dedicated, isolated comparison at \SI{2}{\meter} /
\SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} sharpened this further: the simulated
vehicle settled at \SI{2.067}{\meter} (an extra \SI{0.067}{\meter}),
while the real vehicle settled at \SI{3.91}{\meter} (an extra
\SI{1.90}{\meter}) -- a $\sim$28$\times$ difference for an identical
software command. This result strongly supports a real-hardware-specific
controller/dynamics cause rather than something inherent to the
stop-command approach itself, and directly motivated the calibration
work in the remainder of this chapter.

\section{Throttle Calibration}
\label{sec:throttle-calibration}

\subsection{The Uncalibrated Gain Hypothesis}
\label{sec:throttle-gain-hypothesis}

\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}'s mapping from \texttt{cmd\_vel}'s
\texttt{linear.x} (in \si{\meter\per\second}) to the HAL's PWM duty
cycle had, since early in the project, used a placeholder gain
(\texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN = 1/3}), explicitly documented in its own
source comment as uncalibrated. Direct measurement from the sweep
data above confirmed this mattered: commanding
\SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} produced a real, QCar-local
encoder-measured cruise velocity averaging
$\approx$\SI{0.8}{\meter\per\second} -- roughly $2.6$--$2.7\times$ the
commanded speed, consistent across two independent measurements.
Since coasting distance from momentum scales with the square of
velocity, this alone predicts roughly a $6.9\times$ larger coast
distance than a genuine \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} stop would
produce -- a substantial fraction of the sim-vs-real gap found above,
and a reminder that the sim-vs-real comparison in
Section~\ref{sec:sim-vs-real} was not, at that point, comparing truly
matched real speeds.

\subsection{First Calibration Attempt: A Deadband Discovered, Then Reverted}
\label{sec:deadband-discovery}

A dedicated measurement tool, \texttt{check\_stop\_latency.py}, was
built to measure cruise velocity and stop latency in a single run. An
initial correction -- lowering \texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN} by dividing by
the previously measured $2.67\times$ ratio -- was deployed to
hardware and immediately surfaced a second, independent, hard
non-linearity: at the old gain, a commanded \SI{0.25}{\meter\per\second}
($\sim$8\% duty) sat completely motionless for
$\approx$\SI{2.1}{\second} before suddenly breaking static friction
and moving, while \SIlist{0.20;0.15}{\meter\per\second}
($\sim$6.7\%/5\% duty) never moved at all across
\SIrange{8}{10}{\second} of commanding. This static-friction deadband
is a genuine physical property of the vehicle, not a linear gain
error, and it interacts badly with a naive linear-gain correction: the
lowered gain restored accurate cruise-speed tracking at higher
commanded speeds, but pushed the duty cycle for normal teleoperation
speeds below the deadband threshold entirely, making the vehicle stop
responding to real driving commands. The gain correction was reverted
the same day to restore usable teleoperation.

\paragraph{This is a different friction phenomenon from Section~\ref{sec:friction-theory}'s.}
It is worth being precise about which friction is responsible here,
since this thesis discusses two physically distinct friction
phenomena under similar language. Section~\ref{sec:friction-theory}'s
Coulomb tyre-ground friction (the simulation's \texttt{mu1}/\texttt{mu2})
governs whether a spinning wheel's rotation converts into forward
chassis thrust at all, and is essentially instantaneous -- it has no
notion of a wheel being ``stuck.'' The deadband characterised here is
a different phenomenon internal to the real drivetrain itself (motor
brushes, gearbox mesh, bearing seats): \emph{static} friction (often
called stiction) resists the onset of relative motion between two
surfaces up to some breakaway force threshold, while \emph{kinetic}
friction, which applies once motion has actually begun, is often
measurably lower than that static threshold for the same
surface pair. A commanded duty cycle below the static threshold
produces zero motion no matter how long it is held, since the applied
torque never exceeds the force needed to break static friction in the
first place; once duty is raised just past that threshold, the
\emph{lower} kinetic friction then applies to an already-moving
system, so the same duty cycle that only barely broke static friction
can accelerate substantially further than expected once moving -- the
stick-slip signature Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration} identifies
directly in the duty-sweep data (Table~\ref{tab:duty-sweep}'s
\texttt{0.085} row, which \emph{runs away} rather than settling,
despite that same duty needing no help at all breaking away from a
standstill).

This reframes the calibration problem: gain and deadband are not
independent. Any solution must jointly (a) track commanded speed
accurately at normal operating speeds and (b) keep every one of those
same commands above the static-friction threshold -- which a single
linear multiplier applied to the whole range cannot do, since scaling
the gain down to fix (a) simultaneously worsens (b) for exactly the
commands that were already only barely clearing the threshold.

\subsection{Final Calibration: An Empirical Duty Sweep}
\label{sec:final-calibration}

Given that finding, the calibration approach was reframed entirely:
rather than extrapolating a linear gain from one or two data points,
\texttt{THROTTLE\_GAIN} was forced to zero and a dedicated,
lighter-weight tool (\texttt{drive\_and\_log.py}) was used to sweep
fixed PWM duty values directly, with the vehicle on the ground under
real load throughout. Table~\ref{tab:duty-sweep} summarises the
resulting duty-response curve.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Fixed-duty sweep results (QCar on the ground, real load).}
  \label{tab:duty-sweep}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
    \toprule
    Duty & Observed behaviour \\
    \midrule
    0.050 & No motion at all (confirmed twice, up to \SI{27.5}{\second} of commanding) \\
    0.060--0.061 & Reliable breakaway after $\approx$\SIrange{2.0}{2.1}{\second} of stiction delay; settles to a stable, non-runaway cruise of $\approx$\SIrange{0.24}{0.33}{\meter\per\second} \\
    0.065 & $\approx$\SI{0.39}{\meter\per\second} \\
    0.085 & \textbf{Runs away} to $\approx$\SIrange{0.85}{0.9}{\meter\per\second} -- a stick-slip signature (static friction exceeds kinetic friction, so once moving, the same duty produces far more net accelerating force), confirmed by watching the full velocity trace climb continuously rather than plateau \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

A caution surfaced during this sweep and worth recording explicitly:
the motion/no-motion threshold near duty $\approx 0.06$ is genuinely
noisy, not a hard deterministic cut-off -- a re-test with duty
adjusted by only $+0.0013$ (\texttt{0.0533} vs.\ \texttt{0.052})
flipped a command from ``27\,s of zero motion'' to reliably covering
the full target distance. This floor appears to drift somewhat both
within and across sessions (plausibly floor contact, resting wheel
position, temperature, or battery voltage), and no single threshold
measurement from this sweep should be treated as an exact, permanent
constant.

The deployed calibration combines a deadband floor with a linear gain
above it, fit from the duty=0.061/\SI{0.33}{\meter\per\second} and
duty=0.065/\SI{0.39}{\meter\per\second} points and validated
separately:

\begin{equation}
  \text{duty} = \text{THROTTLE\_DEADBAND} + \text{THROTTLE\_GAIN} \cdot |v_{\text{cmd}}|,\quad
  \text{THROTTLE\_DEADBAND} = 0.04,\ \text{THROTTLE\_GAIN} = 0.0667.
  \label{eq:throttle-calibration}
\end{equation}

Listing~\ref{lst:throttle-formula} shows Equation~\ref{eq:throttle-calibration}
as implemented in \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}'s control loop, together
with the rate limiter that caps how fast \texttt{current\_throttle}
(the value actually written to the HAL) may change per cycle -- a
separate safeguard from the deadband/gain calibration itself, present
throughout this chapter's testing to keep duty-cycle steps within the
documented \SI{100}{\percent\per\second} hardware limit
(Appendix~\ref{app:safety-limits}).

\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Duty-cycle command computation and rate limiting (\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}).},label={lst:throttle-formula}]
if abs(target_linear) < 1e-3:
    desired_throttle = 0.0
else:
    desired_throttle = math.copysign(
        THROTTLE_DEADBAND + THROTTLE_GAIN * abs(target_linear), target_linear)
desired_throttle = max(-THROTTLE_LIMIT, min(THROTTLE_LIMIT, desired_throttle))
max_step = THROTTLE_RATE_LIMIT * dt
delta = max(-max_step, min(max_step, desired_throttle - current_throttle))
current_throttle += delta
\end{lstlisting}

Table~\ref{tab:calibration-validation} presents the resulting
end-to-end validation across four commanded speeds, each from a
dedicated \SI{2}{\meter} drive-and-stop test with cruise velocity
measured directly from \texttt{/odom}.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Throttle calibration validation (Equation~\ref{eq:throttle-calibration}).}
  \label{tab:calibration-validation}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
    \toprule
    Commanded speed & Measured cruise speed & Ratio & Note \\
    \midrule
    \SI{0.2}{\meter\per\second} & unreliable ($\approx$0.24 or no motion) & -- & At the deadband edge \\
    \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} & \SI{0.31}{\meter\per\second} & 1.05 & \\
    \SI{0.4}{\meter\per\second} & \SI{0.42}{\meter\per\second} & 1.05 & \\
    \SI{0.5}{\meter\per\second} & \SI{0.50}{\meter\per\second} & 1.00 & \\

This is a substantial improvement over the original uncalibrated
gain's $2.6$--$2.7\times$ overshoot: commanded speeds of
\SIrange{0.3}{0.5}{\meter\per\second} now track within
$\approx$5\%. Below $\approx$\SIrange{0.25}{0.3}{\meter\per\second},
open-loop duty control against real floor/battery/temperature-dependent
friction is inherently unreliable -- this is treated as a hard
physical limit of the open-loop approach at the tested operating
conditions, not a remaining tuning gap; reliable sub-\SI{0.25}{\meter\per\second}
creep would require closed-loop velocity feedback from the encoder
rather than a fixed duty mapping.

\subsection{A Stray-Process False Positive}
\label{sec:stray-process}

While iterating on this calibration, a separate, purely diagnostic
false alarm is worth recording as a general debugging caution. A
prior \texttt{check\_stop\_latency.py} test process, left running in
the background rather than exiting automatically once its measurement
completed, continued publishing \texttt{linear.x=0.0} on
\texttt{/cmd\_vel} at 20\,Hz, silently racing against a separately
launched teleoperation node publishing on the same topic. The
resulting symptom -- the vehicle briefly registering a throttle
command and then immediately reverting to zero within one control
cycle -- looked exactly like a gain, deadband, or logic bug, and was
initially investigated as one. ROS~2 does not warn about multiple
publishers on the same topic; it simply interleaves messages, with
whichever publisher's message arrives last in a given control cycle
taking effect. The actual fix was operational, not code: kill the
stray process. This project subsequently adopted two standing
practices as a result -- checking \texttt{pgrep -af} for
topic-related script names (or \texttt{ros2 topic info /cmd\_vel
--verbose} for publisher count) before deep-diving into a control-logic
theory whenever real behaviour contradicts an issued command, and
designing one-shot diagnostic nodes to exit automatically once their
measurement is complete rather than spinning indefinitely.

\section{The Hardware Abstraction-Layer Buffering Defect}
\label{sec:readmode-bug}

Even after the throttle calibration of
Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration} made commanded and real cruise
speed match closely, the original stop-distance symptom this chapter
opened with -- a multi-second coast after a stop command, with
substantial extra distance -- was still present, apparently
unaffected by the gain fix. This section documents how that residual
was ultimately traced to a defect in the vendor hardware abstraction
layer itself, not the vehicle's physical dynamics at all -- the
project's single most significant finding, both for its magnitude and
for the methodological lesson in how long an incorrect physical
explanation can survive against evidence that, in hindsight, directly
contradicted it.

\subsection{An Initial, Incomplete Diagnosis}
\label{sec:coast-shape-analysis}

A closer look at the raw coast-phase velocity trace from one of the
calibration validation runs (\SI{0.5}{\meter\per\second}) showed the
coast was \emph{not} a smooth decay: velocity remained essentially
flat -- if anything slightly \emph{elevated} relative to the
preceding cruise average -- for the first $\approx$\SI{2.0}{\second}
after ``stop'' was commanded, and only crashed sharply to zero in the
final \SIrange{0.3}{0.4}{\second}. This flat-plateau-then-cliff shape
is inconsistent with passive drivetrain momentum/friction coasting
(which predicts continuous, gradual decay starting immediately once
power is cut), and instead resembles the real motor continuing to be
\emph{actively driven} for roughly two seconds after the stop command
was issued. A review of the Quanser HAL documentation found no
mention of any drive-motor ramp, filter, or time constant that would
explain a two-second lag of this kind -- only a separate, documented
\SI{0.16}{\second} steering-servo time constant, unrelated to the
drive motor. This shifted the leading hypothesis toward a
command-delivery lag in the project's own bridge software rather than
physical coasting -- a genuine change of theory, captured here because
it turned out to still be one step short of the actual cause. A
diagnostic instrumentation pass (logging commanded velocity, the
bridge's own internally-ramped throttle value, and real encoder
velocity together, all on the QCar's local clock to eliminate network
timing) was begun but interrupted by the test vehicle's battery
running out mid-session, and resumed in a later session on a charged
battery.

\subsection{Disproving Two Hypotheses, and the Argument That Found the Real Cause}
\label{sec:readmode-discovery}

The resumed diagnostic trace showed the bridge's own internal
throttle value reaching exactly zero within \SI{52}{\milli\second} of
the stop command, while the encoder-reported velocity stayed elevated
for roughly two more seconds -- which correctly ruled out the
project's own throttle-ramping logic as the cause, but, as understood
in hindsight, did \emph{not} actually rule out a measurement or
reporting defect in the encoder-velocity reading itself, since the two
values are produced through entirely separate code paths. This
distinction was missed on the first pass through the data.

At this point the person operating the vehicle directly and
repeatedly disputed the emerging conclusion: teleoperating the QCar
from a genuine standstill, the vehicle visibly starts and stops moving
\emph{instantly} in response to a command, flatly contradicting the
$\approx$2-second delay the automated test script was measuring. Two
further hypotheses were tested and disproven with direct hardware data
before the actual cause was found:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Duty-magnitude dependence} (a higher commanded speed
    produces more torque and a faster stiction breakaway): tested at
    \SI{0.7}{\meter\per\second} (duty 0.087, well above the normally
    tested \SIrange{0.052}{0.075} range) -- the stiction delay was
    still \SI{2.092}{\second}, statistically identical to the
    low-speed tests. Disproven.
  \item \textbf{``\texttt{v} is a stale reading, not real motion.''}
    Disproven by the structure of the \texttt{Odometry} class's own
    update code: the reported velocity \texttt{v} and the accumulated
    position \texttt{x} are computed from the exact same
    \texttt{distance} variable within the same loop iteration, so if
    \texttt{v} were falsely indicating motion, the accumulated position
    would have to freeze at the same instant -- and it demonstrably did
    not; distance kept growing smoothly and matched the vehicle's real,
    physically measured settled position.
\end{itemize}

The argument that ultimately identified the true cause was not a
further measurement, but a piece of physical reasoning offered
directly by the vehicle's operator: \emph{an encoder is a real-time
sensor -- it cannot have a built-in two-second lag by itself.} This
was correct, and it redirected the investigation to a question the
prior analysis had not actually asked: not whether the
\texttt{Odometry} class was internally self-consistent (it was), but
whether the value it was consuming as its own input -- the raw
\texttt{car.motorEncoder[0]} read -- was itself stale before the
\texttt{Odometry} class ever saw it. This prompted reading the vendor
HAL's own Python source directly, rather than continuing to reason
about it indirectly from documentation or from the \texttt{Odometry}
class's own behaviour.

\subsection{Root Cause: a Ring-Buffer I/O Mode}
\label{sec:readmode-rootcause}

The root cause, found in the vendor HAL source
(\texttt{pal/products/qcar.py}) on the QCar itself, is exactly the
\texttt{readMode} distinction introduced in
Section~\ref{sec:qcar-platform}. \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} constructed
its \texttt{QCar} object with \texttt{readMode=1} (task-based I/O),
which starts a background acquisition task \emph{at object
construction time} -- before the bridge's listening TCP socket has
even opened -- filling a ring buffer of \texttt{frequency}$\times 2$
samples (at this project's \SI{50}{\hertz} read rate, exactly 100
samples, i.e.\ \SI{2.0}{\second}) with overwrite-on-overflow
behaviour. Each call to \texttt{car.read()} dequeues one buffered
sample. Because \texttt{car.read()} is not actually called until a
relay client connects -- which can take many seconds after the bridge
process starts -- the buffer fills and cycles during that idle gap.
Once reads begin at a consumption rate matching the production rate
exactly, the read stream is permanently stuck approximately 100
samples (\SI{2.0}{\second}) behind real time, because the backlog
never has an opportunity to drain.

\paragraph{Formalising the lag: why it is exactly the buffer depth, forever.}
Let the background task write into the ring buffer at a fixed
production index $p$, incrementing by one every $1/f$ seconds
($f = \SI{50}{\hertz}$ here), and let \texttt{car.read()} calls
advance a separate consumption index $c$, each call returning the
sample at position $c \bmod B$ (buffer capacity $B = 100$) and then
incrementing $c$. Production begins at object construction, $t = 0$;
consumption begins only once a relay client connects, at
$t = T_{\text{idle}}$. During $[0, T_{\text{idle}}]$, $p$ advances
alone (production with no consumption at all), so by the time
consumption starts, $p = f \cdot T_{\text{idle}}$ while $c = 0$ --
a gap of $f \cdot T_{\text{idle}}$ samples between them. If
$T_{\text{idle}} > B/f$ (true here, since a relay connecting takes
several seconds while $B/f = \SI{2.0}{\second}$), the overwrite-on-overflow
buffer has already wrapped around at least once by
$T_{\text{idle}}$, meaning the oldest sample still available to read
is not the very first one produced, but the one produced exactly
$B$ samples before $p$'s current value -- so the very first
\texttt{car.read()} call, at $t = T_{\text{idle}}$, necessarily
returns a sample captured at $t = T_{\text{idle}} - B/f$, a lag of
exactly $B/f = \SI{2.0}{\second}$, regardless of how much larger than
$B/f$ the idle gap $T_{\text{idle}}$ itself was. From that point
onward, because production and consumption both advance at the
identical rate $f$ (one \texttt{car.read()} per control-loop cycle,
matching the background task's own sampling rate), the gap between
$p$ and $c$ -- and therefore the lag between ``now'' and whatever
sample is being read -- stays fixed at exactly $B$ samples
indefinitely: neither index ever gains on the other, so the backlog
that accumulated during the idle gap is carried forward forever
rather than draining over time. This is precisely why the lag proved
so exactly reproducible (always $B/f = \SI{2.0}{\second}$, never more
and never less, regardless of how long the QCar sat idle before a
relay connected) and why it never improved on its own the longer the
system ran.

This single mechanism explains every property of the symptom observed
across this entire chapter: the near-exact \SI{2.0}{\second} to
\SI{2.1}{\second} figure (matching the buffer's mathematically exact
2.0\,s capacity), its remarkable stability across sessions, vehicle
speeds, and physical conditions (a fixed buffer depth is indifferent
to any of these), and its symmetric appearance on both the start side
(the ``stiction delay'' of Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery}) and
the stop side (the ``coast''), since both are read through the same
buffered path.

\textbf{Fix:} \texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} now constructs the \texttt{QCar}
object as shown in Listing~\ref{lst:readmode-fix} -- immediate I/O,
reading current hardware state directly with no background task or
buffer involved at all.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={The one-line HAL construction change that fixed the buffering defect (\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}).},label={lst:readmode-fix}]
# readMode=0 (immediate I/O) - was 1 (task-based I/O), which runs a
# background acquisition task into a 100-sample ring buffer
# (frequency*2) from the moment this object is constructed,
# independent of when car.read() actually starts being called. Since
# this object is created before the listening socket even opens, and
# car.read() isn't called until a relay connects, the buffer fills and
# starts overwriting during that gap - once reads begin at the matched
# 50Hz rate, they get permanently stuck ~100 samples (~2.0s) behind
# real-time, since the backlog never drains. Immediate I/O reads
# current hardware state directly, no task/buffer involved.
car = QCar(readMode=0, frequency=READ_RATE)
\end{lstlisting}

\subsection{Validation}
\label{sec:readmode-validation}

The full calibration test suite from Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration}
was re-run in its entirety on a freshly charged battery, with the
duty formula (Equation~\ref{eq:throttle-calibration}) unchanged, to
isolate the effect of this single fix. Table~\ref{tab:readmode-fix}
presents the results.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Effect of the \texttt{readMode=0} fix on stiction delay, extra distance, and stop latency.}
  \label{tab:readmode-fix}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
    \toprule
    Test & Stiction delay & Extra distance & Stop latency \\
    & (before $\to$ after) & (before $\to$ after) & (before $\to$ after) \\
    \midrule
    \SI{2}{\meter} @ \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.09}{0.117}{\second} & \SIrange{0.520}{0.114}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.37}{0.598}{\second} \\
    \SI{2}{\meter} @ \SI{0.4}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.14}{0.001}{\second} & \SIrange{0.790}{0.114}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.40}{0.501}{\second} \\
    \SI{2}{\meter} @ \SI{0.5}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.14}{0.116}{\second} & \SIrange{0.923}{0.154}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.55}{0.550}{\second} \\
    \SI{1}{\meter} @ \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.14}{0.120}{\second} & \SIrange{0.641}{0.118}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.44}{0.572}{\second} \\
    \SI{3}{\meter} @ \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second} & \SIrange{2.08}{0.088}{\second} & \SIrange{0.583}{0.104}{\meter} & \SIrange{2.35}{0.509}{\second} \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Stiction delay collapses to \SIrange{0.001}{0.12}{\second} -- an
essentially instantaneous breakaway response, matching direct
observation of the vehicle. Extra distance becomes small and roughly
constant, $\approx$\SIrange{0.10}{0.15}{\meter}, regardless of speed
or target distance, rather than scaling with cruise speed as
previously found -- confirming that the earlier ``extra distance
scales with speed'' relationship was itself an artefact of a
fixed-\emph{duration} buffering delay applied to different real
velocities, not a genuine vehicle property.

The small residual that remains after this fix is real, and is fully
accounted for by ordinary physics rather than being a further open
mystery: dividing extra distance by stop latency (an implied average
coast velocity) yields \SIrange{54}{61}{\percent} of cruise velocity
in four of the five tests -- consistent with an ordinary, roughly
linear velocity decay to zero over the stop-latency window (a
perfectly linear decay predicts exactly 50\%). The one outlier
(\SI{2}{\meter} @ \SI{0.3}{\meter\per\second}, 108\%) is attributable
to a data-analysis artefact (the ``cruise average'' window for that
specific test likely had not reached a true steady state, now that
the run has much less runway once stiction delay is near-instant)
rather than a physical inconsistency.

\SI{0.2}{\meter\per\second} remains genuinely unreliable even after
this fix, sometimes failing to move the vehicle at all -- this is the
real, independent static-friction deadband characterised in
Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery}, and is unrelated to the
buffering defect resolved here.

\section{Summary}
\label{sec:calibration-summary}

This chapter's investigation began with a symptom -- travelling
roughly three times the commanded stop distance -- that had at least
three superficially plausible explanations (localisation error,
command-delivery delay, and physical drivetrain coasting), and ended
by identifying two genuinely independent, compounding causes: an
uncalibrated, non-linear throttle-to-speed mapping
(Section~\ref{sec:throttle-calibration}), and a fixed-duration
sensor-read buffering artefact in the vendor hardware abstraction
layer (Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug}) that had, for a period of this
project, been reasonably but incorrectly attributed to genuine
vehicle physics. Neither cause was found by reasoning from
documentation or first principles alone; both required direct,
targeted measurement on the physical robot, and the second was found
only after a direct physical argument from the vehicle's operator
prompted reading the vendor's own source code rather than continuing
to trust an internally self-consistent, but incompletely verified,
software abstraction. Chapter~\ref{ch:nav-integration} builds on this
chapter's calibrated, buffering-free bridge to bring up and validate
full closed-loop Nav2 navigation on the physical vehicle.

54	\section{Custom MPPI Critic: \texttt{EarlyCommitCritic}}
55	\label{sec:mppi-critic}
56	
57	Early navigation testing showed a specific weakness in the stock MPPI
58	critic set (Section~\ref{sec:nav2}) for this vehicle: the standard
59	path-following critics evaluate a sampled trajectory's alignment and
60	progress against the path as a whole, which can leave the controller
61	driving further into an approaching curve before it begins reacting
62	to it, rather than beginning the turn as early as physically sensible
63	-- a behaviour more forgiving for a differential-drive robot's tight
64	turning radius than for an Ackermann-steered vehicle with the
65	finite minimum turning radius of Table~\ref{tab:qcar-geometry}.
66	
67	A custom MPPI critic plugin, \texttt{EarlyCommitCritic}, was
68	developed and built into the navigation package to address this: it
69	scores only the first \texttt{early\_time\_steps} of each sampled
70	trajectory rollout against the bearing to a near-term path point,
71	with no distance or angle gating, so that MPPI is pushed to begin
72	turning toward the path immediately rather than waiting until deeper
73	into the curve. It is gated by an \texttt{active\_path\_points}
74	parameter so that it stops influencing the controller once the
75	vehicle has made genuine progress along the route, avoiding
76	interference with the stock critics' normal path-tracking behaviour
77	during straight segments. A later direction-awareness refinement
78	extended the critic to handle reversing and K-turn path segments
79	correctly, where a naive ``always turn toward the next point''
80	bearing calculation would otherwise fight the vehicle's intended
81	direction of travel.
82	
83	Building this plugin required matching \texttt{xtensor}/\texttt{xsimd}
84	compile definitions exactly against Nav2's own MPPI controller build
85	-- a mismatch here does not produce a compile-time error, but a
86	silent ABI incompatibility that crashes the navigation container on
87	the first control cycle that touches vectorised critic math, making
88	it a notably unforgiving class of build-configuration bug to diagnose
89	from its symptom alone.

92	\texttt{score()} method in full. It computes the bearing from each
93	sampled trajectory's own starting position to a near-term path target
94	(\texttt{offset\_from\_furthest} points ahead of the furthest point
95	the robot has already reached), then, for only the first
96	\texttt{early\_time\_steps} of that trajectory, accumulates the
97	angular distance between the trajectory's actual yaw and that
98	bearing -- scoring every sampled rollout independently, not just the
99	robot's single current pose. The early return on
100	\texttt{active\_path\_points} is what confines this to the start of a
101	path, and the \texttt{forward\_preference\_}-gated minimum of the
102	forward- and reverse-bearing angular distances is the
103	direction-awareness refinement mentioned above, letting a trajectory
104	be scored against whichever of the bearing or its reverse it is
105	actually closer to, rather than penalising a legitimate reversing
106	manoeuvre.

108	\begin{lstlisting}[language=C++,caption={\texttt{EarlyCommitCritic::score()} (\texttt{src/critics/early\_commit\_critic.cpp}).},label={lst:early-commit-critic}]
109	void EarlyCommitCritic::score(CriticData & data)
110	{

112	  utils::setPathFurthestPointIfNotSet(data);
113

115	  // real progress, let the normal path/goal critics take over.
116	  if (*data.furthest_reached_path_point >= active_path_points_) { return; }
117	
118	  const size_t path_size = data.path.x.shape(0) - 1;
119	  const size_t offseted_idx = std::min(
120	    *data.furthest_reached_path_point + offset_from_furthest_, path_size);
121	  const float target_x = data.path.x(offseted_idx);
122	  const float target_y = data.path.y(offseted_idx);
123	
124	  const size_t time_steps = data.trajectories.x.shape(1);
125	  const size_t early_steps = std::min(early_time_steps_, time_steps);
126	  if (early_steps == 0) { return; }
127	
128	  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> x0 = xt::view(data.trajectories.x, xt::all(), 0);
129	  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> y0 = xt::view(data.trajectories.y, xt::all(), 0);
130	  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> bearing = xt::atan2(target_y - y0, target_x - x0);
131	  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> reverse_bearing = bearing + static_cast<float>(M_PI);
132	
133	  xt::xtensor<float, 1> sum_diff = xt::zeros<float>({data.trajectories.x.shape(0)});
134	  for (size_t t = 0; t < early_steps; ++t) {
135	    const xt::xtensor<float, 1> yaw_t = xt::view(data.trajectories.yaws, xt::all(), t);
136	    const xt::xtensor<float, 1> fwd_diff =
137	      xt::abs(utils::shortest_angular_distance(yaw_t, bearing));
138	    if (forward_preference_) {
139	      sum_diff += fwd_diff;
140	    } else {
141	      const xt::xtensor<float, 1> rev_diff =
142	        xt::abs(utils::shortest_angular_distance(yaw_t, reverse_bearing));
143	      sum_diff += xt::minimum(fwd_diff, rev_diff);
144	    }
145	  }
146	  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> cost = sum_diff / static_cast<float>(early_steps);
147	  data.costs += xt::pow(cost * weight_, power_);
148	}
149	\end{lstlisting}
150	
151	\paragraph{How this cost actually changes which trajectory wins.}
152	Connecting this directly to Section~\ref{sec:mppi-math}'s softmax
153	weighting (Equation~\ref{eq:mppi-weight}): \texttt{data.costs} is the
154	same per-trajectory accumulator every enabled critic adds into, so
155	this critic's contribution
156	$\left(\overline{\Delta\theta} \cdot \texttt{weight\_}\right)^{\texttt{power\_}}$
157	(the early-steps-averaged angular difference $\overline{\Delta\theta}$
158	from the listing's \texttt{cost} variable, scaled and exponentiated by
159	its own configured weight and power) is simply summed alongside the
160	stock critics' own contributions into $S(\tau^{(k)})$ before
161	Equation~\ref{eq:mppi-weight}'s exponential weighting is applied.
162	Concretely: of two sampled trajectories approaching the same curve,
163	one that begins turning toward the near-term path point immediately
164	accrues a small $\overline{\Delta\theta}$ over its first
165	\texttt{early\_time\_steps}, while one that continues driving straight
166	before reacting accrues a much larger one -- inflating that second
167	trajectory's total cost $S(\tau^{(k)})$, which Equation~\ref{eq:mppi-weight}
168	translates into an \emph{exponentially} smaller importance weight
169	$w^{(k)}$ relative to the early-turning trajectory. Because the
170	executed control is the weight-averaged sum over all $K$ sampled
171	trajectories, systematically suppressing the weight of every
172	late-turning sample -- rather than merely marking one specific
173	trajectory as disqualified -- is what actually shifts the controller's
174	averaged output toward beginning the turn earlier, without ever
175	needing to identify or select a single ``best'' trajectory explicitly.
176	
177	\section{Phased Hardware Integration}
178	\label{sec:phased-integration}
179	
180	Given the number of independent subsystems involved (TCP bridge,
181	odometry, SLAM, localisation, planning, control), integration
182	proceeded in three deliberately staged phases rather than attempting
183	the full stack at once, so that a failure at any stage could be
184	attributed to a bounded set of newly-added components rather than the
185	entire system:
186	
187	\begin{description}
188	  \item[Phase 1 -- Teleoperation.] Bridge (Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge})
189	    plus manual \texttt{/cmd\_vel} teleoperation only, with no
190	    odometry, mapping, or navigation involved. Confirmed the motor and
191	    steering command path worked correctly end-to-end before any more
192	    complex subsystem was layered on top.
193	  \item[Phase 2 -- SLAM.] Cartographer mapping
194	    (Section~\ref{sec:cartographer}) added on top of Phase~1,
195	    confirmed to require no odometry extension at all given the
196	    \texttt{use\_odometry: false} configuration described in
197	    Section~\ref{sec:cartographer}. A real, growing occupancy grid was
198	    built by driving the vehicle around a bounded space under
199	    teleoperation and saved via \texttt{nav2\_map\_server}'s
200	    \texttt{map\_saver\_cli} -- this saved map is the one used for all
201	    subsequent localisation and navigation testing.
202	  \item[Phase 3 -- Navigation.] The full Nav2 stack (AMCL, planning,
203	    MPPI control) added on top of Phase~2's saved map, requiring the
204	    wheel-odometry extension of Section~\ref{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}
205	    (deferred from Phase~2, where it had not been necessary) and the
206	    steering-trim (Section~\ref{sec:steering-trim}) and throttle
207	    calibration (Section~\ref{sec:throttle-calibration}) work, since
208	    dead-reckoning odometry and AMCL localisation are only as accurate
209	    as the vehicle model producing them.
210	\end{description}
211	
212	The full stack's initial bring-up -- motor bridge, LiDAR node, relay
213	node, and the ported Nav2 launch configuration -- came up cleanly on
214	the first attempt against the saved Phase~2 map: both Nav2 lifecycle
215	managers reported their managed nodes active, all seven configured
216	MPPI critics (the stock six plus \texttt{EarlyCommitCritic}) loaded
217	matching the intended configuration, and the costmap auto-sized
218	correctly to the saved map's dimensions, with no crash loop. A real
219	navigation goal was deliberately not sent during this first bring-up,
220	since dead-reckoning odometry -- and therefore everything built on
221	top of it, including AMCL and planning -- is only as trustworthy as
222	the still-unresolved steering-trim calibration at that point in the
223	project's timeline; that calibration (Section~\ref{sec:steering-trim})
224	was completed before the first real goal was attempted.
225	
226	\section{Diagnosing an Apparent Display-Localisation Artefact}
227	\label{sec:display-lag}
228	
229	After the throttle calibration of Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration}
230	(but before the buffering-defect fix of Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug}),
231	a live Nav2 goal test surfaced a new symptom, described by the
232	vehicle's operator in detail: when driving toward a goal inside an
233	enclosed space, the entire mapped rectangle appeared to shift in
234	RViz, with the LiDAR scan keeping its internal shape but dragging
235	behind the robot's true motion before ``snapping'' back into
236	alignment -- and the same shift-then-correct pattern recurred, after
237	a delay, once the goal was reported reached.
238	
239	\subsection{Ruling Out Simpler Causes}
240	\label{sec:display-lag-rule-out}
241	
242	Several candidate causes were checked directly and eliminated:
243	\texttt{qcar\_clock\_offset} was re-measured fresh and re-applied
244	(with one procedural caution found along the way -- a relay launch
245	command given during this session had omitted the
246	\texttt{qcar\_clock\_offset} argument entirely, silently defaulting
247	it to zero and briefly reintroducing exactly the bug fixed in
248	Section~\ref{sec:clock-offset}, worth checking for explicitly before
249	suspecting the offset value itself); \texttt{map}
250	$\rightarrow$ \texttt{odom} TF was captured directly during active
251	driving and updated in small, smooth, incremental steps rather than
252	sudden jumps; the RViz \texttt{Fixed Frame} configuration was
253	confirmed correct (\texttt{map}); \texttt{base} $\rightarrow$
254	\texttt{lidar} TF is static and therefore not a timing bottleneck;
255	local CPU load was checked and found unremarkable (RViz
256	$\approx$10\%, the Nav2 container $\approx$29\%); network round-trip
257	latency to the QCar was \SIrange{1}{6}{\milli\second}, far too small
258	to explain a multi-second visible effect; and direct
259	receipt-versus-capture latency on \texttt{/odom} and \texttt{/scan}
260	measured $\approx$\SIlist{0.18;0.20}{\second} respectively, small
261	and tightly clustered, ruling out network or relay transit as the
262	source of a large visible lag.
263	
264	\subsection{Instrumentation: \texttt{monitor\_goal\_timing.py}}
265	\label{sec:monitor-goal-timing}
266	
267	A dedicated instrumentation tool was built to timestamp a single Nav2
268	goal end to end: goal-sent, real motion start/stop (from
269	\texttt{/odom}), RViz-displayed motion start/stop (from the
270	\texttt{map} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{base} TF), and goal-reached. Two
271	implementation defects were found and fixed while building this tool,
272	both worth recording as general lessons for any future action-status
273	monitoring code on ROS~2:
274	
275	\begin{enumerate}
276	  \item \textbf{A QoS durability mismatch.} The actual publisher QoS
277	    for \texttt{/navigate\_to\_pose/\_action/status} is
278	    \texttt{RELIABLE} + \texttt{TRANSIENT\_LOCAL}. \texttt{rclpy}'s
279	    default subscription QoS, constructed by passing a plain integer
280	    depth, leaves durability at \texttt{VOLATILE} -- technically
281	    QoS-compatible by specification (a subscriber may request less
282	    than a publisher offers), but this delivered \emph{zero} messages
283	    in practice, confirmed twice on real hardware. The fix required
284	    constructing an explicit \texttt{QoSProfile} matching the
285	    publisher exactly, a reminder that formal QoS compatibility rules
286	    do not guarantee the practical behaviour a developer expects
287	    (Section~\ref{sec:ros2-model}). This is exactly the
288	    \texttt{TRANSIENT\_LOCAL}-publisher / \texttt{VOLATILE}-subscriber
289	    case Table~\ref{tab:qos-compatibility} marks as formally
290	    compatible: durability governs whether \emph{already-published}
291	    samples are replayed to a newly matched subscriber, and a
292	    low-frequency topic like action status may not publish a fresh
293	    sample again for a long time, so a \texttt{VOLATILE} subscriber
294	    that missed the replay is left waiting with no error raised on
295	    either side.
296	  \item \textbf{Goal-detection logic.} The tool originally waited for
297	    status code \texttt{ACCEPTED} specifically to mark ``goal sent'',
298	    but a goal can transition directly from absent to
299	    \texttt{EXECUTING} between two consecutive status publishes,
300	    skipping an independently observable \texttt{ACCEPTED} update
301	    entirely -- this topic's \texttt{TRANSIENT\_LOCAL} history appears
302	    to retain only the latest status per goal, not the full transition
303	    sequence. The fix tracks goal UUIDs instead: the first appearance
304	    of a previously unseen \texttt{goal\_id} (after seeding a known-ID
305	    set from whatever the topic already retained at monitor startup)
306	    marks ``goal sent'', regardless of which status value it first
307	    carries.
308	\end{enumerate}
309	
310	Listing~\ref{lst:status-qos} shows the explicit \texttt{QoSProfile}
311	that fixed the first defect -- matching \texttt{bt\_navigator}'s
312	publisher exactly rather than relying on the default subscription QoS
313	constructed from a plain integer depth.
314	
315	\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Explicit QoS profile matching \texttt{bt\_navigator}'s action-status publisher (\texttt{scripts/monitor\_goal\_timing.py}).},label={lst:status-qos}]
316	STATUS_QOS = QoSProfile(
317	    reliability=QoSReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE,
318	    durability=QoSDurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL,
319	    history=QoSHistoryPolicy.KEEP_LAST,
320	    depth=10,
321	)
322	...
323	self.create_subscription(GoalStatusArray, '/navigate_to_pose/_action/status',
324	                          self.status_cb, STATUS_QOS)
325	\end{lstlisting}
326	
327	Listing~\ref{lst:goal-uuid-tracking} shows the second fix: rather than
328	waiting for a specific status code, the callback seeds a
329	\texttt{known\_goal\_ids} set from whatever the topic already retains
330	at startup (so pre-existing, already-completed goals are not
331	mistaken for a new one), then marks ``goal sent'' the first time a
332	previously unseen goal UUID appears in any status, independent of
333	which status value that UUID first carries.
334	
335	\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Goal-UUID--based ``goal sent'' detection (\texttt{scripts/monitor\_goal\_timing.py}).},label={lst:goal-uuid-tracking}]
336	if not self.known_goal_ids:
337	    for s in msg.status_list:
338	        self.known_goal_ids.add(bytes(s.goal_info.goal_id.uuid))
339	    self.get_logger().info(
340	        'seeded %d pre-existing goal id(s), waiting for a new one'
341	        % len(self.known_goal_ids))
342	    return
343	
344	for s in msg.status_list:
345	    gid = bytes(s.goal_info.goal_id.uuid)
346	    if gid not in self.known_goal_ids:
347	        self.known_goal_ids.add(gid)
348	        if self.goal_sent_t is None:
349	            self.goal_sent_t = now
350	            self.tracked_goal_id = gid
351	\end{lstlisting}
352	
353	An explicit discovery-wait (polling \texttt{get\_publishers\_info\_by\_topic}
354	plus a settle margin) was also required before treating the monitor
355	as ready to observe a goal -- a subscription created and immediately
356	assumed matched can miss a fast goal's status entirely if DDS
357	discovery with the separate \texttt{bt\_navigator} process has not
358	yet completed.
359	
360	\subsection{Measured Result}
361	\label{sec:display-lag-result}
362	
363	Table~\ref{tab:display-lag} presents one complete goal traced with
364	this tool.
365	
366	\begin{table}[htbp]
367	  \centering
368	  \caption{Timing trace of one Nav2 goal (\texttt{monitor\_goal\_timing.py}).}
369	  \label{tab:display-lag}
370	  \begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
371	    \toprule
372	    Event & Offset & Pose \\
373	    \midrule
374	    Goal sent & -- & -- \\
375	    Real start (odom) & +2.145\,s after goal sent & (3.344, 1.674) odom frame \\
376	    RViz start (map$\to$base) & +2.705\,s after goal sent & (0.033, $-$0.031) map frame \\
377	    Goal reached & +6.660\,s after goal sent & -- \\
378	    RViz stop & +2.094\,s after goal reached & (1.257, $-$0.024) \\
379	    Real stop (odom) & +2.238\,s after goal reached & -- \\
380	    \bottomrule
381	  \end{tabular}
382	\end{table}
383	
384	This gives a start gap (RViz minus real) of $+\SI{0.559}{\second}$
385	and a stop gap of $-\SI{0.144}{\second}$ (RViz reporting ``stopped''
386	slightly \emph{before} the real vehicle fully settled -- small, and
387	plausibly within the detection threshold's own noise rather than a
388	separate effect). Note that the real-start offset of
389	\SI{2.145}{\second} already includes the static-friction stiction
390	delay characterised in Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery}, so it is
391	not, by itself, a new timing number.
392	
393	\subsection{Interpretation, and a Necessary Caveat}
394	\label{sec:display-lag-interpretation}
395	
396	This measurement supports two separate, unrelated conclusions. The
397	$\approx$\SI{0.56}{\second} start-of-goal gap is a modest, constant
398	pipeline latency -- network transit, AMCL's scan-matching cycle, and
399	RViz's own subscribe/render overhead stacking up -- between a real
400	event and its appearance on screen; it is not a TF-jump defect (ruled
401	out in Section~\ref{sec:display-lag-rule-out}), and it is not a real
402	navigation-performance problem, since Nav2's own controller consumes
403	\texttt{/odom}/\texttt{/amcl\_pose}/\texttt{/tf} directly at the
404	source, without RViz's additional rendering overhead -- the robot's
405	actual control decisions are working with data less stale than what a
406	human operator sees on screen. The end-of-goal gap, by contrast, is
407	the same stop-latency/coast phenomenon already characterised in
408	Chapter~\ref{ch:calibration}: the real vehicle continuing to move for
409	\SI{2.238}{\second} after ``goal reached'' matches the pre-fix
410	stop-latency figures in Table~\ref{tab:calibration-validation}'s
411	predecessor almost exactly, confirmed here via a completely
412	independent measurement method (a live Nav2 goal rather than the
413	open-loop \texttt{drive\_and\_log.py} test).
414	
415	The necessary caveat, and the reason this section is presented in
416	detail rather than as a closed result: \textbf{this entire
417	measurement was taken while the \texttt{readMode=1} buffering defect
418	of Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug} was still active} in
419	\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} -- it was fixed the following day. Given that
420	defect's confirmed effect on every encoder-derived quantity
421	(Table~\ref{tab:readmode-fix}), the \SI{2.238}{\second} end-of-goal
422	figure here is almost certainly, in large part, the same artefact
423	rather than a distinct navigation-specific finding -- its magnitude
424	matches the buffering defect's characterised effect too closely to be
425	coincidental. The \SI{0.559}{\second} start-gap figure is a different
426	measurement (\texttt{map}$\to$\texttt{base} TF timing rather than
427	\texttt{/odom} velocity thresholding) and is less obviously the same
428	artefact, but since it is also downstream of the same buffered
429	\texttt{/odom} stream, it cannot be treated as a clean, artefact-free
430	measurement of pure network/AMCL/RViz pipeline latency either. The
431	diagnostic methodology and tooling built in this section -- the
432	QoS/goal-detection fixes, and the systematic elimination of TF-jump,
433	Fixed-Frame, and network-latency causes -- remain valid and reusable;
434	only the specific numbers in Table~\ref{tab:display-lag} should be
435	treated as provisional pending a fresh \texttt{monitor\_goal\_timing.py}
436	run with the \texttt{readMode=0} fix in place. % TODO: re-run and report
437	
438	\section{Final Validation}
439	\label{sec:final-validation}
440	
441	Following the \texttt{readMode=0} fix (Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug}),
442	a live Nav2 goal was re-run on the physical vehicle -- full onboard
443	bridge, LiDAR node, and relay node, with AMCL localised against the
444	existing saved map. The vehicle's operator's direct, contemporaneous
445	assessment was unambiguous: navigation was ``working almost
446	perfectly'' -- a strong qualitative result, and one consistent with
447	the buffering defect having been the dominant cause of the
448	``skeleton of the map is moving'' symptom that opened
449	Section~\ref{sec:display-lag}, rather than merely a contributing
450	factor to it. \texttt{monitor\_goal\_timing.py} was not re-run for
451	this specific goal, so the precise post-fix start-gap and
452	end-of-goal figures corresponding to Table~\ref{tab:display-lag}
453	are not available as quantitative numbers in this thesis. % TODO:
454	% capture these numbers with a fresh lab session if at all possible -
455	% this is the single most valuable remaining data point for Ch. 7.
456	
457	\section{Summary}
458	\label{sec:nav-integration-summary}
459	
460	This chapter closes the sim-to-real migration begun in
461	Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}: the physical QCar, connected through the
462	bridge of Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge} and calibrated per
463	Chapter~\ref{ch:calibration}, was shown to complete real, closed-loop
464	Nav2 navigation goals, including an Ackermann-appropriate custom MPPI
465	critic and phased integration that isolated each subsystem's own
466	correctness before combining it with the next. The one significant
467	open item is quantitative: this chapter's display-lag investigation
468	was measured under a bridge configuration later found to be affected
469	by the buffering defect of Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug}, and a
470	qualitative post-fix confirmation exists, but a fresh quantitative
471	re-measurement does not. Chapter~\ref{ch:results} draws together the
472	quantitative results available across this and the preceding two
473	chapters.
474
