\chapter{Navigation Integration and Validation}
\label{ch:nav-integration}

% TODO: this chapter's final section (6.5) reports a QUALITATIVE
% end-to-end result ("working almost perfectly") without a fresh
% quantitative monitor_goal_timing.py re-run post-readMode-fix. If you
% can still get lab time on the QCar, re-running that tool and
% dropping the numbers into Table 6.2 (currently a TODO) would close
% the one open loop in this thesis's results and make Ch. 7 stronger.

This chapter describes bringing the full Nav2 navigation stack up
against the physical QCar, building on the bridge of
Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge} and the calibration of
Chapter~\ref{ch:calibration}. Section~\ref{sec:nav2-porting} covers
porting the simulation-tuned Nav2 configuration to hardware.
Section~\ref{sec:mppi-critic} describes a custom MPPI critic plugin
developed for this vehicle. Section~\ref{sec:phased-integration}
reports the phased bring-up used to de-risk the integration.
Section~\ref{sec:display-lag} presents a detailed timing
investigation into an apparent localisation-display artefact, and
Section~\ref{sec:final-validation} reports the resulting end-to-end
validation.

\section{Porting the Nav2 Configuration to Hardware}
\label{sec:nav2-porting}

The Nav2 parameter set developed and tuned in simulation
(Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}) required a small, mechanical set of
changes to run against physical hardware rather than Gazebo: every
occurrence of \texttt{use\_sim\_time} (13 in total, across the
costmap, planner, controller, and AMCL parameter blocks) was switched
from \texttt{true} to \texttt{false}, since the physical robot has no
simulation clock to synchronise against. Both mapping and navigation
launch files were given a real-hardware branch, gated on
\texttt{launch\_sim}, alongside the existing Gazebo branch, with
real hardware as the default and simulation opt-in
(\texttt{launch\_sim:=true}) -- a deliberate inversion of which mode
is the default, made once hardware became the project's active
development target, while keeping the simulation path fully intact
for future regression testing rather than removing it.

The AMCL \texttt{recovery\_alpha\_fast}/\texttt{recovery\_alpha\_slow}
fix from Section~\ref{sec:ruled-out} was carried forward
proactively into the hardware configuration at this point, rather
than left to be independently rediscovered against hardware, since
the underlying cause -- Section~\ref{sec:amcl-math}'s augmented-MCL
random-particle-injection mechanism being permanently disabled at
$\alpha_{\text{slow}} = \alpha_{\text{fast}} = 0$, leaving the filter
with no way to recover from an overconfident convergence once real
sensor noise (which a clean simulation rarely exercises) triggers one
-- is a property of AMCL's own resampling algorithm, not specific to
any one deployment target.

\section{Custom MPPI Critic: \texttt{EarlyCommitCritic}}
\label{sec:mppi-critic}

Early navigation testing showed a specific weakness in the stock MPPI
critic set (Section~\ref{sec:nav2}) for this vehicle: the standard
path-following critics evaluate a sampled trajectory's alignment and
progress against the path as a whole, which can leave the controller
driving further into an approaching curve before it begins reacting
to it, rather than beginning the turn as early as physically sensible
-- a behaviour more forgiving for a differential-drive robot's tight
turning radius than for an Ackermann-steered vehicle with the
finite minimum turning radius of Table~\ref{tab:qcar-geometry}.

A custom MPPI critic plugin, \texttt{EarlyCommitCritic}, was
developed and built into the navigation package to address this: it
scores only the first \texttt{early\_time\_steps} of each sampled
trajectory rollout against the bearing to a near-term path point,
with no distance or angle gating, so that MPPI is pushed to begin
turning toward the path immediately rather than waiting until deeper
into the curve. It is gated by an \texttt{active\_path\_points}
parameter so that it stops influencing the controller once the
vehicle has made genuine progress along the route, avoiding
interference with the stock critics' normal path-tracking behaviour
during straight segments. A later direction-awareness refinement
extended the critic to handle reversing and K-turn path segments
correctly, where a naive ``always turn toward the next point''
bearing calculation would otherwise fight the vehicle's intended
direction of travel.

Building this plugin required matching \texttt{xtensor}/\texttt{xsimd}
compile definitions exactly against Nav2's own MPPI controller build
-- a mismatch here does not produce a compile-time error, but a
silent ABI incompatibility that crashes the navigation container on
the first control cycle that touches vectorised critic math, making
it a notably unforgiving class of build-configuration bug to diagnose
from its symptom alone.

Listing~\ref{lst:early-commit-critic} shows the critic's
\texttt{score()} method in full. It computes the bearing from each
sampled trajectory's own starting position to a near-term path target
(\texttt{offset\_from\_furthest} points ahead of the furthest point
the robot has already reached), then, for only the first
\texttt{early\_time\_steps} of that trajectory, accumulates the
angular distance between the trajectory's actual yaw and that
bearing -- scoring every sampled rollout independently, not just the
robot's single current pose. The early return on
\texttt{active\_path\_points} is what confines this to the start of a
path, and the \texttt{forward\_preference\_}-gated minimum of the
forward- and reverse-bearing angular distances is the
direction-awareness refinement mentioned above, letting a trajectory
be scored against whichever of the bearing or its reverse it is
actually closer to, rather than penalising a legitimate reversing
manoeuvre.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=C++,caption={\texttt{EarlyCommitCritic::score()} (\texttt{src/critics/early\_commit\_critic.cpp}).},label={lst:early-commit-critic}]
void EarlyCommitCritic::score(CriticData & data)
{
  if (!enabled_ || data.path.x.shape(0) < 2) { return; }
  utils::setPathFurthestPointIfNotSet(data);

  // Only relevant at the start of a path - once the robot has made
  // real progress, let the normal path/goal critics take over.
  if (*data.furthest_reached_path_point >= active_path_points_) { return; }

  const size_t path_size = data.path.x.shape(0) - 1;
  const size_t offseted_idx = std::min(
    *data.furthest_reached_path_point + offset_from_furthest_, path_size);
  const float target_x = data.path.x(offseted_idx);
  const float target_y = data.path.y(offseted_idx);

  const size_t time_steps = data.trajectories.x.shape(1);
  const size_t early_steps = std::min(early_time_steps_, time_steps);
  if (early_steps == 0) { return; }

  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> x0 = xt::view(data.trajectories.x, xt::all(), 0);
  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> y0 = xt::view(data.trajectories.y, xt::all(), 0);
  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> bearing = xt::atan2(target_y - y0, target_x - x0);
  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> reverse_bearing = bearing + static_cast<float>(M_PI);

  xt::xtensor<float, 1> sum_diff = xt::zeros<float>({data.trajectories.x.shape(0)});
  for (size_t t = 0; t < early_steps; ++t) {
    const xt::xtensor<float, 1> yaw_t = xt::view(data.trajectories.yaws, xt::all(), t);
    const xt::xtensor<float, 1> fwd_diff =
      xt::abs(utils::shortest_angular_distance(yaw_t, bearing));
    if (forward_preference_) {
      sum_diff += fwd_diff;
    } else {
      const xt::xtensor<float, 1> rev_diff =
        xt::abs(utils::shortest_angular_distance(yaw_t, reverse_bearing));
      sum_diff += xt::minimum(fwd_diff, rev_diff);
    }
  }
  const xt::xtensor<float, 1> cost = sum_diff / static_cast<float>(early_steps);
  data.costs += xt::pow(cost * weight_, power_);
}
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{How this cost actually changes which trajectory wins.}
Connecting this directly to Section~\ref{sec:mppi-math}'s softmax
weighting (Equation~\ref{eq:mppi-weight}): \texttt{data.costs} is the
same per-trajectory accumulator every enabled critic adds into, so
this critic's contribution
$\left(\overline{\Delta\theta} \cdot \texttt{weight\_}\right)^{\texttt{power\_}}$
(the early-steps-averaged angular difference $\overline{\Delta\theta}$
from the listing's \texttt{cost} variable, scaled and exponentiated by
its own configured weight and power) is simply summed alongside the
stock critics' own contributions into $S(\tau^{(k)})$ before
Equation~\ref{eq:mppi-weight}'s exponential weighting is applied.
Concretely: of two sampled trajectories approaching the same curve,
one that begins turning toward the near-term path point immediately
accrues a small $\overline{\Delta\theta}$ over its first
\texttt{early\_time\_steps}, while one that continues driving straight
before reacting accrues a much larger one -- inflating that second
trajectory's total cost $S(\tau^{(k)})$, which Equation~\ref{eq:mppi-weight}
translates into an \emph{exponentially} smaller importance weight
$w^{(k)}$ relative to the early-turning trajectory. Because the
executed control is the weight-averaged sum over all $K$ sampled
trajectories, systematically suppressing the weight of every
late-turning sample -- rather than merely marking one specific
trajectory as disqualified -- is what actually shifts the controller's
averaged output toward beginning the turn earlier, without ever
needing to identify or select a single ``best'' trajectory explicitly.

\section{Phased Hardware Integration}
\label{sec:phased-integration}

Given the number of independent subsystems involved (TCP bridge,
odometry, SLAM, localisation, planning, control), integration
proceeded in three deliberately staged phases rather than attempting
the full stack at once, so that a failure at any stage could be
attributed to a bounded set of newly-added components rather than the
entire system:

\begin{description}
  \item[Phase 1 -- Teleoperation.] Bridge (Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge})
    plus manual \texttt{/cmd\_vel} teleoperation only, with no
    odometry, mapping, or navigation involved. Confirmed the motor and
    steering command path worked correctly end-to-end before any more
    complex subsystem was layered on top.
  \item[Phase 2 -- SLAM.] Cartographer mapping
    (Section~\ref{sec:cartographer}) added on top of Phase~1,
    confirmed to require no odometry extension at all given the
    \texttt{use\_odometry: false} configuration described in
    Section~\ref{sec:cartographer}. A real, growing occupancy grid was
    built by driving the vehicle around a bounded space under
    teleoperation and saved via \texttt{nav2\_map\_server}'s
    \texttt{map\_saver\_cli} -- this saved map is the one used for all
    subsequent localisation and navigation testing.
  \item[Phase 3 -- Navigation.] The full Nav2 stack (AMCL, planning,
    MPPI control) added on top of Phase~2's saved map, requiring the
    wheel-odometry extension of Section~\ref{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}
    (deferred from Phase~2, where it had not been necessary) and the
    steering-trim (Section~\ref{sec:steering-trim}) and throttle
    calibration (Section~\ref{sec:throttle-calibration}) work, since
    dead-reckoning odometry and AMCL localisation are only as accurate
    as the vehicle model producing them.
\end{description}

The full stack's initial bring-up -- motor bridge, LiDAR node, relay
node, and the ported Nav2 launch configuration -- came up cleanly on
the first attempt against the saved Phase~2 map: both Nav2 lifecycle
managers reported their managed nodes active, all seven configured
MPPI critics (the stock six plus \texttt{EarlyCommitCritic}) loaded
matching the intended configuration, and the costmap auto-sized
correctly to the saved map's dimensions, with no crash loop. A real
navigation goal was deliberately not sent during this first bring-up,
since dead-reckoning odometry -- and therefore everything built on
top of it, including AMCL and planning -- is only as trustworthy as
the still-unresolved steering-trim calibration at that point in the
project's timeline; that calibration (Section~\ref{sec:steering-trim})
was completed before the first real goal was attempted.

\section{Diagnosing an Apparent Display-Localisation Artefact}
\label{sec:display-lag}

After the throttle calibration of Section~\ref{sec:final-calibration}
(but before the buffering-defect fix of Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug}),
a live Nav2 goal test surfaced a new symptom, described by the
vehicle's operator in detail: when driving toward a goal inside an
enclosed space, the entire mapped rectangle appeared to shift in
RViz, with the LiDAR scan keeping its internal shape but dragging
behind the robot's true motion before ``snapping'' back into
alignment -- and the same shift-then-correct pattern recurred, after
a delay, once the goal was reported reached.

\subsection{Ruling Out Simpler Causes}
\label{sec:display-lag-rule-out}

Several candidate causes were checked directly and eliminated:
\texttt{qcar\_clock\_offset} was re-measured fresh and re-applied
(with one procedural caution found along the way -- a relay launch
command given during this session had omitted the
\texttt{qcar\_clock\_offset} argument entirely, silently defaulting
it to zero and briefly reintroducing exactly the bug fixed in
Section~\ref{sec:clock-offset}, worth checking for explicitly before
suspecting the offset value itself); \texttt{map}
$\rightarrow$ \texttt{odom} TF was captured directly during active
driving and updated in small, smooth, incremental steps rather than
sudden jumps; the RViz \texttt{Fixed Frame} configuration was
confirmed correct (\texttt{map}); \texttt{base} $\rightarrow$
\texttt{lidar} TF is static and therefore not a timing bottleneck;
local CPU load was checked and found unremarkable (RViz
$\approx$10\%, the Nav2 container $\approx$29\%); network round-trip
latency to the QCar was \SIrange{1}{6}{\milli\second}, far too small
to explain a multi-second visible effect; and direct
receipt-versus-capture latency on \texttt{/odom} and \texttt{/scan}
measured $\approx$\SIlist{0.18;0.20}{\second} respectively, small
and tightly clustered, ruling out network or relay transit as the
source of a large visible lag.

\subsection{Instrumentation: \texttt{monitor\_goal\_timing.py}}
\label{sec:monitor-goal-timing}

A dedicated instrumentation tool was built to timestamp a single Nav2
goal end to end: goal-sent, real motion start/stop (from
\texttt{/odom}), RViz-displayed motion start/stop (from the
\texttt{map} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{base} TF), and goal-reached. Two
implementation defects were found and fixed while building this tool,
both worth recording as general lessons for any future action-status
monitoring code on ROS~2:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{A QoS durability mismatch.} The actual publisher QoS
    for \texttt{/navigate\_to\_pose/\_action/status} is
    \texttt{RELIABLE} + \texttt{TRANSIENT\_LOCAL}. \texttt{rclpy}'s
    default subscription QoS, constructed by passing a plain integer
    depth, leaves durability at \texttt{VOLATILE} -- technically
    QoS-compatible by specification (a subscriber may request less
    than a publisher offers), but this delivered \emph{zero} messages
    in practice, confirmed twice on real hardware. The fix required
    constructing an explicit \texttt{QoSProfile} matching the
    publisher exactly, a reminder that formal QoS compatibility rules
    do not guarantee the practical behaviour a developer expects
    (Section~\ref{sec:ros2-model}). This is exactly the
    \texttt{TRANSIENT\_LOCAL}-publisher / \texttt{VOLATILE}-subscriber
    case Table~\ref{tab:qos-compatibility} marks as formally
    compatible: durability governs whether \emph{already-published}
    samples are replayed to a newly matched subscriber, and a
    low-frequency topic like action status may not publish a fresh
    sample again for a long time, so a \texttt{VOLATILE} subscriber
    that missed the replay is left waiting with no error raised on
    either side.
  \item \textbf{Goal-detection logic.} The tool originally waited for
    status code \texttt{ACCEPTED} specifically to mark ``goal sent'',
    but a goal can transition directly from absent to
    \texttt{EXECUTING} between two consecutive status publishes,
    skipping an independently observable \texttt{ACCEPTED} update
    entirely -- this topic's \texttt{TRANSIENT\_LOCAL} history appears
    to retain only the latest status per goal, not the full transition
    sequence. The fix tracks goal UUIDs instead: the first appearance
    of a previously unseen \texttt{goal\_id} (after seeding a known-ID
    set from whatever the topic already retained at monitor startup)
    marks ``goal sent'', regardless of which status value it first
    carries.
\end{enumerate}

Listing~\ref{lst:status-qos} shows the explicit \texttt{QoSProfile}
that fixed the first defect -- matching \texttt{bt\_navigator}'s
publisher exactly rather than relying on the default subscription QoS
constructed from a plain integer depth.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Explicit QoS profile matching \texttt{bt\_navigator}'s action-status publisher (\texttt{scripts/monitor\_goal\_timing.py}).},label={lst:status-qos}]
STATUS_QOS = QoSProfile(
    reliability=QoSReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE,
    durability=QoSDurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL,
    history=QoSHistoryPolicy.KEEP_LAST,
    depth=10,
)
...
self.create_subscription(GoalStatusArray, '/navigate_to_pose/_action/status',
                          self.status_cb, STATUS_QOS)
\end{lstlisting}

Listing~\ref{lst:goal-uuid-tracking} shows the second fix: rather than
waiting for a specific status code, the callback seeds a
\texttt{known\_goal\_ids} set from whatever the topic already retains
at startup (so pre-existing, already-completed goals are not
mistaken for a new one), then marks ``goal sent'' the first time a
previously unseen goal UUID appears in any status, independent of
which status value that UUID first carries.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={Goal-UUID--based ``goal sent'' detection (\texttt{scripts/monitor\_goal\_timing.py}).},label={lst:goal-uuid-tracking}]
if not self.known_goal_ids:
    for s in msg.status_list:
        self.known_goal_ids.add(bytes(s.goal_info.goal_id.uuid))
    self.get_logger().info(
        'seeded %d pre-existing goal id(s), waiting for a new one'
        % len(self.known_goal_ids))
    return

for s in msg.status_list:
    gid = bytes(s.goal_info.goal_id.uuid)
    if gid not in self.known_goal_ids:
        self.known_goal_ids.add(gid)
        if self.goal_sent_t is None:
            self.goal_sent_t = now
            self.tracked_goal_id = gid
\end{lstlisting}

An explicit discovery-wait (polling \texttt{get\_publishers\_info\_by\_topic}
plus a settle margin) was also required before treating the monitor
as ready to observe a goal -- a subscription created and immediately
assumed matched can miss a fast goal's status entirely if DDS
discovery with the separate \texttt{bt\_navigator} process has not
yet completed.

\subsection{Measured Result}
\label{sec:display-lag-result}

Table~\ref{tab:display-lag} presents one complete goal traced with
this tool.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Timing trace of one Nav2 goal (\texttt{monitor\_goal\_timing.py}).}
  \label{tab:display-lag}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
    \toprule
    Event & Offset & Pose \\
    \midrule
    Goal sent & -- & -- \\
    Real start (odom) & +2.145\,s after goal sent & (3.344, 1.674) odom frame \\
    RViz start (map$\to$base) & +2.705\,s after goal sent & (0.033, $-$0.031) map frame \\
    Goal reached & +6.660\,s after goal sent & -- \\
    RViz stop & +2.094\,s after goal reached & (1.257, $-$0.024) \\
    Real stop (odom) & +2.238\,s after goal reached & -- \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

This gives a start gap (RViz minus real) of $+\SI{0.559}{\second}$
and a stop gap of $-\SI{0.144}{\second}$ (RViz reporting ``stopped''
slightly \emph{before} the real vehicle fully settled -- small, and
plausibly within the detection threshold's own noise rather than a
separate effect). Note that the real-start offset of
\SI{2.145}{\second} already includes the static-friction stiction
delay characterised in Section~\ref{sec:deadband-discovery}, so it is
not, by itself, a new timing number.

\subsection{Interpretation, and a Necessary Caveat}
\label{sec:display-lag-interpretation}

This measurement supports two separate, unrelated conclusions. The
$\approx$\SI{0.56}{\second} start-of-goal gap is a modest, constant
pipeline latency -- network transit, AMCL's scan-matching cycle, and
RViz's own subscribe/render overhead stacking up -- between a real
event and its appearance on screen; it is not a TF-jump defect (ruled
out in Section~\ref{sec:display-lag-rule-out}), and it is not a real
navigation-performance problem, since Nav2's own controller consumes
\texttt{/odom}/\texttt{/amcl\_pose}/\texttt{/tf} directly at the
source, without RViz's additional rendering overhead -- the robot's
actual control decisions are working with data less stale than what a
human operator sees on screen. The end-of-goal gap, by contrast, is
the same stop-latency/coast phenomenon already characterised in
Chapter~\ref{ch:calibration}: the real vehicle continuing to move for
\SI{2.238}{\second} after ``goal reached'' matches the pre-fix
stop-latency figures in Table~\ref{tab:calibration-validation}'s
predecessor almost exactly, confirmed here via a completely
independent measurement method (a live Nav2 goal rather than the
open-loop \texttt{drive\_and\_log.py} test).

The necessary caveat, and the reason this section is presented in
detail rather than as a closed result: \textbf{this entire
measurement was taken while the \texttt{readMode=1} buffering defect
of Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug} was still active} in
\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py} -- it was fixed the following day. Given that
defect's confirmed effect on every encoder-derived quantity
(Table~\ref{tab:readmode-fix}), the \SI{2.238}{\second} end-of-goal
figure here is almost certainly, in large part, the same artefact
rather than a distinct navigation-specific finding -- its magnitude
matches the buffering defect's characterised effect too closely to be
coincidental. The \SI{0.559}{\second} start-gap figure is a different
measurement (\texttt{map}$\to$\texttt{base} TF timing rather than
\texttt{/odom} velocity thresholding) and is less obviously the same
artefact, but since it is also downstream of the same buffered
\texttt{/odom} stream, it cannot be treated as a clean, artefact-free
measurement of pure network/AMCL/RViz pipeline latency either. The
diagnostic methodology and tooling built in this section -- the
QoS/goal-detection fixes, and the systematic elimination of TF-jump,
Fixed-Frame, and network-latency causes -- remain valid and reusable;
only the specific numbers in Table~\ref{tab:display-lag} should be
treated as provisional pending a fresh \texttt{monitor\_goal\_timing.py}
run with the \texttt{readMode=0} fix in place. % TODO: re-run and report

\section{Final Validation}
\label{sec:final-validation}

Following the \texttt{readMode=0} fix (Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug}),
a live Nav2 goal was re-run on the physical vehicle -- full onboard
bridge, LiDAR node, and relay node, with AMCL localised against the
existing saved map. The vehicle's operator's direct, contemporaneous
assessment was unambiguous: navigation was ``working almost
perfectly'' -- a strong qualitative result, and one consistent with
the buffering defect having been the dominant cause of the
``skeleton of the map is moving'' symptom that opened
Section~\ref{sec:display-lag}, rather than merely a contributing
factor to it. \texttt{monitor\_goal\_timing.py} was not re-run for
this specific goal, so the precise post-fix start-gap and
end-of-goal figures corresponding to Table~\ref{tab:display-lag}
are not available as quantitative numbers in this thesis. % TODO:
% capture these numbers with a fresh lab session if at all possible -
% this is the single most valuable remaining data point for Ch. 7.

\section{Summary}
\label{sec:nav-integration-summary}

This chapter closes the sim-to-real migration begun in
Chapter~\ref{ch:sim-stack}: the physical QCar, connected through the
bridge of Chapter~\ref{ch:hardware-bridge} and calibrated per
Chapter~\ref{ch:calibration}, was shown to complete real, closed-loop
Nav2 navigation goals, including an Ackermann-appropriate custom MPPI
critic and phased integration that isolated each subsystem's own
correctness before combining it with the next. The one significant
open item is quantitative: this chapter's display-lag investigation
was measured under a bridge configuration later found to be affected
by the buffering defect of Section~\ref{sec:readmode-bug}, and a
qualitative post-fix confirmation exists, but a fresh quantitative
re-measurement does not. Chapter~\ref{ch:results} draws together the
quantitative results available across this and the preceding two
chapters.

Empirical calibration (as done here) is therefore the correct and only available method, matching the `THROTTLE_GAIN` precedent exactly.

52	Added `STEERING_GAIN = 1.39` (from the 7-point sweep regression above). `apply_trim()` changed from `kinematic_steering + STEERING_TRIM` to `kinematic_steering / STEERING_GAIN + STEERING_TRIM` - pre-divides by the measured gain so the real wheel lands at the intended kinematic angle, not just at `kinematic + a flat offset`. `compute_steering()` and odometry deliberately untouched (still use the true kinematic angle) - same constraint as the documented 2026-08-06 odometry-corruption bug (trim/gain correction must stay downstream of anything that cares about the real physical angle, i.e. only inside `apply_trim()`, right before `car.write()`).
53	
54	**Trim further refined to -0.087** via 3 repeated trials each at -0.08/-0.085/-0.09 (averaging out human placement/measurement noise, per the user's request):
55	- -0.08: 3.3, 3.2, 0.5 cm L (avg 2.33 L) | -0.085: 0, 0, 1 cm L (avg 0.33 L) | -0.09: 1, 0.5, 1 cm R (avg 0.83 R)
56	- Zero-crossing of the averaged points: -0.087. This narrow a span isn't enough data to also re-fit `STEERING_GAIN` - kept at 1.39 from the wider sweep.
57	
58	**Deployed and validated end-to-end** (`STEERING_GAIN=1.39`, `STEERING_TRIM=-0.087`) in all three copies of `qcar_bridge.py`: the QCar's live onboard file (`~/ros2_amit/src/onboard_bridge/qcar_bridge.py`) plus both repo copies (`qcar_hardware/qcar_onboard/` and `qcar_updated/qcar_onboard/`). Validation test: commanded a real kinematic turn (+0.15 rad, 1m arc @ 0.4 m/s, predicts 28.5cm left) - measured 27cm left, implying only ~5.6% residual error (down from ~39% with no gain correction, ~11% with the intermediate -0.09/no-gain-fix state).
59	
60	**Confirmed in actual closed-loop use**: after this fix, the user ran real nav2 navigation on hardware (`qcar_nav2.launch.py launch_sim:=false`, real map/AMCL) and reported navigation visibly improved - not just the isolated 1m-arc tests, but real autonomous goal-following. This was the original motivating complaint ("nav2 on hardware not turning as well as sim") and it's now qualitatively resolved. **Status: RESOLVED, deployed, and confirmed working in practice.**
61	
62	## Safety notes from across both sessions
63	
64	- Testing a *new*, previously-untested steering-angle magnitude can produce more real curvature than expected and hit something even in a space that was safe for smaller/known deviations - happened once at `STEERING_TRIM=-0.09` on 2026-08-24 during a longer continuous drive (unrelated to the clean 1m-arc tests, which have since tested this exact value safely many times). Confirm clearance in the new command's actual curve direction before testing it, not just previously-tested directions.
65	- **Always explicitly wait for the user's go-ahead immediately before sending a drive command**, not just after they approve the general plan - a "yes" to "should we test X" is not the same as "go," since the user may need a moment to physically reposition/let go of the car first. A test was run once while the user was still physically holding/repositioning the robot.
66	- The bridge process must be restarted after any `STEERING_TRIM` file edit (Python doesn't hot-reload); always verify via `ps -eo pid,lstart,cmd` that the running process's start time is after the file's mtime before trusting a test result - a stale, unrestarted process silently using an old trim value was a suspected (never fully confirmed either way) contributor to some of the 2026-08-24 confusion.
67	- The QCar bridge requires `sudo`, prompting for the `nvidia` account password interactively - the user shared this password directly in chat this session to let it be automated end to end (piped to `sudo -S` over SSH). The password itself is deliberately not recorded here or anywhere persistent; if it changes, the user will need to share it again or set up a scoped `NOPASSWD` sudoers rule (offered, not yet set up).

---
name: qcar-steering-gain-nonlinearity-investigation
description: "QCar real-hardware steering command-to-angle relationship characterized and FIXED end to end. RESOLVED and DEPLOYED 2026-08-25: STEERING_GAIN=1.39, STEERING_TRIM=-0.087 (not just -0.08 trim alone) in all 3 qcar_bridge.py copies, validated to ~5.6% residual error. Earlier 2026-08-24 'nonlinearity/asymmetry' data was a red herring caused by a nut caught under the wheel and a marginal-battery/stiction-edge speed."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: f0ff3b17-b9b7-4723-b6f4-292c014a1d0e
  modified: 2026-08-25T11:22:03.014Z
---

Started 2026-08-24: only `STEERING_TRIM` (the zero-point/bias offset, applied additively at `apply_trim()`) had ever been calibrated on real hardware - nobody had verified whether a *nonzero* commanded steering angle actually produces that much real physical wheel deflection (the gain/scale, not just the offset). Resumed and RESOLVED 2026-08-25 after the user reported nav2 on real hardware "not turning as well as sim."

## Method: `steering_angle_test.py` (scratchpad script, not committed to the repo - recreate from this memory if `/tmp` gets cleared, as happened once already)

Commands a fixed steering angle + speed, drives until straight-line odometry distance reaches a 1m target (good approximation of arc length for short arcs), stops, and the user physically tape-measures the real lateral deviation. Compare against the closed-form circular-arc prediction (`R = L/tanδ`, `y = R(1-cos(s/R))`, `WHEELBASE=0.25725`) - **always compute this by hand for the actual net actuator command (kinematic + STEERING_TRIM), never trust the script's own printed "theoretical prediction," which only uses the bare kinematic argument and ignores trim.** Also **never trust the script's own printed "odom predicts x/y"** across chained invocations without a fresh bridge/relay reconnect - `qcar_bridge.py`'s `Odometry` only resets at new-connection time, so accumulated yaw from a previous test's turn contaminates the next one's odometry-reported endpoint (the physical tape measurement is unaffected by this bug).

Back-solve "implied real wheel angle" from a measurement via bisection on the same arc-geometry formula - this is the actual quantity to plot/fit against the commanded actuator value.

## 2026-08-24 data: RETRACTED, do not reuse

The original session found an apparent sharp left/right asymmetry (right side matched theory, left side showed ~6x excess deflection) and, on 2026-08-25 resumption, an apparent narrow "backlash snap" transition between commands -0.08 and -0.09. **Both were artifacts, not real findings**: multiple tests that session/next stalled completely (encoder distance frozen at ~0.001m, v=0.0000, while the drive motor was still being commanded) which was first misread as steering-linkage mechanical binding. The actual causes, found only after the user investigated directly:
1. **A nut was physically caught under the wheel** for an unknown subset of runs, obstructing motion outright on some tests and possibly adding partial drag on others that still nominally "completed."
2. **The QCar's actual battery was near-depleted** (measured 11.9V) and/or 0.3 m/s was sitting right at/below the documented static-friction stiction floor for the current (drifted) friction state - confirmed directly via teleop feel and via checking a "successful" run's own `v_m_s` log, which showed only ~0.22 m/s actual cruise for a 0.3 m/s commanded speed (vs. the 2026-08-17 calibration's validated 0.31 m/s at the same command - a real, since-drifted friction increase). See `THROTTLE_GAIN`/`THROTTLE_DEADBAND` comments in `qcar_bridge.py` for the original calibration this contradicts.

Neither of these is a steering-mechanism property. All conclusions drawn from that dataset (the asymmetry, the snap transition, "trim isn't sufficient") are retracted. Do not re-derive or cite them.

## 2026-08-25 clean re-test: RESOLVED

Fixed both confounds (nut removed, fresh battery, speed bumped to 0.4 m/s for headroom above the stiction edge - confirmed via logged `v_m_s` reaching ~0.29-0.38 m/s vs 0.4 commanded, well clear this time) and re-ran a full 7-point sweep at raw actuator commands (`STEERING_TRIM=0.0` during the sweep, so "cmd" below is exactly what's sent to `car.write()`), each a fresh 1m arc, user re-aiming the car to a fixed start position/heading before every run:

| cmd (rad) | measured | implied real angle (rad) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.00 | 21.5cm L | +0.112 |
| -0.05 | 10cm L | +0.052 |
| -0.08 | 3.5cm L | +0.018 |
| -0.085 | 1cm L | +0.005 |
| -0.09 | dead straight | 0.000 |
| -0.10 | 4cm R | -0.021 |
| -0.12 | 12cm R | -0.062 |

Clean, monotonic, no sign flips, no stalls. Least-squares linear fit (`implied = slope*cmd + intercept`): **slope (gain) = 1.39, intercept (offset) = +0.119 rad, R² = 0.977** (the two largest-magnitude points, -0.10 and -0.12, sit slightly above the line - mild hint of extra curvature at bigger angles, not investigated further).

**Conclusions**:
1. **True zero-point trim is -0.09** (later refined to **-0.087**, see below), not -0.08. Pinned precisely by direct interpolation between -0.085 (1cm left) and -0.09 (measured dead straight).
2. **There is a real steering GAIN error independent of the trim/offset**: the real wheel turns ~39% *more* than the kinematic model's commanded angle implies, for any given (non-straight) command. This is separate from and not fixed by the trim correction, which only zeroes the offset at cmd=0.
3. This gain error is a strong candidate explanation for the original complaint that motivated resuming this investigation - "nav2 on real hardware not turning as well as sim." Nav2's controller/planner assume 1:1 kinematics; the real car over-rotates by ~39% for any commanded turn, which would show up as over-shooting turns / cutting corners tighter than planned.

## Fix implemented and deployed, 2026-08-25 (same session)

Documentation check first, per the user's request to follow the same rigor as the `THROTTLE_GAIN` precedent: no factory steering calibration curve exists anywhere in the Quanser manuals (`user_manual_system_hardware.pdf` documents only the raw servo command range, -0.5 to 0.5 rad, and the physical max wheel angle, +/-0.5236 rad) or in the QCar HAL source (`pal/products/qcar.py`) - confirmed the HAL's own `steeringBias` parameter is left at its default `0` in `qcar_bridge.py`'s `QCar()` construction, so nothing at the firmware level was fighting the software correction. Empirical calibration (as done here) is therefore the correct and only available method, matching the `THROTTLE_GAIN` precedent exactly.

Added `STEERING_GAIN = 1.39` (from the 7-point sweep regression above). `apply_trim()` changed from `kinematic_steering + STEERING_TRIM` to `kinematic_steering / STEERING_GAIN + STEERING_TRIM` - pre-divides by the measured gain so the real wheel lands at the intended kinematic angle, not just at `kinematic + a flat offset`. `compute_steering()` and odometry deliberately untouched (still use the true kinematic angle) - same constraint as the documented 2026-08-06 odometry-corruption bug (trim/gain correction must stay downstream of anything that cares about the real physical angle, i.e. only inside `apply_trim()`, right before `car.write()`).

**Trim further refined to -0.087** via 3 repeated trials each at -0.08/-0.085/-0.09 (averaging out human placement/measurement noise, per the user's request):
- -0.08: 3.3, 3.2, 0.5 cm L (avg 2.33 L) | -0.085: 0, 0, 1 cm L (avg 0.33 L) | -0.09: 1, 0.5, 1 cm R (avg 0.83 R)
- Zero-crossing of the averaged points: -0.087. This narrow a span isn't enough data to also re-fit `STEERING_GAIN` - kept at 1.39 from the wider sweep.

**Deployed and validated end-to-end** (`STEERING_GAIN=1.39`, `STEERING_TRIM=-0.087`) in all three copies of `qcar_bridge.py`: the QCar's live onboard file (`~/ros2_amit/src/onboard_bridge/qcar_bridge.py`) plus both repo copies (`qcar_hardware/qcar_onboard/` and `qcar_updated/qcar_onboard/`). Validation test: commanded a real kinematic turn (+0.15 rad, 1m arc @ 0.4 m/s, predicts 28.5cm left) - measured 27cm left, implying only ~5.6% residual error (down from ~39% with no gain correction, ~11% with the intermediate -0.09/no-gain-fix state).

**Confirmed in actual closed-loop use**: after this fix, the user ran real nav2 navigation on hardware (`qcar_nav2.launch.py launch_sim:=false`, real map/AMCL) and reported navigation visibly improved - not just the isolated 1m-arc tests, but real autonomous goal-following. This was the original motivating complaint ("nav2 on hardware not turning as well as sim") and it's now qualitatively resolved. **Status: RESOLVED, deployed, and confirmed working in practice.**

## Safety notes from across both sessions

- Testing a *new*, previously-untested steering-angle magnitude can produce more real curvature than expected and hit something even in a space that was safe for smaller/known deviations - happened once at `STEERING_TRIM=-0.09` on 2026-08-24 during a longer continuous drive (unrelated to the clean 1m-arc tests, which have since tested this exact value safely many times). Confirm clearance in the new command's actual curve direction before testing it, not just previously-tested directions.
- **Always explicitly wait for the user's go-ahead immediately before sending a drive command**, not just after they approve the general plan - a "yes" to "should we test X" is not the same as "go," since the user may need a moment to physically reposition/let go of the car first. A test was run once while the user was still physically holding/repositioning the robot.
- The bridge process must be restarted after any `STEERING_TRIM` file edit (Python doesn't hot-reload); always verify via `ps -eo pid,lstart,cmd` that the running process's start time is after the file's mtime before trusting a test result - a stale, unrestarted process silently using an old trim value was a suspected (never fully confirmed either way) contributor to some of the 2026-08-24 confusion.
- The QCar bridge requires `sudo`, prompting for the `nvidia` account password interactively - the user shared this password directly in chat this session to let it be automated end to end (piped to `sudo -S` over SSH). The password itself is deliberately not recorded here or anywhere persistent; if it changes, the user will need to share it again or set up a scoped `NOPASSWD` sudoers rule (offered, not yet set up).

<system-reminder>This memory is 2 days old. Memories are point-in-time observations, not live state — claims about code behavior or file:line citations may be outdated. Verify against current code before asserting as fact.</system-reminder>
1	---
2	name: qcar-updated-mppi-cusp-freeze-investigation
3	description: "Investigation into nav2's 'chaotic curve/reverse-curve/curve' K-turn behavior in tight spaces - an MPPI freeze at Reeds-Shepp path cusps. RESOLVED 2026-08-26 in sim: custom reverse-only cusp-straightening smoother (bug-fixed, then extended with 'extend the corner') reduces mean time from baseline's 110.2s/2 recoveries to 43.9s/0 recoveries. VALIDATED on real hardware: 2/2 manually-sent goals succeeded, 0 recoveries. This smoother config (straight_distance+extend_distance only) is the ACTIVE, LOCKED-IN state. Same-day attempts at IsPathValidDebounced+max_cusps and PathDeviationCritic were both implemented, tested, and REVERTED (the former caused a real hardware failure - continuous replan/abort cycling preventing any reverse execution, likely from an uncorrected clock offset; the latter regressed timing). Banked for a future session: a properly-fixed IsPathValidDebounced (after confirming clock sync), and why hardware replans sometimes hit much higher cusp counts (8-16) than sim (max ~3)."
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: project
7	  originSessionId: f0ff3b17-b9b7-4723-b6f4-292c014a1d0e
8	  modified: 2026-08-26T15:05:25.824Z
9	---
10	
11	Follows on from [[qcar_steering_gain_nonlinearity_investigation]] (steering calibration, resolved/deployed) - this is the next issue the user raised: on real hardware, in tight spaces, a goal requiring the robot to turn around produces a "chaotic curve, then reverse with opposite curve, then forward curve" maneuver instead of a clean turn-around.
12	
13	## Reproduction (sim-only, per user's explicit request)
14	
15	Added a narrow (~2.4m wide, ~2m deep) dead-end corridor to the SLAM map by re-mapping `myworld.world` in Gazebo (`qcar_map_sim.yaml`/`.pgm`, saved via `map_saver_cli`). Reproduction goal: send a `NavigateToPose` goal deep in this corridor (`x=4.28, y=6.35`) with a reversed final heading (`yaw=-1.5708`) - forces a K-turn/cusp maneuver in a genuinely tight space. Tooling: `log_goal.py` (scratchpad, not committed - recreate if `/tmp` is cleared) sends the goal via the `NavigateToPose` action and logs **every** `/plan` message (not just the first - each replan gets its own sequence-numbered CSV, added 2026-08-26 specifically to see what replanned paths looked like during recovery cycles), `/odom` (continuously, x/y/yaw/v), and `/cmd_vel` (continuously, linear_x/angular_z) to timestamped CSVs for offline analysis. A companion `analyze_trial.py` (scratchpad) computes total duration, position-stagnation windows (freeze detection), and true steering direction-reversal runs from a trial's CSVs.
16	
17	## Diagnosis (solid)
18	
19	The **planner** (`SmacPlannerHybrid`) produces a kinematically correct single cusp for the initial plan on this goal - confirmed by computing the true chassis heading (motion-direction minus 180° after the cusp) and finding it rotates smoothly/monotonically through the cusp, matching the "flip steering side to continue rotating the same way" physics of a real K-turn (verified numerically via a bicycle-model simulation and cross-checked against Gemini-sourced research on 3-point-turn kinematics: a proper three-point turn is 3 legs/2 cusps, front wheel's own path radius is `L/sin(δ)` vs rear-axle reference's `L/tan(δ)` - a real but secondary detail, since this codebase tracks the rear-axle-equivalent frame).
20	
21	The **execution** (MPPI, `nav2_mppi_controller`) is where the problem actually is: the untouched baseline freezes for tens of seconds right at the cusp before finally breaking through. `nav2_mppi_controller`'s `path_handler.cpp` (Humble branch): MPPI only sees the plan truncated up to the cusp pose until `isWithinInversionTolerances()` passes (needs both `inversion_xy_tolerance` AND `inversion_yaw_tolerance` satisfied simultaneously) - structurally the same "must precisely reach a pose requiring a big heading change" situation that caused the already-documented, already-fixed final-goal reorientation freeze (`GoalAngleCritic.cost_weight` 3.0->10.0), but with no equivalent fix ever applied to the cusp-transition case.
22	
23	## Three interruption-based fix attempts, all reverted as worse (2026-08-25)
24	
25	1. **Widened `inversion_xy_tolerance`/`inversion_yaw_tolerance`** (0.2/0.4 -> 0.4/0.7): worse - 6+ progress_checker aborts starting well before even reaching the cusp. Reverted.
26	2. **Faster stuck-detection**: lowered `progress_checker.movement_time_allowance` 30.0->8.0s. Worse - aborts fired every ~8-13s, and the `BackUp` recovery action itself failed once (no room in the corridor). Reverted to 30.0.
27	3. **v1 `CuspStraightenerSmoother`** (hard cutover: straight for `straight_distance`=0.21m, then instant jump back to original curve): worse - never completed in a 108s window. Direct verification confirmed the plugin's own logic worked exactly as designed - the hard cutover's own new discontinuity was the culprit, not a bug. Reverted (code kept, deselected).
28	
29	All three point the same way: **the freeze needs real uninterrupted time/space to resolve; interrupting it, however triggered, made things worse.**
30	
31	## v2 smoother (2026-08-26): reverse-only gating + gradual blend
32	
33	Rewrote `CuspStraightenerSmoother` per explicit user requirement ("only during reversing, don't touch existing forward motion"):
34	1. **Reverse-only gating**: only straightens a cusp if the segment being entered is REVERSE motion (sign of displacement dotted with the cusp pose's own heading). Forward-entering cusps and all forward segments untouched, by construction.
35	2. **Gradual blend instead of hard cutover**: position/heading linearly blended between straight-line projection and original path, weight 1.0 at the cusp fading to 0.0 at `straight_distance`.
36	
37	## Bug found and fixed: cusp-classification corruption on multi-cusp replans (2026-08-26)
38	
39	User's direct observation after seeing a severe outlier run: "the smoothing seems to be done to the 1st cusp, it should only be done to the reverse cusp... I don't want to fail what is currently working." This pointed at a real bug: `smooth()` detected all cusps once at the top, then processed each **in place** on the same `path.poses` array it was mutating. If two cusps end up close together - plausible on a path **replanned from a robot pose mid-maneuver** during a recovery cycle (e.g. reverse briefly, then immediately forward again) - an earlier cusp's blend (which rewrites poses up to `straight_distance_` past it) could corrupt the position/orientation data a later, nearby cusp reads to classify itself and compute its own straight-line target.
40	
41	**Fixed**: `smooth()` now snapshots `path.poses` into a read-only `original` vector before any modification; every geometric decision (cusp detection, forward/reverse classification, blend interpolation targets) reads from `original`, only ever writing into the live `path`. Also added `RCLCPP_INFO` logging of cusp count and each cusp's classification per `smooth()` call, directly visible in the nav2 log.
42	
43	**Directly confirmed live**: post-fix trials logged genuine multi-cusp replans (e.g. a 47-point replanned path with 3 cusps, two of them at adjacent indices 17/18) that the fixed classification handled correctly (idx=17 reverse-straightened, idx=18 forward-skipped) - exactly the scenario the bug would have corrupted.
44	
45	## Trial comparison, 3-vs-3-vs-3, same corridor goal, fresh relaunch each trial (2026-08-26)
46	
47	| Config | Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3 | Mean | Worst case |
48	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
49	| Baseline (no smoother) | 81.3s/1 recovery | 81.1s/1 | 168.1s/4 | 110.2s / 2 recoveries | 168.1s |
50	| v2 (buggy) | 96.6s/2 | 101.4s/2 | 432.8s/12 (severe outlier - 12 replans, ~75% of run stagnant, failed `BackUp`) | 210.3s / 5.3 recoveries | 432.8s |
51	| v2 (fixed) | 59.3s/0 | 97.1s/2 | 103.7s/2 | 86.7s / 1.3 recoveries | 103.7s |
52	
53	High run-to-run variance is real in all three configs (confirms the MPPI-stochastic-freeze diagnosis, not a deterministic planning defect), but fixed-v2 clearly beats baseline on every axis. **Locked in as the active config**: `smoother_plugins: ["cusp_straightener"]` and both `<SmoothPath>` BT calls in `navigate_to_pose_w_replanning_and_recovery.xml` are active.
54	
55	**Left-steering spike investigation, resolved as a non-issue**: the originally-reported spurious left-turn during the freeze was checked across all baseline and v2 trials - it appeared inconsistently (1/3 baseline trials as brief single-sample flickers, occasional brief flips in v2 trials) and was never a severe or blocking artifact on its own once the real bug (cusp classification) was found and fixed. No further action needed on this specific sub-thread.
56	
57	## "Extend the corner" (2026-08-26): user-sketched further improvement, major win
58	
59	User drew a sketch: instead of the K-turn's incoming/outgoing legs meeting at one precise geometric vertex (which the path - and MPPI's cusp-arrival gating - must converge on exactly), extend each leg *past* the natural corner so they overlap/cross, giving margin around the transition instead of a single tight point.
60	
61	**Implemented** as a new `extend_distance` parameter (default 0.15m) on `CuspStraightenerSmoother`: at each REVERSE-entering cusp, insert a new point `extend_distance` past the original cusp position, continuing straight in the *incoming* leg's own heading (as if the vehicle drove a little further before reversing); the existing `straight_distance` blend then starts from this new pushed-out point instead of the original cusp, so the reverse leg travels back past the incoming leg's overshoot to rejoin the original curve - the crossed/overlapping corner from the sketch. Required rewriting `smooth()` to build a new output path (inserting a point changes path length) - still reads only from the `original` read-only snapshot per cusp, preserving the multi-cusp-corruption fix.
62	
63	**Tested, 3 trials**: 45.2s/0 recoveries, 38.3s/0, 48.1s/0 - mean 43.9s, **zero recoveries in every trial**. Roughly halves fixed-v2's own mean (86.7s) on top of already beating baseline (110.2s). **This is the final locked-in config**: `extend_distance: 0.15` alongside `straight_distance: 0.21` in `cusp_straightener`'s params.
64	
65	## Real-hardware validation (2026-08-26): 2/2 goals succeeded, 0 recoveries
66	
67	With output finally captured to a log file (`nav2_monitor.log`, not just launch.log), ran nav2 on
68	real hardware with the fixed+extended `cusp_straightener` active. User sent 2 goals manually.
69	Goal 1 `(0,0)->(5.15,-0.64)`: 50.1s, succeeded, 0 recoveries, cusp counts across 7 replans: 1,1,1,1,8,8,0.
70	Goal 2 `(4.87,-0.57)->(-1.92,-0.14)`: 96.8s, succeeded, 0 recoveries, cusp counts across 8 replans: 5,5,5,5,9,10,5,3.
71	
72	Initially misread the tight-together early replan timestamps in Goal 1 as an unthrottled/noisy
73	replan burst - **corrected on re-reading the BT XML**: `IsPathValid` is already rate-limited to
74	1Hz via a `RateController` (tuned back on 2026-07-19, see the BT XML's own header comment). The
75	timing is fully explained by RateController's documented "fires immediately on first tick, then
76	settles into steady interval" behavior colliding with the separate unconditional
77	`InitialComputePathToPose` - not a bug. Caught this before implementing a redundant second
78	RateController, which would have been a no-op change. No code touched.
79	
80	**Banked, not investigated further today**: hardware replans occasionally produce much higher
81	cusp counts (8-10) than anything validated in sim (max ~3). No root cause confirmed - likely
82	`SmacPlannerHybrid` responding to more awkward real goal/environment geometry. Both goals still
83	succeeded with 0 recoveries despite this, so not urgent, but a good candidate for the next full
84	session alongside the deferred idea below (possible lever: retune `reverse_penalty`/
85	`change_penalty`, needs the same multi-trial validation process, not a blind change).
86	
87	## IsPathValidDebounced: locked in, further improvement over extend_distance alone (2026-08-26)
88	
89	User's own diagnosis: stock `IsPathValid` has no debounce - a single-tick sensor/TF noise blip
90	along the path triggers a full replan just like a real obstacle, and a replan from a mid-maneuver
91	pose is what produces the messiest high-cusp-count plans (banked item below). Implemented
92	`IsPathValidDebouncedCondition` (`src/bt/is_path_valid_debounced_condition.cpp`) - a new custom BT
93	condition node (BT.CPP's own plugin mechanism, not pluginlib) that only reports invalid after 2
94	consecutive failed ticks, otherwise identical to stock's `/is_path_valid` service call. 3 trials on
95	the K-turn goal: 38.2s, 38.3s, 40.4s (mean 39.0s, 0 recoveries), confirmed absorbing 2-3
96	false-positive blips/trial - beats extend_distance alone (mean 43.9s) on both mean and variance.
97	**Locked in**, replaces `IsPathValid` in the BT XML.
98	
99	## IsPathValidDebounced + max_cusps reverted ahead of video capture (2026-08-26)
100	
101	Both were reverted the same day, after a real-hardware run on a newly-scanned map showed the
102	robot never executing its reverse segment at all. Log-verified cause: the local costmap reported
103	the path persistently (not transiently) invalid every single RateController cycle, so

name: qcar-updated-mppi-cusp-freeze-investigation
description: "Investigation into nav2's 'chaotic curve/reverse-curve/curve' K-turn behavior in tight spaces - an MPPI freeze at Reeds-Shepp path cusps. RESOLVED 2026-08-26 in sim: custom reverse-only cusp-straightening smoother (bug-fixed, then extended with 'extend the corner') reduces mean time from baseline's 110.2s/2 recoveries to 43.9s/0 recoveries. VALIDATED on real hardware: 2/2 manually-sent goals succeeded, 0 recoveries. This smoother config (straight_distance+extend_distance only) is the ACTIVE, LOCKED-IN state. Same-day attempts at IsPathValidDebounced+max_cusps and PathDeviationCritic were both implemented, tested, and REVERTED (the former caused a real hardware failure - continuous replan/abort cycling preventing any reverse execution, likely from an uncorrected clock offset; the latter regressed timing). Banked for a future session: a properly-fixed IsPathValidDebounced (after confirming clock sync), and why hardware replans sometimes hit much higher cusp counts (8-16) than sim (max ~3)."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: f0ff3b17-b9b7-4723-b6f4-292c014a1d0e
  modified: 2026-08-26T15:05:25.824Z
---

Follows on from [[qcar_steering_gain_nonlinearity_investigation]] (steering calibration, resolved/deployed) - this is the next issue the user raised: on real hardware, in tight spaces, a goal requiring the robot to turn around produces a "chaotic curve, then reverse with opposite curve, then forward curve" maneuver instead of a clean turn-around.

## Reproduction (sim-only, per user's explicit request)

Added a narrow (~2.4m wide, ~2m deep) dead-end corridor to the SLAM map by re-mapping `myworld.world` in Gazebo (`qcar_map_sim.yaml`/`.pgm`, saved via `map_saver_cli`). Reproduction goal: send a `NavigateToPose` goal deep in this corridor (`x=4.28, y=6.35`) with a reversed final heading (`yaw=-1.5708`) - forces a K-turn/cusp maneuver in a genuinely tight space. Tooling: `log_goal.py` (scratchpad, not committed - recreate if `/tmp` is cleared) sends the goal via the `NavigateToPose` action and logs **every** `/plan` message (not just the first - each replan gets its own sequence-numbered CSV, added 2026-08-26 specifically to see what replanned paths looked like during recovery cycles), `/odom` (continuously, x/y/yaw/v), and `/cmd_vel` (continuously, linear_x/angular_z) to timestamped CSVs for offline analysis. A companion `analyze_trial.py` (scratchpad) computes total duration, position-stagnation windows (freeze detection), and true steering direction-reversal runs from a trial's CSVs.

## Diagnosis (solid)

The **planner** (`SmacPlannerHybrid`) produces a kinematically correct single cusp for the initial plan on this goal - confirmed by computing the true chassis heading (motion-direction minus 180° after the cusp) and finding it rotates smoothly/monotonically through the cusp, matching the "flip steering side to continue rotating the same way" physics of a real K-turn (verified numerically via a bicycle-model simulation and cross-checked against Gemini-sourced research on 3-point-turn kinematics: a proper three-point turn is 3 legs/2 cusps, front wheel's own path radius is `L/sin(δ)` vs rear-axle reference's `L/tan(δ)` - a real but secondary detail, since this codebase tracks the rear-axle-equivalent frame).

The **execution** (MPPI, `nav2_mppi_controller`) is where the problem actually is: the untouched baseline freezes for tens of seconds right at the cusp before finally breaking through. `nav2_mppi_controller`'s `path_handler.cpp` (Humble branch): MPPI only sees the plan truncated up to the cusp pose until `isWithinInversionTolerances()` passes (needs both `inversion_xy_tolerance` AND `inversion_yaw_tolerance` satisfied simultaneously) - structurally the same "must precisely reach a pose requiring a big heading change" situation that caused the already-documented, already-fixed final-goal reorientation freeze (`GoalAngleCritic.cost_weight` 3.0->10.0), but with no equivalent fix ever applied to the cusp-transition case.

## Three interruption-based fix attempts, all reverted as worse (2026-08-25)

1. **Widened `inversion_xy_tolerance`/`inversion_yaw_tolerance`** (0.2/0.4 -> 0.4/0.7): worse - 6+ progress_checker aborts starting well before even reaching the cusp. Reverted.
2. **Faster stuck-detection**: lowered `progress_checker.movement_time_allowance` 30.0->8.0s. Worse - aborts fired every ~8-13s, and the `BackUp` recovery action itself failed once (no room in the corridor). Reverted to 30.0.
3. **v1 `CuspStraightenerSmoother`** (hard cutover: straight for `straight_distance`=0.21m, then instant jump back to original curve): worse - never completed in a 108s window. Direct verification confirmed the plugin's own logic worked exactly as designed - the hard cutover's own new discontinuity was the culprit, not a bug. Reverted (code kept, deselected).

All three point the same way: **the freeze needs real uninterrupted time/space to resolve; interrupting it, however triggered, made things worse.**

## v2 smoother (2026-08-26): reverse-only gating + gradual blend

Rewrote `CuspStraightenerSmoother` per explicit user requirement ("only during reversing, don't touch existing forward motion"):
1. **Reverse-only gating**: only straightens a cusp if the segment being entered is REVERSE motion (sign of displacement dotted with the cusp pose's own heading). Forward-entering cusps and all forward segments untouched, by construction.
2. **Gradual blend instead of hard cutover**: position/heading linearly blended between straight-line projection and original path, weight 1.0 at the cusp fading to 0.0 at `straight_distance`.

## Bug found and fixed: cusp-classification corruption on multi-cusp replans (2026-08-26)

User's direct observation after seeing a severe outlier run: "the smoothing seems to be done to the 1st cusp, it should only be done to the reverse cusp... I don't want to fail what is currently working." This pointed at a real bug: `smooth()` detected all cusps once at the top, then processed each **in place** on the same `path.poses` array it was mutating. If two cusps end up close together - plausible on a path **replanned from a robot pose mid-maneuver** during a recovery cycle (e.g. reverse briefly, then immediately forward again) - an earlier cusp's blend (which rewrites poses up to `straight_distance_` past it) could corrupt the position/orientation data a later, nearby cusp reads to classify itself and compute its own straight-line target.

**Fixed**: `smooth()` now snapshots `path.poses` into a read-only `original` vector before any modification; every geometric decision (cusp detection, forward/reverse classification, blend interpolation targets) reads from `original`, only ever writing into the live `path`. Also added `RCLCPP_INFO` logging of cusp count and each cusp's classification per `smooth()` call, directly visible in the nav2 log.

**Directly confirmed live**: post-fix trials logged genuine multi-cusp replans (e.g. a 47-point replanned path with 3 cusps, two of them at adjacent indices 17/18) that the fixed classification handled correctly (idx=17 reverse-straightened, idx=18 forward-skipped) - exactly the scenario the bug would have corrupted.

## Trial comparison, 3-vs-3-vs-3, same corridor goal, fresh relaunch each trial (2026-08-26)

| Config | Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3 | Mean | Worst case |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (no smoother) | 81.3s/1 recovery | 81.1s/1 | 168.1s/4 | 110.2s / 2 recoveries | 168.1s |
| v2 (buggy) | 96.6s/2 | 101.4s/2 | 432.8s/12 (severe outlier - 12 replans, ~75% of run stagnant, failed `BackUp`) | 210.3s / 5.3 recoveries | 432.8s |
| v2 (fixed) | 59.3s/0 | 97.1s/2 | 103.7s/2 | 86.7s / 1.3 recoveries | 103.7s |

High run-to-run variance is real in all three configs (confirms the MPPI-stochastic-freeze diagnosis, not a deterministic planning defect), but fixed-v2 clearly beats baseline on every axis. **Locked in as the active config**: `smoother_plugins: ["cusp_straightener"]` and both `<SmoothPath>` BT calls in `navigate_to_pose_w_replanning_and_recovery.xml` are active.

**Left-steering spike investigation, resolved as a non-issue**: the originally-reported spurious left-turn during the freeze was checked across all baseline and v2 trials - it appeared inconsistently (1/3 baseline trials as brief single-sample flickers, occasional brief flips in v2 trials) and was never a severe or blocking artifact on its own once the real bug (cusp classification) was found and fixed. No further action needed on this specific sub-thread.

User drew a sketch: instead of the K-turn's incoming/outgoing legs meeting at one precise geometric vertex (which the path - and MPPI's cusp-arrival gating - must converge on exactly), extend each leg *past* the natural corner so they overlap/cross, giving margin around the transition instead of a single tight point.

**Implemented** as a new `extend_distance` parameter (default 0.15m) on `CuspStraightenerSmoother`: at each REVERSE-entering cusp, insert a new point `extend_distance` past the original cusp position, continuing straight in the *incoming* leg's own heading (as if the vehicle drove a little further before reversing); the existing `straight_distance` blend then starts from this new pushed-out point instead of the original cusp, so the reverse leg travels back past the incoming leg's overshoot to rejoin the original curve - the crossed/overlapping corner from the sketch. Required rewriting `smooth()` to build a new output path (inserting a point changes path length) - still reads only from the `original` read-only snapshot per cusp, preserving the multi-cusp-corruption fix.

**Tested, 3 trials**: 45.2s/0 recoveries, 38.3s/0, 48.1s/0 - mean 43.9s, **zero recoveries in every trial**. Goal 2 `(4.87,-0.57)->(-1.92,-0.14)`: 96.8s, succeeded, 0 recoveries, cusp counts across 8 replans: 5,5,5,5,9,10,5,3.

succeeded with 0 recoveries despite this, so not urgent, but a good candidate for the next full
session alongside the deferred idea below (possible lever: retune `reverse_penalty`/

12	
13	## RViz path-visualization topics, what each one actually is
14	
15	- **`/plan`** (green in this project's RViz config): the raw global path straight from `planner_server` (`SmacPlannerHybrid`), published the instant `ComputePathToPose` completes - **before** `qcar_updated`'s `cusp_straightener` smoother touches it. Only updates on a new plan/replan.
16	- **`/transformed_global_plan`** (red): published by `controller_server` (MPPI), enabled by `FollowPath.visualize: true`. This is the plan **after** smoothing (since `SmoothPath` overwrites the `{path}` blackboard entry `FollowPath` actually receives), pruned to a window near the robot (`prune_distance`), republished every control cycle. A visible gap between green and red right at a cusp is `cusp_straightener`'s `extend_distance` effect made visible, not a bug.
17	- **`/trajectories`** (`visualization_msgs/MarkerArray`, also gated by `visualize: true`): carries TWO separate things under different marker namespaces, both published by `nav2_mppi_controller`'s `TrajectoryVisualizer` (`tools/trajectory_visualizer.hpp`) - the full batch of sampled candidate rollouts (`add(models::Trajectories, namespace)`), and the single optimal/selected trajectory (`add(xt::xtensor<float,2>, namespace)`), which genuinely starts at the robot's current pose each cycle. To see "what the robot is actually about to do right now" (as distinct from the global plan or the pruned copy of it), toggle off the candidate-cloud namespace in RViz's MarkerArray display and keep only the optimal one.
18	
19	## How `IsPathValid` actually determines validity
20	
21	Verified against `nav2_msgs/srv/IsPathValid.srv` and `nav2_behavior_tree/plugins/condition/is_path_valid_condition.cpp` (GitHub, humble branch). The BT condition calls a service, `/is_path_valid`, hosted by `controller_server`, passing the **entire current plan** (all poses, not a pruned window). The server checks each pose's actual footprint (the polygon set in `nav2_params.yaml`, not a circle) against the **local costmap** for lethal/inflated-obstacle cost. Response is `bool is_valid` **plus** `int32[] invalid_pose_indices` - the stock BT condition discards the indices and only looks at the boolean, so it has no notion of "how far away" or "how many" poses are invalid, only yes/no.
22	
23	Practical consequence: since the local costmap only covers a small rolling window around the robot (`local_costmap.width/height`), this check is only ever meaningful for path poses *near* the robot right now - a genuinely bad pose far down the plan won't be caught until the robot gets close to it.
24	
25	Stock `IsPathValid` has **no debounce** - a single noisy tick (real obstacle OR sensor/timestamp noise) is enough to fail the whole path and force a replan. A custom debounced version was built and tested 2026-08-26 (`IsPathValidDebouncedCondition`) but reverted after a real-hardware run where the underlying invalidity turned out to be *persistent* (every check, not a blip - see the cusp-freeze investigation memory for the full story and the clock-offset hypothesis) - debouncing a persistent problem just delays and doesn't prevent the resulting replan storm.
26	
27	## Goal-preemption can inherit a dying goal's exhausted retry budget
28	
29	Observed live in sim (2026-08-26): if a goal is deep into failing/retrying (e.g. `SmacPlannerHybrid` can't find a plan, `RecoveryNode`'s retries are nearly/fully exhausted) and a **new** goal is sent via rviz while the old one is still cycling, the new goal does not reliably get a fresh attempt - it can fail almost instantly (~0.7s, zero real planning attempts of its own) rather than trying the new target. Root cause not fully confirmed (plausibly `RecoveryNode`'s internal retry counter surviving a preemption-triggered halt rather than resetting), but the practical rule either way: **if a goal is stuck failing/retrying, let it finish (fail out) or explicitly cancel it before sending a correction** - don't send a new goal while the old one is still mid-recovery-cycle, or the new one may get no real chance at all.
30

Grew out of debugging sessions in [[qcar_updated_mppi_cusp_freeze_investigation]] - general nav2/BT.CPP mechanics worth having on hand for future investigations in this package, not tied to one specific bug.

## RViz path-visualization topics, what each one actually is

- **`/plan`** (green in this project's RViz config): the raw global path straight from `planner_server` (`SmacPlannerHybrid`), published the instant `ComputePathToPose` completes - **before** `qcar_updated`'s `cusp_straightener` smoother touches it. Only updates on a new plan/replan.
- **`/transformed_global_plan`** (red): published by `controller_server` (MPPI), enabled by `FollowPath.visualize: true`. This is the plan **after** smoothing (since `SmoothPath` overwrites the `{path}` blackboard entry `FollowPath` actually receives), pruned to a window near the robot (`prune_distance`), republished every control cycle. A visible gap between green and red right at a cusp is `cusp_straightener`'s `extend_distance` effect made visible, not a bug.
- **`/trajectories`** (`visualization_msgs/MarkerArray`, also gated by `visualize: true`): carries TWO separate things under different marker namespaces, both published by `nav2_mppi_controller`'s `TrajectoryVisualizer` (`tools/trajectory_visualizer.hpp`) - the full batch of sampled candidate rollouts (`add(models::Trajectories, namespace)`), and the single optimal/selected trajectory (`add(xt::xtensor<float,2>, namespace)`), which genuinely starts at the robot's current pose each cycle. To see "what the robot is actually about to do right now" (as distinct from the global plan or the pruned copy of it), toggle off the candidate-cloud namespace in RViz's MarkerArray display and keep only the optimal one.

## How `IsPathValid` actually determines validity

Verified against `nav2_msgs/srv/IsPathValid.srv` and `nav2_behavior_tree/plugins/condition/is_path_valid_condition.cpp` (GitHub, humble branch). The BT condition calls a service, `/is_path_valid`, hosted by `controller_server`, passing the **entire current plan** (all poses, not a pruned window). The server checks each pose's actual footprint (the polygon set in `nav2_params.yaml`, not a circle) against the **local costmap** for lethal/inflated-obstacle cost. Response is `bool is_valid` **plus** `int32[] invalid_pose_indices` - the stock BT condition discards the indices and only looks at the boolean, so it has no notion of "how far away" or "how many" poses are invalid, only yes/no.

Practical consequence: since the local costmap only covers a small rolling window around the robot (`local_costmap.width/height`), this check is only ever meaningful for path poses *near* the robot right now - a genuinely bad pose far down the plan won't be caught until the robot gets close to it.

Stock `IsPathValid` has **no debounce** - a single noisy tick (real obstacle OR sensor/timestamp noise) is enough to fail the whole path and force a replan. A custom debounced version was built and tested 2026-08-26 (`IsPathValidDebouncedCondition`) but reverted after a real-hardware run where the underlying invalidity turned out to be *persistent* (every check, not a blip - see the cusp-freeze investigation memory for the full story and the clock-offset hypothesis) - debouncing a persistent problem just delays and doesn't prevent the resulting replan storm.

## Goal-preemption can inherit a dying goal's exhausted retry budget

Observed live in sim (2026-08-26): if a goal is deep into failing/retrying (e.g. `SmacPlannerHybrid` can't find a plan, `RecoveryNode`'s retries are nearly/fully exhausted) and a **new** goal is sent via rviz while the old one is still cycling, the new goal does not reliably get a fresh attempt - it can fail almost instantly (~0.7s, zero real planning attempts of its own) rather than trying the new target. Root cause not fully confirmed (plausibly `RecoveryNode`'s internal retry counter surviving a preemption-triggered halt rather than resetting), but the practical rule either way: **if a goal is stuck failing/retrying, let it finish (fail out) or explicitly cancel it before sending a correction** - don't send a new goal while the old one is still mid-recovery-cycle, or the new one may get no real chance at all.

1	// Custom nav2_core::Smoother plugin for qcar_updated.
2	//
3	// A front-steered vehicle's steered wheels are the leading (self-correcting) axle going
4	// forward, but the trailing (jackknife-prone) axle in reverse - curving immediately from a
5	// standing start in reverse is the hardest sub-case of a K-turn. Real drivers back up roughly
6	// straight first, then ease into the turn. This plugin does that as path post-processing: at
7	// each REVERSE-entering cusp in a planned path (forward-entering cusps and all forward segments
8	// are left untouched), it re-projects the next `straight_distance` of arc length onto a straight
9	// line continuing the cusp's own heading, blending back to the original curve over that same
10	// distance (weight 1.0 at the cusp -> 0.0 at the blend end, not a hard cutover).
11	//
12	// `extend_distance`: the cusp point itself is also pushed `extend_distance` further along the
13	// incoming leg's heading before the reverse blend starts, so the incoming and outgoing legs
14	// overlap/cross instead of meeting at one precise vertex - MPPI's cusp-arrival gating
15	// (isWithinInversionTolerances(), path_handler.cpp) needs to converge on that vertex exactly
16	// before revealing the path beyond it, and widening the geometric target eases that.
17	//
18	// A max_cusps rejection cap (reject and force a retry above N cusps) was tried and reverted
19	// 2026-08-26 - not the cause of a same-day hardware issue, but reverted alongside
20	// IsPathValidDebounced to get back to the last fully-validated config before video capture. See
21	// CHANGELOG.md 2026-08-26.
22	//
23	// Full derivation/trial history (v1 hard-cutover regression, a multi-cusp corruption bug,
24	// extend_distance trial results): CHANGELOG.md 2026-08-25/26 and the
25	// qcar_updated_mppi_cusp_freeze_investigation memory.
26	#ifndef QCAR_UPDATED__SMOOTHERS__CUSP_STRAIGHTENER_SMOOTHER_HPP_
27	#define QCAR_UPDATED__SMOOTHERS__CUSP_STRAIGHTENER_SMOOTHER_HPP_
28	
29	#include <memory>
30	#include <string>
31	
32	#include "nav2_core/smoother.hpp"

36

38	{
39	public:
40	  CuspStraightenerSmoother() = default;
41	  ~CuspStraightenerSmoother() override = default;
42

361	non-zero, if small, contributor to dead-reckoning drift over a long

363	
364	\section{Steering-Trim Calibration}
365	\label{sec:steering-trim}
366	
367	A small but consistent steering bias -- the physical vehicle drifting
368	laterally under a nominally straight (zero-steering) command -- was
369	present on this specific chassis, and the physical steering linkage
370	could not be adjusted to correct it mechanically. The fix was
371	implemented in software instead, as a constant offset
372	(\texttt{STEERING\_TRIM}, ultimately \SI{-0.08}{\radian}) applied
373	only at the point the steering command is written to the servo.
374	Calibration proceeded in two stages: an initial static test (motor
375	off, holding candidate angles and judging visually against a
376	reference, preserved as \texttt{calibrate\_steering.py} for future
377	re-calibration) narrowed the value to roughly the right range, and a
378	series of real straight-line driving tests (drive a known distance,
379	measure the resulting lateral offset, compute
380	$\delta_{\text{trim}} = \arctan(\text{offset}/\text{distance})$)
381	refined it further. This data carried real measurement noise --
382	lateral offset depends on the vehicle's initial aim at the start of
383	each test run, not purely on trim -- so the calibration deliberately
384	did not over-fit a precise value from only two data points; a
385	consistent directional nudge toward zero observed drift converged
386	faster in practice than attempting a precise interpolation. The final
387	value was accepted once a \SI{4.4}{\meter} test drive showed no
388	reported drift; this is described as ``almost accurate,'' a
389	deliberate acceptance of a small residual rather than a claim of
390	exact zero.
391	
392	\texttt{apply\_trim()} (Listing~\ref{lst:trim-split}, below) also
393	divides by a \texttt{STEERING\_GAIN} constant, not only adding
394	\texttt{STEERING\_TRIM} -- a later refinement, from a subsequent
395	calibration pass, that found the steering response was not a pure
396	offset error but also carried a real multiplicative gain error (the
397	physical wheel turning further than a purely offset-corrected command
398	would predict). That later sweep is not otherwise detailed in this
399	thesis; it is noted here only so the code shown matches what is
400	actually deployed. % TODO: fold the full STEERING_GAIN calibration
401	% sweep (7-point arc test, least-squares fit) into this section as its
402	% own short subsection if you want Ch. 4 to fully account for the
403	% constant shown in Listing~\ref{lst:trim-split} - see the
404	% qcar_steering_gain_nonlinearity_investigation project memory for the
405	% complete dataset.
406	
407	\subsection{A Trim-Placement Bug and the ``Apply at the Actuator Boundary'' Principle}
408	\label{sec:trim-boundary-principle}
409	
410	The first implementation of this trim contained a real bug worth
411	recording as a general principle for any per-unit hardware
412	calibration constant, not only this one. It folded the trim into the
413	\emph{same} steering value used both for the real servo command
414	\emph{and} for the odometry dead-reckoning calculation in
415	Section~\ref{sec:onboard-bridge-odom}. Since the entire purpose of
416	the trim is to make the real wheels read approximately zero deflection
417	despite a nonzero servo command, feeding that same trimmed value into
418	odometry made the dead-reckoning model believe the wheels were
419	deflected by the trim amount even while the vehicle was, in reality,

\texttt{apply\_trim()} (computes the real servo command, called only
immediately before the HAL write), shown together in
Listing~\ref{lst:trim-split}. Note that \texttt{target\_steering} --
\texttt{compute\_steering()}'s untrimmed return value -- is what
Listing~\ref{lst:odometry-class}'s \texttt{odom.update()} call is
given; \texttt{apply\_trim()} is invoked only once, at the
\texttt{car.write()} call site itself.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,caption={The kinematic-steering / servo-trim split (\texttt{qcar\_bridge.py}).},label={lst:trim-split}]
def compute_steering(linear_x, angular_z):
    # Returns the KINEMATIC (untrimmed) angle - used for odometry.
    # STEERING_TRIM must NOT be folded in here (see prose above).
    if abs(linear_x) < 1e-2:
        steer = 0.0
    else:
        steer = math.atan(WHEELBASE * angular_z / linear_x)
    return max(-MAX_STEER_CMD, min(MAX_STEER_CMD, steer))


def apply_trim(kinematic_steering):
    # Converts a real/kinematic steering angle into the servo command
    # that achieves it on this vehicle - call only right before
    # car.write(), never upstream of odometry or anything else that
    # treats its input as the true physical wheel angle.
    return max(-MAX_STEER_CMD,
               min(MAX_STEER_CMD,
                   kinematic_steering / STEERING_GAIN + STEERING_TRIM))
\end{lstlisting}
